It is for the Holland Creek Development, (Lot 1, Block 192, District Lot 103, Oyster District), on Dogwood Dr. near Arbut us Cres., in Ladysmith, B.C, The propo sed development includes 28 lots, and a new street called Rollie Rose Dr. At the time of assessment, the site had been cleared and the rough layout had been completed. The purpose of this report was to identi fy potential hazard trees along the Phase 1 boundary, behind lots 8-10 and 14-28, that had been left behind after initial clearing. The areas behind Lot 10 and Lots 14-28 fall under BC Provincial Riparian Area Regulations (RAR). These areas are tributaries from nearby Heart Creek. On the site maps , they are labelled Tributary 1 and Tributary 2. Tributary 1 runs down the south side of Rollie Rose Dr., into a new storm drain at the back of Lot 10. Tribu tary 2 runs along the back of lots 14-28. Riparian Area Regulations define the Rit arian Assessment Area (RAA) for a stream as “the 30 meter strip on both sides of the stream, measured from the hij water mark”. These areas had been marked out and flagged at the time of assessment, and any trees within the RAR area have been noted on the Tree Index. Hazard trees locate d inside the RAR were to be felled into the Riparian Area and all debris left with no further Proce ssing required. The field assessment for this Frepor t was conducted on Oct 3, 2017, betw een 8:30 am and 12:30 pm. Assessment began at the back of Lot 28 and proceeded down the slope to Lot 14, then from Lot 8 to Lot 10. The trees are numbered in order accor ding to this route. As mentioned above, all trees listed ‘on the Tree Index are deemed poten tial hazards for proposed or existi ng dwellings, (specifically 178, 182, 186 Arbutus Crescent), and are therefore recommended for removal. There were (35) trees deemed poten tial hazards at the time of assessmen t. All trees were marked with pink spray paint, with a yellow numbered tag in the center of the paint, except @ group of dead/dying Red for Tree #1; Alders (Alnus rubra). A few trees in this group were fairly inaccessible at the time of assessment, It should be understood that any dead/dying trees in this group ing are deemed hazardous and are to be removed immediately. Attached to this report is a list of all trees in the index with more detailed notes on their condition at the time of asse ssment. Clough Consulting age ae 1 oF Page 25 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 26 Introduction: This report is a Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP) to protect the Riparian Area during the construction related to road construction for the multi-lot subdivision in Ladysmith B.C. near Holland Creek. The legal description of the property is Lot A, Plan EPP63594, Block 192 and District Lot 103, Oyster District. Riparian Areas Assessment A Riparian Area Regulation (RAR # 3279A) Assessment was submitted by D.R. Clough Consulting in 2014 on behalf of this development. The RAR identified Holland Creek Tributaries 1 and 2 (non fish) as well as Heart Creek (fish). Each of these channels has a SPEA result of 10m from the Top of Bank. The RAR also identified the Measures to Protect the SPEA addressing the issues of Danger Trees, Wind Throw, Slope Stability, Protection of Trees, Encroachment, and Erosion/Sediment Control. This report is to provide guidance to contractors on a Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP) to protect the SPEA areas Scope of Report This report was written to address the civil construction phase involving road construction. It does not address individual lot development which will be addressed by subcontractors whom must have their own CEMP in order to protect the SPEA. This report addresses the Sediment and Erosion Control required for construction and protection of the 10m SPEA from Encroachment. Project Environmental Description and Location: The property is located on the south side of Holland Creek watershed. There are four watercourses in the property area; * Tributary 1 located near the Dogwood Road access running under Rollie Rose Road in a culvert and off property to a water fall above Holland Creek. It is adjacent lots 1-12. * Tributary 2 is located flowing along the north side of Rollie Rose Drive adjacent lot 13-28. * Heart Creek lies further northwest away from the current phase of construction. * Holland Creek is the catchment for all tributaries and is a located north downstream and is a year round salmon and trout stream. Each of these streams has a Riparian Area that is flagged in the field and marked on the construction maps. The SPEAS are located 10m from the top of bank of the streams. The streams have established tree canopies of primarily second growth Red Cedar, Douglas Fir and Bigleaf Maple. The understory shrubbery is mostly native Sword Fern as well as invasive Himalayan Blackberry and English Ivy. There are open Prepared for Prepared By Page 2 of4 Holland Creek Estates DAR. Clough Consulting Page 26 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 27 areas under the Hydro line easements of Scotch Broom, Himalayan Blackberry and Red Alder. Construction Environmental Management Plan 1. Pre-Work — A job safety and environmental pre-work meeting will be done to ensure that all workers understand the environmental objectives and have clear understanding on their roles and responsibilities. SPEA - Environmentally sensitive areas must first be identified. They are to be flagged and a sediment fence will be used to isolate the location. Encroachment - There will be no disturbance of the SPEA, which is located 10 m from the top of bank on the property. The SPEA has been flagged and staked to show where the outer limits are located. Spill Kits — Spill kits must located on each piece of heavy equipment. Spills of any kind must be reported to the environmental monitor. Erosion Control —. 5.1 Erosion control coverings such as plastic, tarps and hay bales must be used to cover any exposed ground. 5.2 Heavy equipment access (trucking route) must be surfaced with a non-erodible firm substrate (e.g, road crush blanketing geotextile) to eliminate sedimentation and rutting during the movement of heavy equipment in and out of the site. 5.3 Drainage in the work site must be managed to be detained, filtered and infiltrated before it enters the tributaries. Monitoring — Site monitoring will be conducted at start-up and routinely as work is conducted to ensure the SPEA boundary is marked and not disturbed. This will be documented in routine monitoring reports . Weather — Wet weather shutdown applies. In any circumstance (whether raining or not) where a potential exists for sediment to escape into the SPEA, the activity must be stopped. . Post Construction — Exposed areas outside the SPEA will be re-seeded with grass seed or covered with other non-erodible materials. All construction materials are to be removed from the site. Limitations of Environmental Oversight This document has been prepared on behalf of Holland Estates for the civil component of construction. The construction beyond this scope is not part of Holland Estates or D.R. Clough Consulting responsibility. This property development is subject to RAR and will require further environmental oversight and reporting to regulatory agencies upon completion. We recommend the future property owners or contractors retain an environmental professional for the remaining phases of construction. Prepared for Prepared By Page 3 of 4 7 Holland Creek Estates D.R. Other DPA conditions; See the Measures to Protect below in RAR 3.) RAR Results A RAR report was submitted by D.R. Clough Consulting in November 2014 and registered as 3279A. The report identifies the SPEAS for the development. Many of the single family lots are situated within the 30m Riparian Assessment Area (RAA). Within the RAA the stream channels have a SPEA of 10m from the top of bank. (Fig.1) All DPA conditions are identified in the RAR Assessment Report under the Section 4 Measures to Protect and Maintain the SPEA; Since the RAR was submitted there has been the following actions taken with respect to the measures 1.) Danger Trees and Windthrow -an assessment report and tree remediation has been done by VI Trees Services Ltd. (Appendix 1). 2.) Clough Consulting Page 53 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 54 Introduction: This report is a Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP) to protect the Riparian Areas during the construction for the multi-lot subdivision in Ladysmith B.C. near Holland Creek. The legal description of the property is Lot A, Plan EPP63594, Block 192 and District Lot 103, Oyster District. Riparian Areas The property is located on the south side of Holland Creek watershed situated directly upslope of Holland Creek Trail Park. There are four watercourses in the area; e Tributary 1 located near the Dogwood Road running under Rollie Rose Road in a culvert and off property to a water fall above Holland Creek. It is adjacent lots 1-12. e Tributary 2 is located flowing along the north side of Rollie Rose Drive adjacent lots 13-28. e Heart Creek lies further northwest away from the phase 1 of the development. e Holland Creek is off property and the catchment for these tributaries. It is a year round salmon and trout stream. Riparian Area Results A Riparian Area Regulation (RAR # 3279A) Assessment was submitted by D.R. Clough Consulting in 2014 on behalf of this development. The assessment determined the Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA) within the 30m Riparian Assessment Area (RAA). The assessment resulted in a 10m SPEA width from top of bank. The SPEAS are 10m from the top of bank of the development streams. Each of the streams (Tributary1, Tributary 2 & Heart Creek) in the development has the SPEA marked along the channels with flags and signs as well as on the lot plan. The RAR report also identified the Measures to Protect the SPEA addressing the issues of Danger Trees, Wind Throw, Slope Stability, Protection of Trees, Encroachment, and Erosion/Sediment Control Property Owner Responsibility These are legal requirements of property owners under the Fish Protection Act; e The SPEA areas must not be encroached, altered or impacted by construction. e All Property owners building within the RAA (30m) of the stream channels are required to follow this a construction sediment management plan that protects the SPEA area. © The property owner must follow the guidelines in this construction environmental plan e The property owner must consult a Qualified Environmental Professional to approve, inspect and submit a completion report for the development. Prepared for Prepared By Page Holland Creek Estates D.R. Clough Consulting 9 2 of 6 Page 54 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 55 Construction Environmental Management Plan Guidance on sediment and erosion control as lots are developed can be taken from the BC Government publication; “Develop With Care — Environmental Guidelines for Urban and Rural Land Development in B.C. Best Management”. 1. SPEA - Environmentally sensitive areas are identified. They are flagged and marked with Riparian Area signage (not to be removed). 2. Encroachment — 2.1 House and other building locations must be within the proposed building area on the lot plan 2.2 There will be no disturbance of the Riparian Area SPEA, which is located 10 m from the top of bank on the property. The SPEA boundary has been flagged, survey staked and signage hung at every lot location 2.3. There will be no storage of materials, burning, garbage or trails in the SPEA. 3. Construction Pre-Work — the construction crew must conduct an environmental pre-work meeting will be done to ensure that all workers understand the environmental areas and have clear understanding on protection of the SPEA. 4. Weather —Weather shutdown applies. In any circumstance where a potential exists for sediment to escape into the SPEA, the activity must be stopped, and mitigative actions taken. 5. Heavy Equipment Operation — 5.1 Spill kits must located on each piece of heavy equipment. Spills of any kind must be reported to the environmental monitor. 5.2. The machinery must not be fueled within 30m of a watercourse 5.3 Trees and tree roots within the SPEA must be protected, machinery must be operated to minimize disturbance of ground and not encroach into the SPEA. 6. Erosion Control 6.1 Erosion control coverings such as plastic, tarps and straw bales must be used to cover any exposed ground. This is very important during foundation excavation and for spoil piles which must be protected during heavy rains. 6.2 Runoff in the work site must be managed to be detained, filtered or infiltrated such that it is clean when it leaves the property. 7. Post Construction — a completion report to RAR BC is required. The property owner must notify a QEP whom will report after the permanent dwelling on the property has been completed and landscaped to confirm there has been no impact in the SPEA. Introduction: On behalf of Holland Creek Development on November 20, 2014 a Riparian Area Regulation (RAR) Assessment was Submitted (# 3279A). The result was protected areas were identified in the RAR report as the Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA). This report is a biological opinion to defend no serious harm will result in a flex to the area of the SPEA for lots 9 and 10 in phase 1 of the development. Description of Lot 9 and 10 SPEA The RAR report identifies the SPEAS for the development (Fig.1). Many of the single-family lots are situated within the 30m Riparian Assessment Area (RAA). Within the RAA the stream channels have a SPEA of 10m from the top of bank. In Phase 1 of the development, lots 9 and 10 are situated adjacent the culvert entrance of Tributary 1. The south sides of these lots border the dedicated Park area owned by the Town of Ladysmith. The standard RAR SPEA was assigned to the tributary line at 90 degrees to flow as the stream enters the culvert. Figure 1 shows there is a small triangle in red of the SPEA projecting laterally from the Park dedication. The SPEA line is approximately 5 m at its widest on both lots 9 and 10. This SPEA projection blocks the already narrow entrance to the lot and isolates the entrance area of the property. Discussion The owner has requested moving the SPEA areas on lot 9 and 10 inward to follow the dedicated Park boundary. This results in a shortening of the front of the SPEA width from 10m to about 5m at the culvert to allow property access. The SPEA remains 10m wide on the rest of the properties. The riparian area adjacent lots 9 and 10 is much larger than the SPEA dedication as there is additional dedicated Park area that increases the width from 10m to over 50m upstream. This results in a large off setting of area. The south side has a tall stand of trees on a hillside in the SPEA /Park that significantly shades the area. The stream is further protected by an incised valley that results in SPEAS at the top of ravine bank. The closed culvert is not affected by riparian needs. Holland Ck RAR Flex Lots 9-10 DRCv2.docx Page 61 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 62 Conclusions The objective of the SPEA in this site is to preserve and protect the water quality of this stream channel feeding into Holland Creek. The remaining SPEA, Park area and small area affected, ensures that this flex of the SPEA will not harm the creek. Yours Truly David R. Clough, RPBio List of Figures Figure 1. The Permittee, as a condition of the issuance of this Permit, agrees: a) To protect the Streamside Protection and Enhancement Areas (SPEAs) adjacent to proposed lots 9, 10 and 14 to 28 (as shown in Schedule A) by adhering to the following environmental management procedures in the Riparian Assessment Area (RAA): PRIOR TO CONSTRUCTION i) Prior to construction and at the time of building permit application a property owner must: e Provide a survey plan showing the location of the SPEA and the proposed building location, e Consult a Qualified Environmental Professional (QEP) to approve, inspect and submit a completion report for the development, ¢ Submit to the Town the QEP name and contact information, e Ensure that the QEP inspects at start-up and routinely as work is conducted to ensure the SPEA boundary is marked and not disturbed, and to identify measures to protect the SPEA during and after construction. ii) A job pre-work meeting will be done with the QEP to ensure that all workers understand the environmental objectives and _ clear understanding of roles and responsibilities to protect the SPEA. iii) The SPEA must be identified with signage, stakes, flagging and a sediment control fence. DURING CONSTRUCTION iv) The SPEA areas must not be encroached, altered or impacted by construction. There must be no storage of materials, garbage or construction of trails in the SPEA. Page 2 of 4 Page 66 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 67 v) If the root zone of a tree in the SPEA is within the area of proposed lots 9, 10 and 14 to 28 then the root zone must be clearly identified with stakes and flagging prior to lot preparation and construction; and must be protected as recommended by the QEP. Machinery is not to disturb these trees and their roots in any way. vi) Erosion control coverings such as plastic, tarps and hay bales must be used to cover any exposed ground in the riparian assessment area. This is very important during foundation excavation and for spoil piles which must be covered during heavy rains. vii) Drainage and runoff in the work site must be managed and detained, filtered, or infiltrated such that it is clean when it leaves the lot and enters a SPEA. viii) Heavy equipment access must be surfaced with a non-erodible firm substrate to eliminate sedimentation and rutting during the movement of heavy equipment in and out of the site. ix) Spill kits must be located on each piece of heavy equipment. Spills of any kind must be reported to the environmental monitor. x) Machinery and equipment must not be fueled within 30 metres of a watercourse. xi) In any circumstance, whether raining or not, where a potential exists for sediment to escape into the SPEA, the activity must be stopped and mitigating actions taken. xii) After construction exposed areas outside the SPEA must be re-seeded with grass seed or covered with other non-erodible materials. All construction materials are to be removed from the site. b) At the time of final inspection and prior to issuance of an Occupancy Permit on proposed lots 9,10 and 14 to 28 (as shown in Schedule A) the owner must complete the following steps: i) Provide a post-construction monitoring_report to the Town of Ladysmith. This report shows the measures to protect for the environmental features in accordance with bylaws from the Town Of Ladysmith as well as the B.C. Riparian Area Regulation under the B.C. Fish Protection Act. 1. Legal Description of Development Property Newcastle Engineering PLA Diagram (Fig. 1) shows the perimeter of the Phase 2 boundary and the individual lot numbers. This figure also shows the Riparian Area of Phase 2. Single family Lots 1--38 ; Legal description: Lot A, Plan EPP63594, Block 192 and District Lot 103, Oyster District - PID: 030-139-520. 2. Ladysmith Bylaws: The Development Permit Area (DPA) will follow the bylaw conditions “protection of the natural environment, its ecosystems and biological diversity” (Local Government Act, section 488(1)(a))”” regulated by the Town of Ladysmith. The Holland Creek development is in the Town of Ladysmith Development Permit Area 6 — Riparian Development Permit Area. The Ladysmith DPA requires a Riparian Area Regulation (RAR)? assessment followed by instructions on protection of the Riparian Area. 3. Riparian Area Regulation — Fish Protection Act The Riparian Area Regulation of the Fish Protection Act requires an assessment of the property following the RAR guidebook. A RAR report was submitted by D.R. Clough Consulting on behalf of Holland Creek Development in November 2014 and registered (RARNSS site as number 3279A. The RAR report describes the environmental areas, provides the determination of the SPEAS and instructions on the Measures to Protect during development. The RAR determined which lots are situated within the 30m Riparian Assessment Area (RAA), these lots are within the DPA 6. Within the RAA, the detailed RAR assessment calculated the stream channels to have a Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA) of 10m from the top of bank (Fig.1) This development is in the Holland Creek Watershed. Holland Creek consists of approximately 5 km long mainstem draining Holland Lake. It also has several tributaries draining from steep side hills including Heart Creek out of Heart Lake. The mainstem of Holland Creek is home to Salmon and Trout with ocean access upstream 3 km to Crystal Falls adjacent Colonia Avenue. Upstream of the falls in lake fed waterways are resident trout. The detailed assessment of the Phase 2 development identified Tributary 1 and 2 that enter Holland Creek. While neither of these streams are fish bearing, they are important to supplying water and nutrients to fish habitat. Protecting the health of these tributaries on this property through the Measures to Protect the SPEA ensures Holland Creek has year round flow and a salmon population. 1 Riparian Areas Guidebook for Local Governments, Aug. 1, 2016, Min FLNRO. ? Riparian Areas Regulation enabled by the Fish Protection Act, March 31, 2005. 3 RARNS — Riparian Areas Notification System. Measures to Protect the SPEA The DPA conditions are identified in the RAR Assessment Report under Section 4 - Measures to Protect and Maintain the SPEA:; Since the RAR was submitted there have been the following actions taken with respect to the measures 1.) Danger Trees and Windthrow —a danger tree assessment report and follow up tree remediation has been done by VI Trees Services Ltd. (Appendix 1). 2. Slope Stability - a Terrain Assessment has been completed by Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. in a report dated Feb. 7, 2014. As part of the rezoning of the property a restrictive covenant (CA60463367) was registered on title defining what future actions were to be taken with respect to geotechnical hazards. Attached in Appendix 2 are copies of all the relevant pages of the covenant. (Appendix 2) 3.) Encroachment of SPEA and Protection of trees - included in the RAR and these areas are mapped by Land Surveyor, flagged and signs installed by RP Bio and Developer in field (Appendix 3). 4.) Sediment and Erosion Control — a plan for Phase 2 was developed by geotechnical (LEA Ltd.) and civil engineering (Newcastle Eng. Ltd.) professionals (Appendix 4) 5.) Earthworks/Stormwater Management — An earthworks and stormwater management plan for the subdivision has been developed by Newcastle Engineering Ltd. (Appendix 5 & 6), and approved for construction by the Town of Ladysmith. 6.) Floodplain Management (no flood concern is identified using RAR guidebook) 4.) Phase 2 Map; The Phase 2 map shows the location of Lots 1-38. The map shows Tributary 1 located to the east and Tributary 2 to the west of Phase 2. There is a 10m setback for the SPEA from the top of bank. Many areas along the tributaries had steep banks. 5.) DPA Terms and Conditions The terms and conditions for the DPA are to be reviewed by the Town of Ladysmith and formalized into a DPA agreement with the developer. The aspects of the terms are determined from the Riparian Areas report and the Town of Ladysmith bylaws. It is expected the protective aspects of the RAR report in section 3 will be included in the DPA. All pertinent reports that apply to the “Measures to Protect” should be submitted to the Town of Ladysmith. The lot owner and builder must follow the DPA recommendations to protect the SPEAS in this report. The developer will employ a Qualified Environmental Professional (QEP) to conduct monitoring of construction to ensure the lot owner and builder follow the RAR. The DPA requires the developer or their QEP to halt or amend any operations that do not follow the RAR. The Developer and QEP must submit a completion report to the B.C. RAR depository for development of lots in the RAA. 6.) Conclusions With the RAR, Map and supporting documents, the Town should have all the information to accommodate the DPA conditions that will protect the environment of Holland Creek. All trees listed on the tree inventory table have been deemed potential hazards for the proposed diellings and recommended to be removed. There are 21 trees (including a cluster of four Alders) deemed potentially hazardous at the time of the assessment. Tree’s should be felled parallel to the line or fallen into open lot and moved parallel to line. Tree sections shall be left as coarse woody debris and branch debris shall be hauled off site to eliminate fire hazard, Limitations: Arborists cannot detect every condition that could possibly lead to the structural failure of a tree. The Permittee, as a condition of the issuance of this Permit, agrees: a) To protect the Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA) shown in Schedule B by adhering to the following environmental management procedures in the Riparian Assessment Area (RAA): PRIOR TO CONSTRUCTION i) Prior to construction and at the time of building permit application a property owner must: e Provide a survey plan showing the location of the SPEA and the proposed building location, ¢ Consult a Qualified Environmental Professional (QEP) to approve, inspect, and submit a completion report for the development, Submit to the Town the QEP name and contact information, Ensure that the QEP inspects at start-up and routinely as work is conducted to ensure the SPEA boundary is marked and not disturbed, and to identify measures to protect the SPEA during and after construction. ii) Prior to construction a job pre-work meeting will be done with the QEP to ensure that all workers understand the environmental objectives and clearly understand the roles and responsibilities to protect the SPEA. iii) Prior to construction the SPEA must be identified with signage, stakes, flagging and a sediment control fence. DURING CONSTRUCTION iv) The SPEA areas must not be encroached, altered or impacted by construction. There must be no storage of materials, garbage or construction of trails in the SPEA. v) If the root zone of a tree in the SPEA is within the RAA then the toot zone must be clearly identified with stakes and flagging prior to lot preparation and construction; and must be protected as recommended by the QEP. Machinery is not to disturb these trees and their roots in any way. Page 2 of 4 Page 89 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 90 vi) Erosion control coverings such as plastic, tarps and hay bales must be used to cover any exposed ground in the RAA. This is very important during foundation excavation and for spoil piles which must be covered during heavy rains. vii) Drainage and runoff in the work site must be managed and detained, filtered, or infiltrated such that it is clean when it leaves the lot and enters a SPEA. viii) | Heavy equipment access must be surfaced with a non-erodible firm substrate to eliminate sedimentation and rutting during the movement of heavy equipment in and out of the site. ix) Spill kits must be located on each piece of heavy equipment. Spills of any kind must be reported to the environmental monitor. x) Machinery and equipment must not be fueled within 30 metres of a watercourse. xi) In any circumstance, whether raining or not, where a potential exists for sediment to escape into the SPEA, the activity must be stopped and mitigating actions taken. xii) After construction exposed areas outside of the SPEA must be re-seeded with grass seed or covered with other non-erodibie materials. V9G 1A2 By e-mail Dear Sir: Re: Malone Road Subdivision, Phases 1 & 2, Lot A, District Lot 126, Oyster District, Plan VIP73132 Stormwater Management Memo Town of Ladysmith File 3320-20-02 We understand that covenant CA3452774 has been placed on the subject property and as such, a stormwater management plan must be accepted by the Town of Ladysmith prior to subdivision of the land. As requested, we have provided below a description of our proposed stormwater management plan to address the conditions of covenant CA3452774: Stormwater Management at the Catchment Level: Existing conditions of the subject property currently allow surface runoff to drain into three different downstream locations including: Rocky Creek, Brown Drive Park, and a storm water headwall located at the west end of the constructed portion of Malone Road. In order to minimize adverse impacts of altering natural drainage patterns, the post development tributary areas have designed to be sized within 1% of pre development tributary areas discharging into each of these locations. Since a single storm sewer pipe directs storm water north down Road A toward Rocky Creek and Brown Drive Park, we have designed a flow splitting manhole to address stormwater distribution to each catchment area, The flow splitting manhole utilizes varying pipe sizes and gradients exiting the manhole to convey an appropriate stormwater volume to each of Rocky Creek and Brown Drive Park. Post development flows along the extension of Malone Road will be directed toward the existing storm sewer headwall located at the west end of the constructed portion of Malone Road, Stormwater Infiltration: In order to mitigate the effects of increasing the impervious area on the subject property post development, the following storm water infiltration systems have been specified: Page 102 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 103 Exfiltration Lawn Basin Storm Service: Exfiltration lawn basins have been specified on lots where the rear property line is adjacent to the Park, This style lawn basin has a bottomless design and is placed on 200mm thick pad of drain rock to promote infiltration, During heavy flows (when the flowrate into the lawn basin is greater than the infiltration rate into the subsoil), the stormwater will overflow out of the grate and into the Park mimicking the pre development condition, Rock Pit Storm Service with Connection to Storm Sewer: Rock pits on the storm services have been specified on all single-family lots that do not share a property line with the Park. These rock pits have a large volume of crushed rock located below a section of perforated pipe that allows for underground storage/infiltration for storm water. Once the underground storage reservoir is full and infiltration capacity of the subsoils has been exploited, storm water will enter the storm sewer mains. Exfiltration Manhole: Storm water flows exiting the flow splitting manhole toward Rock Creek enters an exfiltration manhole. Low flows are designed to infiltrate into the ground and slowly enter the creek subsurface. During periods of significant flows, any runoff exceeding the infiltration capacity of the subsoils surrounding the exfiltration manhole will flow out of the grate and travel down a rip rap channel into Rocky Creek. Allowance for On-site Detention Facilities: Future multifamily sites will address storm water management via on-site detention and exfiltration systems to be designed at the time of development. Mosquito Management: We have not proposed any storm water retention on this project (open pond that is not designed to drain completely) and have proposed exfiltration lawn basins and manholes where possible. With these measures, there will be no additional long-term areas of standing water post development during mosquito hatching season than pre development. Access for Routine Maintenance: Storm water infrastructure not accessible by vehicle has been designed with low maintenance as a priority. All storm water infrastructure will be accessible by foot, Control of Surface Water to Adjacent Properties: Proposed lots that are located adjacent to existing dwellings are proposed to have a rock pit and storm sewer connection to the storm sewer main, This will allow for a direct connection between the storm sewer main and the future homes roof leaders and/or perimeter drain, This will result in the large majority of future impervious surfaces to drain into the rock pit (or storm sewer main) and away from existing dwellings. Form 1 Page 2 of 14 Page 105 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 106 FORM 1 Riparian Areas Protection Regulation - Qualified Environmental Professional - Assessment Report Section 1. Description of Fisheries Resources Values and a Description of the Development proposal (Provide as a minimum: Species present, type of fish habitat present, description of current riparian vegetation condition, connectivity to downstream habitats, nature of development, specific activities proposed, timelines) Introduction and Parcel Description: 7531 Cowichan Lake Road is located east of Cowichan Lake and is situated between the Cowichan Valley Highway to the north and Cowichan Lake Road to the south with Cowichan River Provincial Park land to the southeast and private property to the west. The parcel is long (~930m long) and narrow (up to ~150m wide) with a total area of 21 acres (8.5 ha) located at the following coordinates: 48° 49’ 40.50” N / 124° 00’ 43.43” W. The property is legally identified as follows: LOT 4 BLOCK 29 COWICHAN LAKE DISTRICT, PLAN 47390 (PID 012-490-920). The subject parcel is located in Electoral Area F — Cowichan Lake South/Skutz Falls within the Cowichan Valley Regional District (CVRD). The majority of the property is fully forested by a second growth conifer forest. A single house exists in a small cleared portion of the east side of the parcel. As understood, the property owner wishes to subdivide the property into 4 parcels: Lot A (2.1 ha), Lot B (2.0 ha), Lot C (2.0 ha) and Lot D where the existing house is located (2.4 ha). The subject parcel has four small watercourses bisecting it and a small wetland so the application process requires that a Riparian Areas Protection Regulation (RAPR) assessment be completed as part of the subdivision application. Aquaparian has prepared a separate Biophysical Assessment as a requirement of the subdivision application. A site location map of the study area has been included in this RAPR report as Figure 1. The site survey of the property produced by McElhanney has been included as Figure 2. Aquaparian has labelled the water features on this figure. Figure 3a & 3b show the SPEA and associated setbacks overlaid onto the site plan. A selection of site photographs taken during the site survey have been included within this document as Appendix A. Watercourses Descriptions: A watercourse named Golding Brook was identified to bisect the east side of the parcel as mapped on the CVRD map and on the provincial database Habitat Wizard. Site reconnaissance did not identify any watercourses located where this stream was mapped. It is unclear if the stream is located elsewhere on the parcel or outside of the parcel. Regardless, four small watercourses were identified during site visits conducted on July 5" and 7", 2021 as well as a small wetland. For the purpose of this report, the watercourses will be identified as Watercourses 1, 2, 3 & 4 (west to east) and the Form 1 Page 3 of 14 Page 106 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 107 FORM 1 Riparian Areas Protection Regulation - Qualified Environmental Professional - Assessment Report wetland as Wetland 1. Two ditches recognized as fish-bearing are also included, identified as Ditch 1 and Ditch 2. See Figure 2. Watercourses 1 to 4 and Wetland 1 all drain into a sizeable roadside ditch (Ditch #1) located along Cowichan River Road (south boundary) where they flow either east or west, depending on topography. Culverts in the ditch direct flows further south under Cowichan Lake Road and into forested stream channels to the Cowichan River downstream, located approximately 300m south of the parcel. A small section of ditch (Ditch #2) also extends northeast along the driveway and is located within the adjacent property to the east. No obvious physical fish barriers were identified (i.e. crushed culverts, hanging culverts, steep slopes etc.) between the drainages and Ditch 1, or along downstream ditch connections to the river, so the drainages are to be considered fish-bearing and subject to the RAPR. Watercourses 1,3 & 4 are fed by culverts that provide flows from the hillside above the Cowichan Valley Highway and ditch along the highway along the north boundary of the property. Watercourse 2 appears to collect surface water from surrounding forest within the property. Ditch 1 along Cowichan Lake Road should be considered a channelized section of stream due to the fact that the watercourses are considered headwater streams and part of a historical drainage pattern within the Cowichan / Koksilah Watershed. The parcel topography within the site includes a sleep slope below the Cowichan Valley Highway that then transitions to a gentler slope toward the south boundary. The entire property has a south sloping aspect. Watercourses have a step-pool morphology in upper channel sections but are predominantly riffle-pool in morphology within most of the property. In-stream substrate is dominated by boulder and cobble with gravel and some accumulations of fines. Ditch substrate includes cobble and gravel with some boulders and some fines. Fisheries Resource Values: The Cowichan River, which receives flows from water features identified within the subject parcel, is recorded to support the following species: ¢ Brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalus) e Brown catfish (Ameiurus nebulosus) e Brown trout (Sa/mo trutta) e Dolly Varden (Salvelinus malma) e Chinook salmon (O. tshawytscha) e Chum salmon (O. keta) ¢ Coastal cutthroat trout « Anadromous and resident cutthroat trout ¢ Coastrange sculpin (Cottus aleuticus) e Prickly sculpin (Cottus asper) e Coho salmon (O. kisutch) Form 1 Page 4 of 14 Page 107 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 108 FORM 1 Riparian Areas Protection Regulation - Qualified Environmental Professional - Assessment Report e Kokanee (O. nerka) e Rainbow trout and steelhead (O. mykiss) ¢ Stickleback, and e Lamprey. Riparian Conditions: Creek side vegetation along the multiple small watercourses throughout the parcel includes a canopy of western redcedar, Douglas-fir, and red alder (A/nus rubra) over salal (Gaultheria shallon), false-lily-of-the-valley (Maianthemum dilatatum), fringecup (Tellima grandiflora), herb-Robert (Geranium robertianum), trailing blackberry (Rubus ursinus), pathfinder (Adenocaulon bicolor), skunk cabbage (Lysichiton americanum), Pacific bleeding heart (Dicentra formosa), sweet scented bedstraw (Galium triflorum), stinging nettle (Urtica dioica), maidenhair fern (Adiantum pedatum), lady fern (Athyrium filix-femina), sword fern (Polystichum munitum), foam flower ( Tiarella trifoliata), vanilla leaf (Achlys triphylla), young grand fir (Abies grandis), star flower (Trientalis sp.) and common snowberry (Symphoricarpos albus). The small wetland located centrally within the parcel has a canopy dominated by red alder and an understory dominated by salmonberry (Rubus spectabilis), skunk cabbage, lady fern, deer fern (Blechum spicant) and stinging nettle. The wetland is approximately 100m’ in area. Ditch 1 has a canopy dominated by bigleaf maple, black cottonwood (Populus trichocarpa) and Douglas-fir and the ditch channel and banks are vegetated with slough sedge (Carex obnupta), small-flowered bulrush (Scirpus microcarpus), marsh skullcap (Scutellaria galericulata), common horsetail (Equisetum arvense), cow parsnip (Heracleum maximum), thimbleberry (Rubus parviflorus), bracken fern, young bigleaf maple, broadleaf dock (Rumex obtusifolius), stinging nettle, trailing blackberry, oxeye daisy (Leucanthemum vulgare), smooth hawk’s-beard (Crepis capillaris), pearly everlasting (Anaphalis margaritacea), St. John’s wort (Hypericum perforatum), Scotch broom (Cytisus scoparius), sheep sorrel (Rumex acetosella) and grasses. Ditch 2 has a canopy of western redcedar, Douglas-fir, red alder and bigleaf maple with an understory of pathfinder, dull Oregon-grape (Mahonia nervosa), star flower, trailing blackberry, common snowberry, salal, sword fern, vanilla leaf and young grand fir. Note: Form 1 “riparian length” is an estimated total of all riparian measurements for Watercourses 1 to 4 (160m, 45m, 111m, 50m), Wetland 1 (60m), Ditch 1 (860m) and Ditch 2 (50m). The estimated total riparian length is 1336m. Comments This watercourse has a 1988 Covenant applied to it. Provincial and municipal databases do not identify the stream to have a name, but the current property owner referred to it as Josiah Creek. However, provincial and municipal mapping databases identify Josiah Creek to be much farther east than the boundaries of the subject parcel. The covenant refers to Josiah Creek having a 7.5m setback from the centreline and Cowichan River having a 30m setback from the centreline. The covenant is expected to have been instated when the parcel was part of a larger forestry tenure parcel. It is unclear if the covenant document is referring to the subject creek as Josiah Creek or whether Josiah Creek was captured in the larger land parcel prior to subdivision into the smaller subject parcel. Sediment and Erosion Control At the subdivision stage the extent of soil disturbance and proximity of work near the watercourses is unknown. When planning the development stage, ensure that work near the watercourses employs sufficient sediment and erosion control plans to prevent migration of fines and sediments into watercourses or their SPEAs. The following are some general mitigation measures to be followed to reduce the risk of sediment and erosion issues during development: ¢ Earthworks are to be completed during the dry season to prevent sediment migration into the watercourses and wetland. If earthworks cannot be completed during the dry months, sediment and erosion measures are to be implemented (i.e. silt fence) to prevent migrating sediments from entering the watercourses; e Any future development should be designed to minimize vegetation removal and retain mature trees if possible. Minimizing vegetation removal preserves the integrity of soils and slope stability; * No sediment is to enter drainages — additional measures (such as additional silt fencing, straw bales, interceptor ditching, sediment control ponds, sediment traps, staged gravel filters, or other methods) may be required depending on weather conditions and construction method; e Management of stockpiled soils including no Form 1 Page 9 of 14 Page 132 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 133 FORM 1 Riparian Areas Protection Regulation - Qualified Environmental Professional - Assessment Report stockpiling within the SPEAs of the watercourses, covering soil piles with plastic if left on site for extended periods in the rainy season etc; « Do not leave soils exposed to rainfall and potential run-off. Seeding exposed soils immediately upon completion and if necessary, temporarily covering with 1” straw to prevent surface erosion until grass germinates; and, « Avoid tracking sediments onto roadways. Stormwater runoff from roadways has the potential to capture loose sediments and flow into roadside ditches and subsequently into the Cowichan River. Sweep up any tracked sediments. Description of Fisheries Resources Values and a Description of the Development proposal (Provide as a minimum: Species present, type of fish habitat present, description of current riparian vegetation condition, connectivity to downstream habitats, nature of development, specific activities proposed, timelines) Description of Proposed Development The proposed development of 128 Rollie Rose Drive (Lot 12), of the Phase 1 Holland Creek Residential Development Project is situated on a total lot area of 0.190 ha located in the Cowichan Valley Regional District by the Town of Ladysmith. The proposed development along Tributary 1 (T1), will be adjacent to and about 40 m of riparian habitat on the northwest side of T1, which eventually discharges into Holland Creek. The proposed development includes the construction of low density multi family residential homes consisting of three townhouses with a total of seven units, other portions will remain as greenspace or be used as roads/right of ways. The total area covered by housing footprints, access roads and other structures is proposed to be 0.130 ha. The site plan map is available in Section 3 of this report. A detailed RAPR was completed as part of the process for a development permit of multi family residential for the proposed development. The RAPR will be used as a planning document for the measures to protect and maintain the SPEA required for the proposed development. Description of Fisheries Resources Value The proposed development area and associated riparian assessment area (RAA) has previous disturbance and alteration in and around T1. This non fish tributary flows into Holland Creek over a falls near the Dogwood Avenue bridge. The T1 channel is comprised of several reach segments (R1-3): T1-R1, T1-R2, T1-R3; however, the proposed development area only occurs along T1- R1. The area was logged in the past using clear-cut methods and allowed to regenerate naturally. The regenerating area appears to be approximately 3 to 80 years old, which may require a Condition and Impact Assessment report if requested by the Town of Ladysmith or the Ministry. This is due to previous clearing operations during the Phase 1 Holland Creek Residential Development Project within the RAA. Clearing did not occur within the previous SPEA as determined by the 2014 RAR completed for the overall project area, which included T1. A mixture of regenerating Red Cedar, Douglas Fir, Red Alder and Broad Leaf Maple comprise the dominant tree species in the RAA as well as the surrounding area. No old growth trees were observed in the RAA. Extensive areas of the RAA were dominated by moss (in and near T1-R1), salal and ferns as well as by weedy species such as Spurge-Laurel, Foxglove, Himalayan Blackberry, Canada Thistle, and Queen Anne's Lace. In and around T1-R1 and the proposed development area, the channel was historically redirected for logging, service of BC Hydro electrical lines, a water line corridor, as well as access for a garbage dump. In the upper reaches above the proposed development area, the BC Hydro transmission line, Fortis Natural Gas line and forestry road corridors disrupted the channels with poorly located culverts or lack of culverts, alternate routes, drainage ditches and braiding. Reach 1 begins at the confluence with Holland Creek above an 8 m bedrock waterfall which flows year-round from ground water seepage and provides critical summer flow to Holland Creek. The reach is 370 m in length, has an average width of 2.1 m, and an relatively low gradient of 4-12%. It is comprised of step pool complexes. Large woody debris is scattered throughout the reach, in channel and along the banks. This reach ends above the proposed development area, when T1 Form 1 Page 3 of 20 Page 149 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 150 FORM 1 Riparian Areas Protection Regulation - Qualified Environmental Professional - Assessment Report becomes confined in a small valley and gradient increases indicating a reach break into Reach 2). The proposed development area is within the Coastal Douglas Fir Biogeoclimatic Zone which is a Red Listed Plant Community. No specific Red or Blue listed plants other than the CDF Community are found in the B.C. Government Ecosystem Explorer for this site. Coastal Cutthroat Trout and Red Legged Frogs are two provincial blue listed endangered species historically observed during the previous study? around the lower fish bearing drainages. Fish Assessment T1 does not support anadromous or residential fish populations. It is located above the 8 m bedrock waterfall which acts as a fish barrier located at the confluence with Holland Creek. The steep gradients in Reach 2 and intermittently dry channel in Reach 1 eliminate the potential for resident fish. An electroshock of the wetted areas of the lower end of T1 in 2010 confirmed there were no fish‘. Holland Creek, the downstream receiving waters from T1 is located outside of the proposed development area. The creek has perennial flow and anadromous fish access from its’ lower reaches to water falls upstream which act as a fish barrier. The creek supports a diverse mix of anadromous and resident fish species including cutthroat and rainbow trout along with chum and coho salmon’. There has been enhancement of coho and chum salmon through small numbers of hatchery fry augmentation as well as extensive and successful habitat restoration with construction of four different off channel sites as well as much instream work to stabilize the banks and create fish habitat®. Danger Five trees were assessed as potential hazard trees, four of the trees were Trees recommended for treatment, and the one remaining assessed tree was deemed safe to retain. Recommended hazard mitigation includes felling (into the SPEA). Where safe, high stumping and coppicing of maples is recommended to retain value for wildlife. Where not safe, consider retaining Coarse Woody Debris for SPEA to enhance biodiversity. Vegetation management and mitigation measures will be undertaken in multiple ways such as planting and enhancement to bolster the vegetation in and around the SPEA which will increase biodiversity and habitat values. Forest cover on the northwest side of Tributary 1 was assessed. Windthrow risk Windthrow was rated as MODERATE. Likelihood of windthrow was rated MODERATE. The eastern portion of the RAA along Tributary 1 is windward to prevailing winds, and more prone to wind damage; both the windward and leeward segments contained hazardous trees according to the assessment. Treatment to prevent windthrow should follow standard strategies to minimize disturbance to rooting layers during clearing and construction, including not creating windthrow, protecting trees in the SPEA (especially along the SPEA boundary), and retaining wildlife trees in the SPEA. Care must be taken during development to avoid disturbance within the drip line of trees in and along the SPEA and overlap area with the remaining RAA. Management and mitigation measures will be undertaken to avoid disturbance to existing trees, plant new vegetation, increase coarse woody debris, all of which will decrease the potential for additional hazard trees, enhance biodiversity, and help to maintain a carbon sink. Protection | It is important to take steps and protect trees within the SPEA as they can be of Trees damaged by construction activities. Tree roots may extend outwards from their base to multiple times their own height, thus making them susceptible even if ground disturbance is outside the SPEA and within the remaining RAA approved for development. Activities that must not take place near SPEA trees are: significant changes to ground level, release of pollutants, moving equipment, parking or storing construction equipment. An environmental monitor will observe for compliance during inspections and any other practices that may impact SPEA tree health. The trees within the SPEA are not be disturbed. Removal of any danger trees in the SPEA will require the services of a professional danger tree assessor. Work identified as being harmful to the SPEA but not within such as excavation, clearing, erection of permanent structures has to be done in such a way to protect the SPEA trees from harm. A drip zone beyond the marked SPEA is to be implemented to protect trees and their roots from harm. A default 7.5m drip zone will be adhered to, unless the calculated drip zone based off tree height is greater than 7.5m, of which the latter measurement shall than apply. Vegetation management and mitigation measures will be undertaken in multiple ways such as planting and enhancement to bolster the vegetation in and around the SPEA which will increase biodiversity and habitat values. A qualified environmental professional will be retained as the environmental monitor by the developer. The environmental monitor will be available in the event of significant rainfall, drainage problems, erosion and sediment control problems, and general project area wide conditions during emergency events. The qualified environmental professional will be experienced in sediment and erosion control measures, and will have the authority to shut down project area works if necessary to protect the SPEA. The qualified environmental professional will ensure all development activities remain outside of the SPEA, tree protection measures are being followed, fencing and sediment and erosion control measures are in working order, and storm water management structures are functioning correctly and all other relevant measures to protect are followed. Environmental monitoring is planned to protect the drainages, riparian areas, slope stability, and general condition of the proposed project area during clearing and grubbing activities and toad and property construction. Monitoring is to be completed weekly, or during key construction activities or extreme weather conditions (i.e. high rainfall). A post development environmental completion report is a required part of this permit to ensure all measures to protect were followed. This report is submitted to agencies as a final signoff. All relevant document files pertaining to environmental monitoring activities are attached to this report. VOR 2HO Ph/Fax: 250-390-2901 Cell: 250-714-5416 email:drclough@shaw.ca March 20, 2013 Attn: 0885538BC Ltd and Stzuminus First Nation c/o Glenn Carey, Project Manager 6774 Dickinson Road Nanaimo, BC V9V 1A2 Ph: 250-390-1475 email: s.22 RE: Holland Creek Watershed, Ladysmith B.C. Environmental Assessment Introduction: In the proposal for the development on property on the south side of Holland Creek we were asked to provide a preliminary Biological assessment during the winter. The objectives of the assessment were to determine; 1.) Stream and drainage mapping: There are two unnamed drainages as well as Heart Creek and Holland Creek in the development area. We will identify the location in the field with flagging and GPS the location of the unnamed drainages for upload files preliminary planning maps. 2.) Stream Fish Habitat values: The streams will be assessed with a standard fish habitat assessment to determine the physical status of the channel as well as potential for fish presence and type. Po Inspect the proposed bridge crossing area on Heart Creek. Consultation: The importance of this watershed to Stzuminus First Nations, Ladysmith Sportsmen Club and Town of Ladysmith will result in consultation to determine their interest and input in fisheries values. There will be a site visit and meeting to explain findings and listen to concerns. Methods Stream mapping Brad Remillard, RPBio and Dave Clough, RPBio undertook the stream channel assessments in January and February 2013. We began at either the top or bottom of the major drainages and flagged stations and tributaries as we inspected the channels for habitat characteristics. Hand held Garmin (450) GPS was used with a cellular GPS application (Everytrail) and a photo and location reference as well. GPS data was edited on Garmin Mapsource software and uploaded to Google Earth for display. The survey area is bounded by Holland Creek on the north east and the Hydro line on the south west. Stream Habitat Each stream was inspected bya biologist for fish habitat suitability. Fish habitat features such as barriers, rearing and spawning habitat as well as flow regimes were analyzed. We also referred to past fish presence information from past electroshock surveys and information from local stream stewardship groups. Holland Ck Lot 103 Biological Assessment DRCMar13.doc 1 Page 167 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 168 Bridge Site Inspection The general area (taken from the preliminary mapping) suggested approximately 100m of area along Heart Creek. This area was walked to determine the best site based on a narrow confined channel that would result in least impact to fish habitat values. Consultation The Stzuminus First Nation was consulted at their bad office on January 27, 2013 to discuss the development and the possibility of a fish hatchery. The Ladysmith Sportsmen attended on-site tour with the proponent and a follow up inspection of hatchery locations on the 27" of February. Results Study Area Overview; Holland Creek is a salmon and trout stream its entire length adjacent the subject property. The salmon swim upstream under the E&N Railway culvert adjacent the island Highway Bridge then upstream approximately 400m inside the Holland Creek Park to the Dogwood Avenue Bridge. To this point the river is heavily utilized by Chum salmon spawners in October and November. The river then continues upstream past the Lot 103 tributaries in a confined valley. Salmon access lives approximately 1.8km above Dogwood Avenue at Crystal falls, a 10m bedrock barrier. The reach above Dogwood is used by Coho spawners as well as Cutthroat. Crystal Falls is the first of many in a long (8.5 km) steep climb up to Holland Lake (670m elev.). There are resident Cutthroat trout and Rainbow Trout above the falls to Holland Lake. Holland Lake is impounded and used as part of the Town of Ladysmith water supply (Company Dam). Holland Creek is protected by a second growth forest that is 30 to 100m in width on each side to the park boundaries and beyond. The forest was logged; the stumps show it was historically dominated by Douglas Fir with Red Cedar near the water. The forest is regenerating with those species as well as Red Alder, Broad Leaf Maple and many shrub species including Willow, Indian Plum, Ocean Spray, Salmonberry, Sword Fern and Blackberry. There are a few veteran Douglas Fir in the forest. This same forest type extends upland into Lot 103 area with the largest trees found in the Heart Creek valley. Lot 103 also has many polygons of younger stands of trees just emerging from the brush as well as a recent logging above either side of Heart Creek. The Holland Creek foot trail encircles the creek on both sides, with a bridge over each of the Lot 103 tributaries near their entrance to Holland Creek. The Hydro line provides the southwest boundary to the property and Holland Creek/Heart Creek are on the northeast boundary of the lot. The Holland Creek watershed has seen a concerted effort of salmon enhancement and habitat restoration over the last 20 years. There are now hundreds of pieces of wood debris placed for fish habitat. Four sidechannel areas have been dug out in the lower reaches increasing the summer wetted habitat and winter flood refuge significantly in Holland Creek. This work has been done bya partnership led by the Ladysmith Sportsmen Club working with Stzuminus First Nation Fisheries Program and Town of Ladysmith. There is a hatchery on Bush Creek that incubates approximately 15,000 coho fry and 50,000 Chum fry from this creek annually. There are plans to consider relocation of the Bush Creek hatchery to Holland Creek due to the better water quality, easier access and safety. Assessment results are presented overleaf with a Map, and Photos for each drainage. Stream Mapping/Fish Habitat Streams were at medium to high flow levels during the survey allowing for identification of the mainstems as well as smaller tributaries. There are three Holland Creek tributaries that drain the proposed development area; Tributary 1, 2 and Heart Creek respectively from downstream to up (Figure 1). Holland Ck Lot 103 Biological Assessment DRCMar13.doc 2 Page 168 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 169 Tributaries 1 and 2 are unnamed drainages that enter Holland Creek over bedrock water falls (5m) with no fish access. Table 1) Holland Creek Lot 103 Fish Habitat Summary. Drainage Fish Access/Habitat Holland Creek Yes Tributary 1 No Tributary 2 No Heart Creek Yes Tributary 1 The mainstem is 830 m long through the property from the hydro line to Holland Creek. It enters over a 5m bedrock falls just north of the Dogwood Avenue Bridge parking lot. The channel is approximately 2.1m wide. The lower reach to the first hydro line (200m) is relatively low gradient at 4-11%. This reach appears to have been diverted from its historic route as the channel has evidence of recent formation with no natural stream characteristics. It was likely diverted west to make way for Dogwood Avenue. Above the old Hydro right of way the channel appears natural but disturbed by historic logging lacking large woody debris. The channel gradient increases to more than 20% and is confined in a small valley with vegetated sidewalls to just below (150m) the Hydro Line where it is fed by three seasonal channels T1, T1-2, T1-3, that braid across the Hydro Line. The channel furthest north is the strongest (T1). The Hydro Line and logging roads appear to have disrupted the natural course in this area such that the historical location is difficult to determine above the split in channels. There is no fish access into this channel. An electroshock in 2010 found no fish in the 200 m along the lower reach where the gradient is less than 20%. The tributary has perennial water flow to Holland Creek. Tributary 2 The main channel of Tributary 2 is 930m long upstream Hydro line crossing. It has two short tributaries (2B, 2C,) that enter it within the Lot 103 area. Beginning at Holland Creek there is a 4.5m bedrock falls that denies fish access. Upstream this channel was disturbed by historic logging lacking pools and large woody debris. It lies in a semi-confined channel with vegetated sidewalls. The creek channel is 1.7m wide in the lower reach on a gradient of 1-7% above the barrier. It loses its confinement at the Hydro line crossing where it is dry in summer. Water flow is perennial to Holland Creek and in summer this water accrues below the hydro line. Heart Creek This is the longest and largest tributary with length of 1.2 km from the Hydro line to Holland Creek. Heart Creek has a 240m long reach of salmon access, ending at a 5m bedrock water falls. Above the falls there is a confined and deep (20-50m) treed valley that creates an isolated reach of Heart Creek to the Hydro Line where the canyon ends. The average channel width was 4.1m on a 10% slope. Heart Creek goes approximately 1.0 km further upstream to its source at Heart Lake. The entire length of Heart Creek is habitat for resident Cutthroat & Rainbow Trout which occupy the lake as well as perennial pockets in the lower reach. The fish are seeded into the entire length of the stream from Heart Lake. The upper reaches above the Hydro line are more disturbed by historic logging and are seasonal while below the Hydro line, there is flow recovery in summer with perennial flow into Holland Creek. Heart Creek Bridge Site Inspection The mid reach of Heart Creek is the location of a proposed road location. We inspected the stream channel widths in this area and found the channel width and floodplain ranged between 5.0 and 6.3m. The cross section sites were flagged in the field as XS (see Fig.1). The valley walls in the area were 25% slope on the south and 50% slope on a 10m bank on the north side. There were no significant fish habitat features in the area, pools were shallow and the channel had little LWD. The banks were steep but Holland Ck Lot 103 Biological Assessment DRCMar13.doc 3 Page 169 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 170 vegetated and stable. The stream substrates are Boulder/Cobble/Gravel. There were no significant veteran trees in the vicinity. Consultation/Planning for Hatchery Ladysmith Sportsmen Club operate the Bush Creek Hatchery. They built the hatchery with the full support of the Stzuminus First Nation in 1995 after both parties agreed there was a local need. Since then there has been a shared use of the facility. The hatchery enhances Chum and Coho stocks in five local streams; Stocking, Holland, Bush, Walker and the Chemainus River. They have 10 heath stacks and a capacity for 400,000 eggs. Over the years since the hatchery was developed the water quality in Bush Creek has declined. The gravity fed water is colder, carries more sediment and dries to a trickle in early summer. The water supply plugged this year and the eggs were all transported to Nanaimo Hatchery by the club in January. The hatchery also has no electrical power other than a generator so the alarm and fish feeders work off solar power. Its remote location 2.5 km up a logging road has resulted in vandalism and robbery constantly. The new location is next to town and walking distance from local schools allowing the education programs conducted by the Club to expand. The new building may have a classroom for workshops and school programs. The developers of the property have offered their land for a hatchery at a time when the operators of the hatchery were considering relocation. Consultation meetings have been held this winter, the relocation was discussed by both groups, and they walked the sites. There is an opportunity to use T1 and T2 as well as Heart Creek which all have flowing water year round. An inspection this winter found the water temperatures to be 1-3C warmer than Bush Creek which hasa significant effect on egg development timing. The Holland Creek hatchery idea was taken to the DFO Community Programs Community Advisor for advice and permitting. This permit will require a more detailed design to identify the flow and space requirements. CONCLUSIONS The assessment of the drainages was made to determine preliminary planning for a residential development. No lot or road determinations are finalized. The developer had instructed us to provide this environmental information such that they could plan around the environmental aspects. The environmental aspects of this area show Tributary 1 and 2 to be lacking fish access but important water supplies to Holland Creek. The summer water flow contribution of these two streams is approximately 25%. Heart Creek is a fish bearing channel which has a salmon reach to the base of the falls and is populated with resident trout above. Heart Creek is protected by a deep treed ravine which provides shade and habitat to the stream. The T1 and T2 channels are confined or semi-confined in treed depressions. To determine the riparian setback of these channels a Riparian Area Assessment (RAR) will need to be done. The RAR identifies the requirement for building setbacks as well as stormwater management, construction environmental protection as well as Danger Trees, Windthrow, Floodplain, Slope Stability, and Tree Protection. The development of the hatchery will follow a series of regulatory steps, which are out of the control of the proponents but the DFO are indicating their support (they haven't said no) and they should be able to assist in getting the approvals from their auditors and provincial agencies.
