Description of the Development Proposal and Fisheries Resources Values The subject site a 1.1ha lot, 3636 Yellow Point Road, in the Cowichan Valley Regional District (Figures 1, 2 and 3). It is the location of a previously developed single family home, which be removed to construct a new dwelling. On December 10, 2021 Lehna Malmkvist, RPBio, and lan Cruickshank, BSc, visited the site to conduct Riparian Areas Protection Regulation (RAPR) assessment and Sensitive Ecosystem Assessment required by the proposed project. Long Lake Creek crosses the southern portion of the property flowing from west to east, into the marine environment in Nicholson Cove. Watershed Context and Fisheries Resource Values The stream is at the downstream end of the watershed, in the last reach which discharges to the marine environment. No gazetted stream name could be found in the provincial mapping for the stream, however, the 1997 Management Direction Statement for Ladysmith Bog Ecological Reserve for BC Parks (know known as Yellow Point Bog Ecological Reserve), describes the stream as Long Lake Creek flowing out of the Reserve from Long Lake / Green Lake (two different names are used in mapping sources). The lake is located on the BC iMap (920-354500-39600 Waterbody ID 306841). The BC Fisheries Inventory Data Queries (FIDQ) database (January 26, 2022) for the lake describes, rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) and cutthroat trout (O. clarkii) as stocked and observed. Given upstream fish populations and unobstructed access from the marine environment, the stream is determined to be fish-bearing and the RAPR applies. The stream channel meanders through the forest from the culvert under Yellow Point Road to the marine environment in a cascade pool channel type, with sections of bedrock substrated, and sections of rock, cobble and gravel. With the exception of the presences of some invasive species (primarily English ivy), the adjacent SPEA and riparian vegetation on both sides is undisturbed. Site Assessment The RAPR assessment reviewed the subject property with a focus on the Riparian Assessment Area (RAA) (30 m from the Top of Bank) and the proposed work area (Figures 2 and 3). The RAA encompasses most of the lot, and the Streamside Protection & Enhancement Areas (SPEA), and stream encompasses the southern half of the lot. The property is previously developed, with an (Figures 2 and 3; Photos 1-9): existing house (unoccupied) (to be removed and new house built in the same location) separate suite/cottage (partially within the SPEA) well and pump house (in the SPEA) foot bridge over the stream driveway (small part in the SPEA) stairs to the marine shoreline (outside the SPEA) existing septic tank (to be removed) The vegetation on the property is lawn and landscaping on the north side of the driveway, with a fringe of conifer trees around the perimeter (Photos 1-3, 8, 9). The second growth forest south of the driveway on both sides of the stream consisting of is a mature, second growth, dry coastal Swell Environmental Consulting Ltd. 480 Beach Drive, Victoria, BC V8S 2M6 ph. 250-217-9190 __ e. lehna@swell.ca Page 286 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 287 Riparian Areas Protection Regulation Report: 3636 Yellow Point Road Page 5 of 34 forest (Photos ). It is a 8-18, 20, 21). Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii) dominated forest, with large component of western redcedar (Thuja plicata), bigleaf maple (Acer marcophyllum), and a few red alder (Alnus rubra) and grand fir (Abies grandis), with understory dominated by dull Oregon- grape (Mahonia nervosa), sword fern (Polystichum munitum), salal (Gaultheria shallon), with June plum (Oemelaria cerasiformis), oceanspray (Holodiscus discolor), red huckleberry (Vaccinium parvifolium), hairy honeysuckle (Lonicera hispidula), trailing blackberry (Rubus ursinus), etc. Along the stream edge, additional species are willow (Salix sp.), salmonberry (Rubus parviflorus), and slough sedge (Carex obnupta). The Douglas-fir/Oregon-grape forest type is a provincially red-listed (threatened) forest ecosystem. This forest is contiguous with forest in Blue Heron Park providing excellent riparian habitat for the stream and general bird and wildlife habitat. The marine shoreline vegetation in the RAA, but outside the SPEA consists of Douglas-fir, bigleaf maple, and arbutus (Arbutus menziesii) with and understory of willow (Salix sp., Nootka rose (Rosa nutkana), hairy honeysuckle, and bracken fern (Pteridium aquifolium), with ornamental plantings, and invasive species (Photo 19). Invasive, non-native species on the property include: extensive English ivy (Hedra helix), sporadic spurge laurel (Daphne laureola) and English holly (lex aquifolium), Scotch broom (Cytisus scoparius), yellow archangel (Lamium galeobdon), periwinkle (Vinca minor), Himalayan blackberry (Rubus armeniacus), non-native rose (Rosa sp.), bur-chervil (Anthriscus caucalis), thistle (Cirsium sp.), foxglove (Digitalis purpurea), herb-robert (Geranium robertianum),wall lettuce (Lactuca muralis), bindweed (Convolvulus sepium), reed canary grass (Phalaris arundinacea), and other escaped ornamental species (particularly on the shoreline slope). Pre-Clearing Nesting Bird Survey Given the potential habitat for Western Screech-Owl in the forest adjacent to the proposed construction, a nesting survey should be conducted if development activities that could disturb owls during breeding will occur during their nesting season, March through May. The survey would be a call-playback and/or automated recording unit surveys for presence of vocal screech-ows. Additionally, while no tree or understory clearing is proposed for the development, if there are changes to the proposed plan during in the detailed design stage (eg. for the stormwater or septic design), a standard pre-clearing nesting bird survey would be required, as described below. Nesting birds and their nests are protected by both the federal Migratory Bird Convention Act and Section 34 of the BC Wildlife Act, and care must be taken to avoid destruction of nests when clearing and/or developing any property. Section 34 of the BC Wildlife Act protects birds and their eggs from possession, molestation or destruction. The nests of eagles, peregrine falcons, gyrfalcons, ospreys, herons, and burrowing owls are protected at all times of the year. The nests of all other species are protected when the birds or their eggs are in the nest. o If apermanently protected nest is adjacent to the construction footprint, the bird biologist will provide recommendations for buffers and protection during construction, as described with the Guidelines for Raptor Conservation during Urban and Rural Land Development in British Columbia (2013): = https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/environment/natural-resource- stewardship/best-management- practices/raptor_conservation_guidelines_2013.pdf Tree removal and vegetation clearing should be conducted between August 15 and February 1 to minimize the risk of damaging nests. Pre-clearing nesting bird surveys should be conducted if tree or vegetation removal will occur during breeding season. While the period between August 15 and March 15 has been identified by Environment Canada and the BC Ministry of Environment as the general period least likely to involve active bird nesting, this time period does not coincide with the breeding and nesting habits of eagles, many owls species, or herons (Grant Bracher, FLNR and Ann Nightingale, VNHS pers. comm. 2018), therefore we recommend a nesting bird survey be conducted if tree and vegetation clearing will occur between February 1 and August 15. The nesting bird survey should be conducted within 1-2 days of the initiation of clearing, depending on the timing during the nesting season. The rest of the calendar dates are zero percent. https:/Awww.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/avoiding-harm-migratory- birds/general-nesting-periods/nesting-periods.html#_zoneA_calendar When work must be conducted within the breeding window, the following document provides information on steps that can be taken to reduce the risk of disturbing a bird nest. https:/Avww.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/avoiding-harm-migratory- birds/reduce-risk-migratory-birds.html Ideally, vegetation removal should be done outside of the breeding season, but the property owners should be aware that there are some birds (Anna’s Hummingbird, Red Crossbill, Great Horned Owl) that nest during the “off” season. In addition to the actual detection of a nest during vegetation removal, the crew should also watch for signs of high agitation by bird, indicating a nest or young are in the immediate area. If during tree and vegetation removal, a nest is discovered: o halt all disruptive activities in the nesting area o move away as quickly and quietly as possible o avoid disturbing the surrounding vegetation, and avoid making a trail to and from the nest o protect the nest with a buffer zone o avoid the immediate area until the young have naturally left the vicinity of the nest If a nest with young has been exposed to the elements or predation by removal of surrounding vegetation, the nest with young should immediately be taken to the nearest Wildlife Rehabilitation Centre. Environmental Monitoring The owner has been informed of the obligation to protect the Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA) and has agreed to retain a QEP to provide environmental monitoring during construction. At a minimum, environmental monitoring should include: ¢ A pre-construction meeting on-site with the QEP and the contractor. © Site visits timed to coincide with key construction activities and based on weather conditions to ensure all development activities remain outside of the SPEA and E&SC protective structures are in good working order, if needed. o After environmental protection measures are installed (e.g. site flagging, and sediment fencing) o During excavation o Heavy rainfall events (e.g. >15 mm) until such time that the QEP is satisfied that the erosion & sediment control and other protective structures are containing heavy rainfall as designed and no sediment laden runoff is leaving the site o Emergencies (e.g. spills). A post-development visit to inspect works for the conformance statement and post- development report. Photo-point monitoring and site visit checklists should be used for clarity of post-development reporting. The owner must notify the QEP a minimum of 2 weeks prior to the project start up to arrange for the pre-construction meeting. The owner has been informed of the obligation of a QEP to submit a conformance statement and post-development report to the RAR Notification System and have agreed to obtain the services of a QEP to complete this task. A post development report will include a field inspection of the development site and SPEA to ensure that the measures in the RAR report and in Environmental Monitoring plans have been implemented and that no damage has occurred or is expected to occur to the integrity of the SPEA. Reports generated by the Environmental Monitor during construction will be reviewed and the site will be photo-documented. If a QEP is not retained to monitor the project, it may not be possible to provide assurance that the work-site procedures were followed appropriately or the work completed to an acceptable standard, or to sign a conformance statement and submit a post-development report. Description of Fisheries Resources Values and a Description of the Development proposal (Provide as a minimum: Species present, type of fish habitat present, description of current riparian vegetation condition, connectivity to downstream habitats, nature of development, specific activities proposed, timelines) Description of Proposed Development The proposed development of Stage 6 and Stage 7 of Holland Creek Estates is part ofa multi year and multi staged development process. Stage 6 and Stage 7 are situated on 3.74 ha ofa total lot area of 22.02 ha located off of Rollie Rose Drive in the Town of Ladysmith. The proposed development along Tributary 1 (T1), will be adjacent to approximately 347 m of riparian habitat on the northwest side of T1, 95 m on the southeast side of T1, and 133 m on the northeast side of Ditch 1 (D1). T1 eventually discharges into Holland Creek. The proposed development includes the subdivision of lots and a road right of way over T1 with culvert crossing to connect the lot parcels between Stage 6 and Stage 7. Under Section 11 of the Water Sustainability Act (WAS) a Change Approval and Notification (Changes In and About a Stream) was submitted to Forests, Lands and Natural Resource Operations (FLNRO) for a culvert crossing at T1 on April 30th, 2021; a Change Approval for the culvert installation was approved under Section 11 of the WSA and received on August 30th, 2021 (File 1005133). The majority of the proposed lots are slated for the construction of single-family residential homes, other portions will remain as greenspace or be used as road right of ways. The total area covered by housing footprints, access roads and other structures will not be available until the lots are registered, sold, and a building permit is applied for and approved. The Site Plan map is available in Section 3 of this report. T1 and D1 fall within the Development Permit Area (DPA) 6 of the Town of Ladysmith. A detailed Riparian Areas Protection Regulation (RAPR) is required to obtain a Development Permit (DP) for the proposed subdivision of lots, the proposed culvert crossing and road right of way, and construction of residential housing in Stage 6 and Stage 7. Recently site preparation activities including clearing vegetation occurred between 2020 and 2021, without an approved development permit in DPA 6. These activities occurred within the RAAs of T1 and D1 of Stage 6 and 7. A Condition and Impact Assessment (CIA) report was required to address the historically completed site preparation activities with further detailed measures to protect, maintain, and enhance the SPEA. The CIA report is attached to this detailed RAPR. This detailed RAPR with supporting reports/documents and CIA will be used as a planning document for the DP process with the Town of Ladysmith. This document sets the framework for SPEA protection, maintenance, and enhancement associated with the proposed development activities within Stage 6 and Stage 7. Description of Fisheries Resources Value A site visit was completed on the 1% of October 2021 with D.R. Clough Consulting. Stream and ditch survey data for this detailed RAPR assessment report for T1 and D1 was supplied by D.R. Clough Consulting. A second Site visit for the CIA was completed on the 24" of March 2022. The CIA Site inspection focused on assessing potential impacts to the SPEAs from unauthorized historical vegetation clearing in the RAA/DPA of Tributary 1 and D1 as well as identifying mitigation measures. Tributary 1 is a non fish tributary that flows into Holland Creek near the Dogwood Avenue bridge. T1 has had considerable disturbance and alteration of the channel within the proposed Form 1 Page 3 of 27 Page 322 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 323 FORM 1 Riparian Areas Protection Regulation - Qualified Environmental Professional - Assessment Report development areas and associated RAAs within Stage 6 and 7. The T1 channel is comprised of several reach segments: T1-R1, T1-R2, T1-R3. The proposed development area was logged in the past using clear-cut methods and allowed to regenerate naturally. There are active logging roads as well as abandoned roads that are completely grown in with trees. A mixture of regenerating Red Cedar, Douglas Fir, Red Alder and Broad Leaf Maple comprise the dominant tree species in the RAA as well as the total development area. No old growth trees were observed in the RAA. Extensive areas of the RAA were dominated by moss (in and near T1), salal and ferns as well as by weedy species such as Spurge-Laurel, Foxglove, Himalayan Blackberry, Canada Thistle, Queen Anne's Lace. In the lower reaches below the development area in Stage 6 and 7, the channel was historically redirected for logging, service of BC Hydro electrical lines, a water line corridor, as well as access for a garbage dump. In the upper reaches above the Stage 6 and 7 development area, the BC Hydro transmission line, Fortis Natural Gas line and forestry road corridors disrupted the channels with poorly located culverts or lack of culverts, alternate routes, drainage ditches and braiding. Reach 1 begins at the confluence with Holland Creek above an 8 m bedrock waterfall which flows year-round from ground water seepage and provides critical summer flow to Holland Creek. The reach is 370 m in length, has an average width of 2.17 m, and an average gradient of 9%. It is comprised of step pool complexes. Large woody debris is scattered throughout the reach, in channel and along the banks. This reach ends below the Stage 6 and 7 proposed development area. The lower portion of Reach 1 outside of the proposed development area has been developed under an earlier phase of works. The watercourse was culverted underneath a road right of way and runs along the side of the road heading north to Holland Creek. Reach 2 begins approximately at the downstream end of the proposed development for Stage 6 on the northwest bank, which coincides with a Hydro line crossing. Upstream on the east bank the proposed development for Stage 7 is present. This section is confined in a ravine for most of it's 320 m length. This reach also provides summer flow via groundwater seepage to Holland Creek. The average width of this reach is 2.86 m with a much steeper gradient of 21% when compared to Reach 1. It is comprised of step pool complexes. Large woody debris is scattered throughout the reach, in channel and along the banks. Reach 3 begins at the presence of unconfined channel and lower gradient near the proposed toad right of way on the property, which connects Stage 6 and Stage 7. The reach is 140 m in length, has an average width of 2.07 m, and an average gradient of 9%. This reach was significantly altered by historic logging activities and road building. It has seasonal flow and is fed by steep slopes and groundwater above the BC Hydro transmission line, Fortis Natural Gas line and forestry road corridors which have disturbed the capture of water for T1. There is ditching with recent machine maintenance where road runoff collects along the BC hydro line road and right of way that discharges into D1 and into T1-R3. Ditch 1 is a 120m long non fish bearing drainage. The ditch is manmade, it is a machine dug channel with segments along an old logging/skid road to accommodate runoff, it discharges into T1-R3. This waterway drains from the BC hydro line road and right of way which includes a Fortis Natural Gas line and forestry road corridors. This ditch and others were dug to accommodate logging and draining the BC hydro line road and right of way. It has ephemeral flow. The proposed development area is within the Coastal Douglas Fir Biogeoclimatic Zone which is a Red Listed Plant Community. No specific Red or Blue listed plants other than the CDF Community are found in the B.C. Government Ecosystem Explorer for this site. Coastal Cutthroat Form 1 Page 4 of 27 Page 323 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 324 FORM 1 Riparian Areas Protection Regulation - Qualified Environmental Professional - Assessment Report Trout and Red Legged Frogs are two provincial blue listed endangered species historically observed during previous studies’? around the lower fish bearing drainages. Fish Assessment T1 does not support anadromous or residential fish populations. It is located above the 8 m bedrock waterfall which acts as a fish barrier located at the confluence with Holland Creek. The steep gradients in Reach 2 and intermittently dry channel in Reach 1 eliminate the potential for resident fish. An electroshock of the wetted areas of the lower end of T1 in 2010 confirmed there were no fish®. Holland Creek, the downstream receiving waters from T1 is located outside of the proposed development area. The creek has perennial flow and anadromous fish access from its’ lower reaches to water falls upstream which act as a fish barrier. The creek supports a diverse mix of anadromous and resident fish species including cutthroat and rainbow trout along with chum and coho salmon‘. There has been enhancement of coho and chum salmon through small numbers of hatchery fry augmentation as well as extensive and successful habitat restoration with construction of four different off channel sites as well as much instream work to stabilize the banks and create fish habitat’. Comments Reach 1 begins at the confluence with Holland Creek above an 8 m bedrock waterfall which flows year-round from ground water seepage and provides critical summer flow to Holland Creek. The reach is 370 m in length, has an average width of 2.17 m, and an average gradient of 9%. It is comprised of step pool complexes. The lower portion of Reach 1 outside of the proposed development area has been developed under an earlier phase of works. The watercourse was culverted underneath a road right of way and runs along the side of the road heading north to Holland Creek. If a specific measure is not being recommendeda justification must be provided. 1. Danger Eleven trees were assessed as hazard trees and are recommended for removal Trees (falling into the SPEA). Where safe, high stumping is recommended to retain value for wildlife. Where not safe, consider retaining Coarse Woody Debris for SPEA to enhance biodiversity. Vegetation management and mitigation measures will be undertaken in multiple ways such as tree replacement planting and enhancement to bolster the vegetation in and around the SPEA which will increase biodiversity and habitat values. This is an extensive riparian area with potential for further danger trees over time, however the drainages are generally incised in SPEA areas putting the trees in the SPEA at lower elevations than potential building areas. As lots are sold, it is recommended that all houses and development be located to allow for setbacks away from the SPEA beyond the effect of potential new danger trees over time, as determined by a QEP under the new lot owner. Encroach | SPEA encroachment is a significant cause of riparian habitat loss and stream ment degradation. Plant disturbance and loss due to construction activities, dumping and yard waste, trampling due to hiking, and domesticated animals all contribute to riparian degradation. As plants and stream bank stabilization decrease due to disturbance, run off and siltation may occur harming the aquatic ecosystem including fish, their spawning gravels, and aquatic invertebrates (fish food sources). The developer understands that the access to SPEAs in the long term needs to be restricted. There should be no encroachment into SPEAs including any dwellings, clearings, people, domestic animals or vehicles. The SPEAS will be flagged and marked with signage along the lot boundaries asking that the public stay out of and respect the sensitive riparian habitat, as well as the potential for permanent fencing as a barrier. Property owners will be advised about SPEA locations on bills of sale with copies of the RAPR report. A qualified environmental professional will be retained as the environmental monitor by the developer. The environmental monitor will be available in the event significant rainfall, drainage problems, erosion and sediment control problems, and general project area wide conditions during emergency events. The qualified environmental professional will be experienced in sediment and erosion control measures, and will have the authority to shut down project area works if necessary to protect the SPEA. The qualified environmental professional will ensure all development activities remain outside of the SPEA, tree protection measures are being followed, fencing and sediment and erosion control measures are in working order, and storm water management structures are functioning correctly and all other relevant measures to protect are followed. Environmental monitoring is planned to protect the drainages, riparian areas, slope stability, and general condition of the proposed project area during clearing and grubbing activities and toad and property construction. Monitoring is to be completed weekly, or during key construction activities or extreme weather conditions (i.e. high rainfall). A post development environmental completion report is a required part of this permit to ensure all measures to protect were followed. This report is submitted to agencies as a final signoff. (TerraWest) was retained by Jim Dickinson and represented by GlenCar Consultants Inc. (the ‘Client') to complete a Condition and Impact Assessment (CIA) of the property located at the Stage 6 and 7 area of Holland Creek Estates development in Ladysmith, BC, herein referred to as the ‘Subject Property’ and/or the ‘Site’. Activities conducted within the defined Site boundaries are herein referred to as “on-Site”. 2.0 Background Prior to the initiation of development activities on the Subject Property, the Client obtained a Qualified Environmental Professional (QEP) to complete a Riparian Areas Regulation (RAR) assessment in 2014. The RAR report (no. 3279A) was completed and notification of approval was received by the Town of Ladysmith on November 26", 2014 from Forests, Lands and Natural Resource Operations (FLNRO) of British Columbia. The Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA), for the Site was determined to be 10m for Tributary 1, Reach 1, 2 and 3 (T1-R1, T1-R2 and T1-R3), and 2m for the associated Ditches (D1, D2, and D3). The Client was given verbal approval from BC Hydro to complete maintenance and repair the ditch line along the BC hydro line road and right of way. This maintenance was completed off Site, south of Stage 6 and 7. Current runoff Environmental Management and Consulting Page 348 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 349 Zg \/ Condition and Impact Assessment Holland Creek Partnership TerraWest Project: JDHC22-02 Page 2 of 8 collected along the BC hydro line road and right of way discharges solely into D3 (D1 under the 2021 RAPR), and into Tributary 1. Under Section 11 of the Water Sustainability Act (WAS) a Change Approval and Notification (Changes In and About a Stream) was submitted to FLNRO for a culvert crossing on Tributary 1 to connect Stage 6 and 7 on April 30t, 2021; a Change Approval for the culvert installation was approved under Section 11 of the WSA and received on August 30', 2021 (File 1005133). Based on the results and previous approval of the 2014 detailed riparian assessment, the verbal approval from BC Hydro for road water management ditching activities on their right of way, and the Change Approval from FLNRO for the culvert installation on Tributary 1, the Client completed Site preparation activities. These activities occurred within the Development Permit Area (DPA) 6 prior to the acquisition of a relevant Development Permit (DP) from the Town of Ladysmith. The Client was under the impression that the 2014 RAR was still applicable and thus the Change Approval from FLNRO was as well to the current proposed road right of way subdivision and for the proposed subdivision of lots and construction of residential housing on the Site; and that conducting clearing activities in the Riparian Assessment Areas (RAAs) but outside of the SPEAs, with the exception of the Tributary 1 crossing as per the Section 11 approval, was acceptable. The Client was also under the impression since road ditching was changed along the BC Hydro right of way and D1 was redirected off Site into D3, D1 was no longer a functional ditch within the Site and subsequently was cleared. TerraWest was retained by the Client in October of 2021 to complete a new detailed assessment under the current Riparian Areas Protection Regulation (RAPR) due to the time lapsed from the original RAR in 2014. RAR/RAPR as of the updated 2019 Riparian Areas Protection Regulation now expire within five years of which a copy of the report is provided to the local government. Due to the fact Site preparation activities within the RAAs of Stage 6 and 7 occurred between 2020 and 2021, more than five years after the 2014 RAR, and prior to the Site assessment and submission of the current 2021 RAPR or the acquisition of a DP, a Condition and Impact Assessment (CIA) was required to address the historically completed site preparation activities. The local government, being the Town of Ladysmith, is required to review and approve this CIA. Once written approval of the CIA is obtained by the Town of Ladysmith, both documents will be submitted as attachments along with the updated RAPR to the province. Once the RAPR package is approved by the province it will be used to assist in the Development Permit application and approval process through the Town of Ladysmith prior to any new development on Site. The 2021 RAPR was carried out identifying a tributary and a ditch on the Site, RAA/DPA and SPEA boundaries are identified in the RAPR and shown on the Site Plan where determined, see Appendix A. Tributary 1 and Ditch 1 boundary locations and development boundaries were based on previous surveys supplied by the Client's current contractor Bennett Land Surveying (Coastal) Ltd. Environmental Management and Consulting Page 349 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 350 Zg \/ Condition and Impact Assessment Holland Creek Partnership TerraWest Project: JDHC22-02 Page 3 of 8 3.0 Riparian Impact Assessment This CIA outlines the historical disturbance that has occurred inside the RAA/DPA of Tributary 1 and D1. With an approved Section 11 Notification for culvert installation and road construction the CIA generally does not include clearing inside a road right of way, however it is provided here for context. Aerial photos in Appendix B show the progression of historical development activities in and around the Subject Property. Vegetation clearing on Site within the SPEA has occurred, clearing was only observed to be within the surveyed road right of way of Tributary 1. The clearing was completed as part of the approved Section 11 works for the culvert installation and construction of road crossing on Tributary 1 in order to connect Stage 6 and 7. The Subject Property has had site preparation activities including vegetation clearing occur inside the RAA/DPA of Tributary 1 as well as D1, however the SPEA remained intact as confirmed during the detailed 2021 RAPR field assessment and March 24th, 2022 CIA Site inspection; see March 24th, 2022 Site photos in Appendix C. The CIA Site inspection focused on assessing potential impacts to the SPEAs from unauthorized historical vegetation clearing in the RAA/DPA of Tributary 1 and D1 as well as identifying mitigation measures. RARP reports are to be submitted and approved prior to development activities inside RAA/DPA areas. This ensures appropriate measures will be set up and in place to protect SPEAs prior to development activities. It is important to protect the biological functions of the SPEAs associated with the different Zones of Sensitivity (ZOS). The ZOS within the SPEA provides benefit to fish and fish habitat by way of Large Woody Debris/Bank Stability, Litter Fall and Insect Drop, and Shade. Each of the ZOS are determined by field measurements based on the application of current RAPR methodology. Based on the current RAPR methodology the SPEAs of Tributary 1 (10m) and D1 (2m) were determined. 4.0 SPEA Protective Measures 4.1. Danger Trees and Windthrow A windthrow and hazard tree assessment of the Site was completed by Strathcona Forestry Consulting in October 2021. The assessment was prompted due to the clearing of vegetation and removal of trees outside of the determined SPEA but within the RAA/DPA areas along Tributary 1 and D1 of Site. The clearing activities created an exposed tree line along the edge of the SPEA. Forest cover on Site along the east and west sides of Tributary 1 was assessed, resulting in a moderate windthrow risk classification. The eastern portion of the RAA is windward to prevailing winds, and more prone to wind damage. There were no observations of windthrow during the Site assessment, however observations of some trees along the SPEA edge indicated signs of physical damage. The damage most likely was the result of previous land clearing in the RAA/DPA. Environmental Management and Consulting Page 350 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 351 TerraWest Project: JDHC22-02 Page 4 of 8 Hazard mitigation was recommended for hazard trees, identified hazard trees have defects which could increase susceptibility to wind damage. Hazard trees pose a risk to workers, future residents/homes, and increased fire risk. The assessment resulted in eleven (11) trees assessed as hazard trees. Best management for these trees is determined to be removal (directional falling into the SPEA). Where determined safe, high stumping is recommended to retain value for wildlife, and where determined not safe consider retaining for Coarse Woody Debris within the SPEA for enhanced biodiversity. Tree replacement is to occur for each hazard tree that is slated for removal as part of enhancing a remediating the SPEA. Implementation of mitigative actions will be overseen by a QEP (e.g., hazard tree treatment and remediation of the SPEA) as discussed in the windthrow and hazard tree assessment with recommended guidelines in conjunction with the provincial RAR Revegetation Guidelines will yield a net environmental improvement. In the case of needing to replace trees, BC provincial criteria must be followed for tree replacement as per the guidelines below. ¢ Omm- 151 mm (6") dbh 2 replacement trees (min height 1.5 m), or, 4 shrubs (for up to 50% of trees being replaced in this range); e =152 mm - 304mm (12") dbh 3 replacement trees (min height 1.5 m); e 305mm - 456mm (18") dbh 4 replacement trees (min height 2.0 m); e 457mm - 60? mm (24") dbh_ 6 replacement trees (min height >" 2.0 m); e 610mm -914mm (36") dbh 8 replacement trees (min height > 2.0 m) o Trees > 914 mm dbh (36") will require individual approval and replacement criteria prior to removal. o Every effort must be made to retain 20% of trees > 304 mm dbh (12") as wildlife snags at minimum height of 3 m. If the measures identified in the windthrow and hazard tree assessment are followed and implemented by the developer to protect the integrity of the SPEA and surrounding riparian habitat, it is determined there will be no harmful alteration, disruption or destruction of natural features, functions and conditions that support fish life processes in (and/or downstream of) the riparian assessment area. 4.2 Slope Stability Previous land clearing activities in the affected RAA/DPA have not resulted in impacts related to slope stability. 4.3 Protection of Trees It is important to take steps and protect trees within the SPEA as they can be damaged by construction activities taking place on adjacent land outside of the SPEA. Tree roots may extend outwards from their base to multiple times their own height, thus making them susceptible even if ground disturbance is outside the SPEA. In addition, the Environmental Management and Consulting Page 351 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 352 Zg \/ Condition and Impact Assessment Holland Creek Partnership TerraWest Project: JDHC22-02 Page $ of 8 operation of heavy equipment close to the SPEA has the potential to cause damage to trees. Indirect impacts may also occur over the rooting zone in the form of paving or altering the ground level under trees. Observations during the windthrow and hazard tree assessment of some trees along the SPEA edge, outside the surveyed road right of way of Tributary 1, indicated some signs of physical damage. The damage most likely was the result of previous land clearing in the RAA/DPA. There has been no apparent deep excavations or large soil moving activities (only clearing and grubbing observed), inside the affected RAA/DPA areas on Site which suggests the tree drip zones have most likely been maintained. To protect the trees from harm a 7.5m drip zone beyond the marked SPEA is to be implemented to protect the tree roots as well as the placement of fencing along SPEA buffers. Activities that must not take place near SPEA trees are: significant changes to ground level, release of pollutants, moving equipment, parking or storing construction equipment. A QEP will observe for compliance during development inspections and any other practices that may impact SPEA tree health. Removal of any danger trees in the SPEA will require the services of a professional danger tree assessor. Work identified as being harmful to the SPEA but not within such as excavation, clearing, erection of permanent structures has to be done in such a way to protect the SPEA trees from harm. The approved Section 11 Notification for culvert installation and road construction in this CIA generally does not include clearing inside a road right of way, however it is provided here for context. The SPEA conditions prior to clearing were observed during a previous breeding bird nest survey conducted on March 23’, 2021 for D.R. Clough Consulting by TerraWest Environmental. The SPEA conditions prior to vegetation removal were consistent with the current upstream/downstream right/left bank SPEA habitat on Site. TerraWest Environmental was not involved in assessing the culvert crossing location and road right of way for mitigation methods and submission of the Section 11 application. The clearing inside of the designed road right of way appears to conform to the Site plans, it is unknown how many trees were removed during the clearing activities from the SPEA. The clearing works has not appeared to have impacted the upstream/downstream, right/left bank trees growing adjacent in the SPEA. The currently approved Section 11 Notification for culvert installation and road construction was received on August 30'", 2021 (File 1005133). 4.4 Encroachment SPEA encroachment is a significant cause of riparian habitat loss and stream degradation. Plant disturbance and loss due to construction activities, dumping and yard waste, trampling due to hiking, and domesticated animals all contribute to riparian degradation. As plants and stream bank stabilization decrease due to disturbance, run off and siltation may occur harming the aquatic ecosystem including fish, their spawning Environmental Management and Consulting Page 352 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 353 Zg \/ Condition and Impact Assessment Holland Creek Partnership TerraWest Project: JDHC22-02 Page 6 of 8 gravels, and aquatic invertebrates (fish food sources). Apart from the clearance of vegetation as part of the yet to come Culvert installation and road construction on Tributary 1, there has been no other observed SPEA encroachment based on the 2021 Detailed RAPR Assessment. Unauthorized encroachment into the RAA/DPA areas on Site have occurred which is the trigger for this CIA. In order to prevent any further encroachment into the RAA/DPA 30m setback, as shown on the Site Plan, high visibility orange “snow fencing” must be erected and maintained along the RAA/DPA extant. Currently snow fencing is erected along the northwest RAA Tributary 1 boundary within Stage 6, as well as at the clearing boundaries of the road right of way over Tributary 1. Snow fencing was not erected along the southeast RAA Tributary 1/D1 boundary within Stage 7; however this was deemed acceptable based on no further works taking place in the area. No further clearing or grubbing has been or will be completed in Stage 6 or 7 until an approved DP from the Town of Ladysmith is in place. A QEP will perform a Site visit to confirm the snow fencing has been erected. Disturbance within the RAA/DPA will only be permitted upon approval of the Detailed Assessment submitted under RAPR and successfully obtaining a development permit from the Town of Ladysmith. The developer understands that the access to SPEAs in the long term needs to be restricted. There should be no encroachment into SPEAs including any dwellings, clearings, people, domestic animals or vehicles. The SPEAS will be flagged and marked with signage along the lot boundaries asking that the public stay out of and respect the sensitive riparian habitat, as well as the potential for permanent fencing as a barrier. Property owners will be advised about SPEA locations on bills of sale with copies of the RAPR report. Even though the Change Approval and Notification (Changes In and About a Stream) was submitted to FLNRO for the culvert crossing on Tributary 1 to connect Stage 6 and 7 on April 30%, 2021; and a Change Approval for the culvert installation was approved under Section 11 of the WSA and received on August 30", 2021 (File 1005133), the Town of Ladysmith requires that these activities only proceed after obtaining an approved DP. The approved Section 11 activities involve the installation of a culvert on Tributary 1 to allow for road construction in the road right of way. These construction activities involve SPEA encroachment as permitted under the approved Section 11 (File 1005133). 4.5 Erosion and Sediment Control (ESC) SPEA areas and stream channels must be protected from the proposed property developments from erosion and sediment issues. An erosion and sediment control plan by Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. was developed and implemented in 2021 for Stage 5 and 6 of the Site which had been cleared and grubbed in the RAA/DPA; Stage 7 of the Site is currently only cleared within the RAA/DPA. Stage 7 ground conditions were left rough after tree clearing within the RAA/DPA, with stumps left in place, woody debris left on the ground, and shrubs/herbs present. This ground cover is currently acting as a form sediment and erosion control, decreasing the chance of sedimentation and runoff Environmental Management and Consulting Page 353 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 354 Zg \/ Condition and Impact Assessment Holland Creek Partnership TerraWest Project: JDHC22-02 Page 7 of 8 leading downslope into Tributary 1. Prior to development activities in Stage 7, an erosion and sediment control plan must be completed, and once activities begin it must be implemented. A QEP will complete Site inspections to ensure the implementation of erosion and sediment control measure are correctly in place and maintained. Further guidance on sediment and erosion control as land clearing and development occurs can be taken from the Develop With Care - Environmental Guidelines for Urban and Rural Land Development in B.C. Best Management. 4.6 Stormwater Management The majority of the RAA/DPA area around Tributary 1 and D1 consists low lying vegetation in Stage 7 and bare soil in Stage 6 and is considered raw and undeveloped. Clearing activities within the RAA/DPA have not appeared to cause increases in stormwater runoff into the SPEA and subsequently Tributary 1 or D1. The future development of the Site must ensure that runoff patterns and water quality are not altered. Impermeable surfaces increase stormwater runoff and could impact Tributary 1 and D1 if not managed correctly. Site servicing and stormwater management plans were prepared by Newcastle Engineering Ltd. for the Site. Further guidance and practices as lots are developed can be found in the publication; Stormwater Planning; A Guide for British Columbia. 4.7 Floodplain Concerns Clearing activities withing the RAA/DPA of Tributary 1 and D1 have not been observed to cause concerns related to floodplains. 5.0 Closure The unauthorized clearing activities that occurred without an approved Development Permit from the Town of Ladysmith on Site within the RAA/DPAs associated with Tributary 1 and D1, appear to have had very little, if any effect on their associated SPEAs. As discussed in Section 4.4, activities involving SPEA encroachment did occur as permitted under the approved Section 11 (File 1005133), which involved vegetation clearing in preparation for the installation of a culvert on Tributary 1 to allow for road construction in the road right of way. However even though an approved Section 11 was obtained clearing activities were completed again prior to receiving an approved Development Permit. It is imperative that this CIA along with the current RAPR are approved by local and provincial government prior to any further disturbances or works within the RAA/DPA areas on Site. One immediate requirement that must be met is the installation of further snow fencing and the maintenance of currently installed snow fencing for the identification of the RAA/DPA 30m boundary on Site. A follow up Site visit will be Environmental Management and Consulting Page 354 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 355 \; Condition and impact Assessment Hollond Creek Partnership Terrawest Project: JOHC22-02 Page 8 of8 completed to ensure the fencing has been placed in the correct locations and no further disturbances have occurred withing the RAA/DPA. We trust this meets your requirements, and if there are any questions regarding the above please do not hesitate to contact the undersigned below. Environmental Management and Consulting Page 367 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 368 D. R. Clough Consulting Fisheries Resource Consultants 6966 Leland Road Lantzville B.C. VOR 2HO Ph/Fax: 250-390-2901 Cell: 250-714-5416 email:drclough@shaw.ca March 20, 2013 Attn: 0885538BC Ltd and Stzuminus First Nation c/o Glenn Carey, Project Manager 6774 Dickinson Road Nanaimo, BC V9V 1A2 Ph: 250-390-1475 email:s.22 RE: Holland Creek Watershed, Ladysmith B.C. Environmental Assessment Introduction: In the proposal for the development on property on the south side of Holland Creek we were asked to provide a preliminary Biological assessment during the winter. The objectives of the assessment were to determine; 1.) Stream and drainage mapping: There are two unnamed drainages as well as Heart Creek and Holland Creek in the development area. We will identify the location in the field with flagging and GPS the location of the unnamed drainages for upload files preliminary planning maps. 2.) Stream Fish Habitat values: The streams will be assessed with a standard fish habitat assessment to determine the physical status of the channel as well as potential for fish presence and type. Po Inspect the proposed bridge crossing area on Heart Creek. Consultation: The importance of this watershed to Stzuminus First Nations, Ladysmith Sportsmen Club and Town of Ladysmith will result in consultation to determine their interest and input in fisheries values. There will be a site visit and meeting to explain findings and listen to concerns. Methods Stream mapping Brad Remillard, RPBio and Dave Clough, RPBio undertook the stream channel assessments in January and February 2013. We began at either the top or bottom of the major drainages and flagged stations and tributaries as we inspected the channels for habitat characteristics. Hand held Garmin (450) GPS was used with a cellular GPS application (Everytrail) and a photo and location reference as well. GPS data was edited on Garmin Mapsource software and uploaded to Google Earth for display. The survey area is bounded by Holland Creek on the north east and the Hydro line on the south west. Stream Habitat Each stream was inspected bya biologist for fish habitat suitability. Fish habitat features such as barriers, rearing and spawning habitat as well as flow regimes were analyzed. We also referred to past fish presence information from past electroshock surveys and information from local stream stewardship groups. Holland Ck Lot 103 Biological Assessment DRCMar13.doc 1 Page 368 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 369 Bridge Site Inspection The general area (taken from the preliminary mapping) suggested approximately 100m of area along Heart Creek. This area was walked to determine the best site based on a narrow confined channel that would result in least impact to fish habitat values. Consultation The Stzuminus First Nation was consulted at their bad office on January 27, 2013 to discuss the development and the possibility of a fish hatchery. The Ladysmith Sportsmen attended on-site tour with the proponent and a follow up inspection of hatchery locations on the 27" of February. Results Study Area Overview; Holland Creek is a salmon and trout stream its entire length adjacent the subject property. The salmon swim upstream under the E&N Railway culvert adjacent the island Highway Bridge then upstream approximately 400m inside the Holland Creek Park to the Dogwood Avenue Bridge. To this point the river is heavily utilized by Chum salmon spawners in October and November. The river then continues upstream past the Lot 103 tributaries in a confined valley. Salmon access lives approximately 1.8km above Dogwood Avenue at Crystal falls, a 10m bedrock barrier. The reach above Dogwood is used by Coho spawners as well as Cutthroat. Crystal Falls is the first of many in a long (8.5 km) steep climb up to Holland Lake (670m elev.). There are resident Cutthroat trout and Rainbow Trout above the falls to Holland Lake. Holland Lake is impounded and used as part of the Town of Ladysmith water supply (Company Dam). Holland Creek is protected by a second growth forest that is 30 to 100m in width on each side to the park boundaries and beyond. The forest was logged; the stumps show it was historically dominated by Douglas Fir with Red Cedar near the water. The forest is regenerating with those species as well as Red Alder, Broad Leaf Maple and many shrub species including Willow, Indian Plum, Ocean Spray, Salmonberry, Sword Fern and Blackberry. There are a few veteran Douglas Fir in the forest. This same forest type extends upland into Lot 103 area with the largest trees found in the Heart Creek valley. Lot 103 also has many polygons of younger stands of trees just emerging from the brush as well as a recent logging above either side of Heart Creek. The Holland Creek foot trail encircles the creek on both sides, with a bridge over each of the Lot 103 tributaries near their entrance to Holland Creek. The Hydro line provides the southwest boundary to the property and Holland Creek/Heart Creek are on the northeast boundary of the lot. The Holland Creek watershed has seen a concerted effort of salmon enhancement and habitat restoration over the last 20 years. There are now hundreds of pieces of wood debris placed for fish habitat. Four sidechannel areas have been dug out in the lower reaches increasing the summer wetted habitat and winter flood refuge significantly in Holland Creek. This work has been done bya partnership led by the Ladysmith Sportsmen Club working with Stzuminus First Nation Fisheries Program and Town of Ladysmith. There is a hatchery on Bush Creek that incubates approximately 15,000 coho fry and 50,000 Chum fry from this creek annually. There are plans to consider relocation of the Bush Creek hatchery to Holland Creek due to the better water quality, easier access and safety. Assessment results are presented overleaf with a Map, and Photos for each drainage. Stream Mapping/Fish Habitat Streams were at medium to high flow levels during the survey allowing for identification of the mainstems as well as smaller tributaries. There are three Holland Creek tributaries that drain the proposed development area; Tributary 1, 2 and Heart Creek respectively from downstream to up (Figure 1). Holland Ck Lot 103 Biological Assessment DRCMar13.doc 2 Page 369 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 370 Tributaries 1 and 2 are unnamed drainages that enter Holland Creek over bedrock water falls (5m) with no fish access. Table 1) Holland Creek Lot 103 Fish Habitat Summary. Drainage Fish Access/Habitat Holland Creek Yes Tributary 1 No Tributary 2 No Heart Creek Yes Tributary 1 The mainstem is 830 m long through the property from the hydro line to Holland Creek. It enters over a 5m bedrock falls just north of the Dogwood Avenue Bridge parking lot. The channel is approximately 2.1m wide. The lower reach to the first hydro line (200m) is relatively low gradient at 4-11%. This reach appears to have been diverted from its historic route as the channel has evidence of recent formation with no natural stream characteristics. It was likely diverted west to make way for Dogwood Avenue. Above the old Hydro right of way the channel appears natural but disturbed by historic logging lacking large woody debris. The channel gradient increases to more than 20% and is confined in a small valley with vegetated sidewalls to just below (150m) the Hydro Line where it is fed by three seasonal channels T1, T1-2, T1-3, that braid across the Hydro Line. The channel furthest north is the strongest (T1). The Hydro Line and logging roads appear to have disrupted the natural course in this area such that the historical location is difficult to determine above the split in channels. There is no fish access into this channel. An electroshock in 2010 found no fish in the 200 m along the lower reach where the gradient is less than 20%. The tributary has perennial water flow to Holland Creek. Tributary 2 The main channel of Tributary 2 is 930m long upstream Hydro line crossing. It has two short tributaries (2B, 2C,) that enter it within the Lot 103 area. Beginning at Holland Creek there is a 4.5m bedrock falls that denies fish access. Upstream this channel was disturbed by historic logging lacking pools and large woody debris. It lies in a semi-confined channel with vegetated sidewalls. The creek channel is 1.7m wide in the lower reach on a gradient of 1-7% above the barrier. It loses its confinement at the Hydro line crossing where it is dry in summer. Water flow is perennial to Holland Creek and in summer this water accrues below the hydro line. Heart Creek This is the longest and largest tributary with length of 1.2 km from the Hydro line to Holland Creek. Heart Creek has a 240m long reach of salmon access, ending at a 5m bedrock water falls. Above the falls there is a confined and deep (20-50m) treed valley that creates an isolated reach of Heart Creek to the Hydro Line where the canyon ends. The average channel width was 4.1m on a 10% slope. Heart Creek goes approximately 1.0 km further upstream to its source at Heart Lake. The entire length of Heart Creek is habitat for resident Cutthroat & Rainbow Trout which occupy the lake as well as perennial pockets in the lower reach. The fish are seeded into the entire length of the stream from Heart Lake. The upper reaches above the Hydro line are more disturbed by historic logging and are seasonal while below the Hydro line, there is flow recovery in summer with perennial flow into Holland Creek. Heart Creek Bridge Site Inspection The mid reach of Heart Creek is the location of a proposed road location. We inspected the stream channel widths in this area and found the channel width and floodplain ranged between 5.0 and 6.3m. The cross section sites were flagged in the field as XS (see Fig.1). The valley walls in the area were 25% slope on the south and 50% slope on a 10m bank on the north side. There were no significant fish habitat features in the area, pools were shallow and the channel had little LWD. The banks were steep but Holland Ck Lot 103 Biological Assessment DRCMar13.doc 3 Page 370 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 371 vegetated and stable. The stream substrates are Boulder/Cobble/Gravel. There were no significant veteran trees in the vicinity. Consultation/Planning for Hatchery Ladysmith Sportsmen Club operate the Bush Creek Hatchery. They built the hatchery with the full support of the Stzuminus First Nation in 1995 after both parties agreed there was a local need. Since then there has been a shared use of the facility. The hatchery enhances Chum and Coho stocks in five local streams; Stocking, Holland, Bush, Walker and the Chemainus River. They have 10 heath stacks and a capacity for 400,000 eggs. Over the years since the hatchery was developed the water quality in Bush Creek has declined. The gravity fed water is colder, carries more sediment and dries to a trickle in early summer. The water supply plugged this year and the eggs were all transported to Nanaimo Hatchery by the club in January. The hatchery also has no electrical power other than a generator so the alarm and fish feeders work off solar power. Its remote location 2.5 km up a logging road has resulted in vandalism and robbery constantly. The new location is next to town and walking distance from local schools allowing the education programs conducted by the Club to expand. The new building may have a classroom for workshops and school programs. The developers of the property have offered their land for a hatchery at a time when the operators of the hatchery were considering relocation. Consultation meetings have been held this winter, the relocation was discussed by both groups, and they walked the sites. There is an opportunity to use T1 and T2 as well as Heart Creek which all have flowing water year round. An inspection this winter found the water temperatures to be 1-3C warmer than Bush Creek which hasa significant effect on egg development timing. The Holland Creek hatchery idea was taken to the DFO Community Programs Community Advisor for advice and permitting. This permit will require a more detailed design to identify the flow and space requirements. CONCLUSIONS The assessment of the drainages was made to determine preliminary planning for a residential development. No lot or road determinations are finalized. The developer had instructed us to provide this environmental information such that they could plan around the environmental aspects. The environmental aspects of this area show Tributary 1 and 2 to be lacking fish access but important water supplies to Holland Creek. The summer water flow contribution of these two streams is approximately 25%. Heart Creek is a fish bearing channel which has a salmon reach to the base of the falls and is populated with resident trout above. Heart Creek is protected by a deep treed ravine which provides shade and habitat to the stream. The T1 and T2 channels are confined or semi-confined in treed depressions. To determine the riparian setback of these channels a Riparian Area Assessment (RAR) will need to be done. The RAR identifies the requirement for building setbacks as well as stormwater management, construction environmental protection as well as Danger Trees, Windthrow, Floodplain, Slope Stability, and Tree Protection. The development of the hatchery will follow a series of regulatory steps, which are out of the control of the proponents but the DFO are indicating their support (they haven't said no) and they should be able to assist in getting the approvals from their auditors and provincial agencies. Prepared by: Strathcona Forestry Consulting PO Box 387 Stn Mn Duncan BC V9L 3X5 strathcona.fc@shaw.ca 24 October 2021 Hoe Pes Page 377 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 378 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Executive Summary Strathcona Forestry Consulting was retained by Jim Dickenson, property owner, c/o Glenn Carey, Project Manager, GlenCar Consultants Inc., to prepare a_windthrow and hazard tree assessment of the riparian area at Stages 6 & 7 of the Holland Creek Partnership. Stages 6 & 7 comprise residential lots being developed on Colonia Drive, off Rollie Rose Drive, in Ladysmith, B.C. The development straddles Tributary 1 of Holland Creek. The RARP (Riparian Areas Protection Regulation) Project lead is Derek Nickel RPBio at Terra West Environmental Inc. The Riparian Assessment Area (RAA) boundary is 30m; the Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA) is 10 m forTributary 1 and 2 m for Ditch 1. Boundaries were determined by TerraWest Environmental Inc., D.R.Clough Consulting, and Bennett Land Surveying (Coastal) Ltd. A Post-Clearing Tree Risk Assessment conducted by Vancouver Island Tree Service in July 2021 identified trees deemed to have an elevated likelihood of failure. The purpose of this report is to determine whether there are windthrow concerns within and adjacent to the SPEA as a result of the proposed development, and, where necessary, to prescribe windthrow protection measures. Forest cover at two edge segments (east and west sides of Tributary 1) was assessed. Windthrow risk at was rated MODERATE. Likelihood of windthrow was rated MODERATE. The eastern portion of the RAA is windward to prevailing winds, and more prone to wind damage; both the windward and leeward segments contained hazardous trees. Eleven trees, including eight (8) big-leaf maples, were identified as hazard trees. Recommended hazard mitigation comprises felling (including options for high stumping and/or retention of coarse woody debris) and coppicing (maple). Coppicing will reduce tree height and remove any dangerous limbs, while encouraging lateral branching. High stumping will retain perching and nesting sites, while also providing opportunities for installing nesting boxes and bat boxes. Planting with ecologically suitable native trees and shrubs is recommended to rehabilitate the SPEA. Page 378 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 379 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Treatment to prevent windthrow should follow standard strategies to minimize disturbance to rooting layers during clearing and construction, including not creating windthrow, protecting trees in the SPEA (especially along the SPEA boundary), and retaining wildlife trees in the SPEA. Measures to avoid disturbance to existing trees will decrease potential for additional hazard trees, enhance biodiversity, and help to maintain a carbon sink. If the measures identified in this report to protect the integrity of the SPEA and surrounding riparian habitat are implemented by the developer, there will be no harmful alteration, disruption or destruction of natural features, functions and conditions that support fish life processes downstream of the riparian assessment area. Mitigative actions (treatment of hazardous trees and remediation of the SPEA) will yield a net environmental improvement. Recommended strategies will enhance local biodiversity of both riparian and upland forest areas by increasing resiliency. Additionally, if the recommendations contained in this report are followed during planning and construction, risks associated with windthrow and hazard trees can be mitigated to reduce long-term maintenance while also enhancing safety within and surrounding the riparian forest stand. Page 379 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 380 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Introduction Strathcona Forestry Consulting was retained by Jim Dickenson, property owner, c/o Glenn Carey, Project Manager, GlenCar Consultants Inc., to prepare a windthrow and hazard tree assessment at Stages 6 & 7 of the Holland Creek Partnership. Stages 6 & 7 comprise residential lots being developed on Colonia Drive, off Rollie Rose Drive, in Ladysmith, B.C. Tributary 1 of Holland Creek flows northeast between Stages 6 & 7. The RARP Project lead is Derek Nickel RPBio at Terra West Environmental Inc. The Riparian Assessment Area (RAA) boundary is 30m; the Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA) is 10 m forTributary 1 and 2 m for Ditch 1. Boundaries were determined by TerraWest Environmental Inc., D.R.Clough Consulting, and Bennett Land Surveying (Coastal) Ltd. A Post-Clearing Tree Risk Assessment conducted by Vancouver Island Tree Service in July 2021 identified five (5) big leaf maple trees “deemed to have an elevated likelihood of failure, and which pose an unacceptable level of risk to proposed structures and dwellings.” The report recommended that these (5) trees be removed to mitigate the risk. The report also noted that large maples at the north-east side of the development (bottom of the slope) should be pruned to remove any large diameter deadwood from the canopy. The purpose of this report is to determine whether there are windthrow concerns within and adjacent to the SPEA as a result of the proposed development, and, where necessary, to prescribe windthrow protection measures. The intent is to maintain tree cover where safely possible in conjunction with the planned development. The Riparian Area is to be dedicated to the Town of Ladysmith as parkland. Riparian Areas Protection Regulation The Riparian Areas Protection Regulation (RAPR) defines “stream” to encompass any watercourse — natural or human-made-—that provides fish habitat, contains water on a perennial or seasonal basis, is scoured by water or contains observable deposits of mineral alluvium, and has a continuous channel bed, including a watercourse that is Page 380 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 381 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting obscured by overhanging or bridging vegetation or soil mats. A watercourse may not itself be inhabited by fish, but may provide water, food and nutrients to streams that do support fish. Under the Riparian Areas Regulation, a proponent must prepare a Riparian Assessment report in support of their application to local government for development approval if development is proposed within 30 m of a stream or the top of a ravine bank of a stream. The Assessment Report must be prepared by a Qualified Environmental Professional (or group of professionals) who understands the interaction of various features, functions, and conditions of riparian areas. The RAR Assessment Report prescribes the specific requirements of the SPEA (streamside protection and enhancement area) and ZOS (zone of sensitivity). The width of the SPEA, determined through appropriate methodology, outlines required measures to maintain the integrity of the SPEA. The ZOS, determined through detailed assessment procedures under the RAR, identifies a zone of sensitivity adjacent to a waterbody within which disturbance is restricted, i.e., an undisturbed riparian buffer. The effects of the biophysical processes through which riparian vegetation influences in stream conditions vary continuously with buffer width. Under the RAPR, a fixed buffer width is generally selected in order to maintain in stream conditions similar to those found in undisturbed forests, and/or to target specific species such as salmonid fishes. Specific experts (i.e., geotechnical advisors, windthrow specialists) may be called on to provide their relative expertise on site characteristics that may pose specific problems or concerns. The Riparian Assessment report for the proposal must demonstrate appropriate assessment methods have been followed, and must certify: |. if the development is implemented as proposed there will be no harmful alteration, disruption, or destruction of natural features, functions, and conditions that support fish life processes in the riparian assessment area, or ll. if the streamside protection and enhancement areas identified in the report are protected from the development and the measures identified in the report as necessary to protect the integrity of those areas from the effects of the development are implemented by the developer, there will be no harmful alteration, disruption or destruction of natural features, functions and conditions that support fish life processes in the riparian assessment area Page 381 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 382 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Next pages: Holland Creek RAR and Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek Partnership Page 382 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 383 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting SKETCH PLAN TO ACCOMPANY RIPARIAN AREAS PROTECTION REGULATION REPORT FOR STAGE 6 AND STAGE 7 OF HOLLAND CREEK HOLLAND CREEK ‘ra Ps hows TH LOCATION OF LE FEATURES CRY, WO DOES HOT IRscaTe oreeo CENAES Tat HAY ENT ON OR ARON To DORSET ‘commen comecr bennett o {ano SURVEWING (COASTAN LTD. tsar omeer eae weer Seoevemn co a Roma commen ATES STANT SS SO ORAS ESP SETONESER TORT Ts POUANO REAR) ET IONS Holland Creek RAR. ROLLIE ROSE DRIVE A PART oF LOT ‘terme A BLOCK 28 cor ses ovata Stage 7 (bolded) Map provided by client Oct. 2021 Page 384 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 385 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Stage 6 (bolded) Map provided by client Oct. 2021 Page 385 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 386 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Stage 5 PLA (bolded) Map provided by client Oct. 2021 10 Page 386 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 387 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Site Description Stages 6 & 7 are located on the upper slope of Colonia Drive, approximately 1 km south of the centre of Ladysmith town centre, and 0.5 km west of the TransCanada Highway (Highway 1). To the west are cleared areas with new and future residential development, to the south (upslope) is a BC Hydro right-of-way; immediately to the northeast is forest, while further to the northeast is established residential development along Dogwood Drive and Arbutus Crescent. To the east is mature forest (scheduled for future development). The SPEA is dedicated to the Town of Ladysmith for parkland. Signs of previous human activities (e.g. historical logging) were evidenced by a brushed- in, old skid trail and partially buried choker cables. The Town of Ladysmith does not have a Tree Protection bylaw. Water Courses Tributary 1 of Holland Creek flows northeast between Stages 6 & 7 and discharges into Holland Creek, which discharges into Ladysmith Harbour, less than a kilometre to the northeast. Biogeoclimatic Classification The subject site is classified in the Coastal Douglas-fir Moist Maritime Subzone (CDFmm). The CDFmm has warm dry summers and moist mild winters. Prevailing winds in winter are generally southeasterly (to southwesterly). Ecosystems in the assessed area were classified as CDFmm_04/05/01. Vegetation The SPEA is forested with mature to maturing second-growth forest cover. Forest cover is “mixed” — with coniferous and deciduous trees. Coniferous trees dominate - mainly Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga heterophylla), with lesser amounts of western redcedar (Thuja plicata), and a minor components of grand fir (Abies grandis), and western hemlock (Tsuga heterophylla). Deciduous cover is dominated by big leaf maple (Acer Page 387 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 388 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting macrophyllum), with a lesser component of red alder (A/nus rubra). Many of the big leaf maples are dominant trees in the canopy. The understorey is characterized by a discontinuous shrub layer (sword fern, salal, and Oregon grape) and a discontinuous moss layer (Hylocomium splendens, Kindbergia oregana, Rhytidiadelphus triquetus). Observations of historical blowdown indicate trees in the local area are fairly windfirm. Forest cover was recently removed from lands on either side of Tributary 1 in conjunction with development of Phases 6 and 7. After the prolonged drought in the summer of 2021, trees could be vulnerable to windthrow this fall and winter, especially if saturation from heavy rains coincides with strong windstorms. Forest cover along the eastern side ofthe SPEA is likely more vulnerable to blowdown due to direction of prevailing winds in winter. Soils in the area developed in moderately deep, sandy gravelly fluvial, fluvioglacial and/or marine deposits. Soils are well to imperfectly drained. Very gravelly to gravelly loamy sand is the usual texture in the upper horizons; subsoils consist of very gravelly loamy and or very gravelly sand. The coarse fragment content is at least 35% and usually exceeds 50% by volume. A weak to moderate cemented layer is generally present at depths between 35 and 90 cm; relatively unweathered parent material is encountered at depths between 1.5 and 2 m. The usual taxonomic classification is Orthic Dystric Brunisol; the lesser common soil is a Duric Dystric Brunisol (MoE Technical Report 17). Site Visit Field work took place on October 14, 2021. At the time of the assessment, the Top of Bank (Top of Bank) and SPEA were flagged and surveyed in with hard pins. The development site had been cleared up to the RAPR setbacks. Lots were not marked. Trees had not been previously tagged. As part of this study, potentially hazardous trees were flagged and numbered, but were not GPS referenced, due to inclement weather on the day of the assessment. 12 Page 388 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 389 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Stages 6 and 7 and Holland Creek Tributary 1 SPEA Stages 6 & 7- Development site cleared up to the RAR setback. Right: Physical damage (from construction) to stem of tree on edge of SPEA. 14 Page 390 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 391 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Efforts are encouraged to retain wildlife trees in the SPEA / future parkland. 15 Page 391 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 392 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Windthrow - Background Discussion Windthrow (Tree fall) — tree uprooting or stem breakage that results when wind loads exceed stem or anchorage strength. The purpose of windthrow assessment is to determine whether there are windthrow concerns as a result of proposed development and prescribe windthrow protection measures outside of the SPEA. In coastal BC, the most common cause of stand damaging winds is the western movement of extra-tropical low pressure systems from the Pacific Ocean. These storms produce counter-clockwise rotating regional-scale wind fields that interact with local geography and terrain. Pacific low pressure systems are strongest during the coolest months (i.e. October to April) when they are accompanied by gusty winds and high rainfall. The long duration of these storms and the high rainfall can be significant factors in windthrow risk because root-soil cohesion breaks down as trees rock back and forth in wet soil. In routine events, local geography and terrain produce predictable differences in local wind speeds. Catastrophic damage patterns during intense systems are less dependent on local terrain. WIND TURNING MOMENT During strong Pacific low systems with wind and heavy rains, root-soil cohesion breaks down as trees rock back and forth in wet soil (left). Intense winds can cause boles to “snap” (right). 16 Page 392 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 393 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting The other large scale weather systems which can cause stand damaging winds are arctic ridges of high pressure. These cold, dry systems occasionally move south over the interior of BC and outward toward the coast. Strong outflow winds through major valleys are associated with these winter systems, particularly when there is an offshore low pressure system and therefore a steep differential gradient in surface air pressure (high to low). In the summer, local wind effects are created where strong differences in air temperature develop. On-shore winds develop in the afternoon as the land heats up relative to the ocean. Windthrow Assessment Windthrow hazard and likelihood assessment is conducted on those areas in the stand (edge segments) that have a risk to values or objectives as a result of windthrow. 1. A set of diagnostic questions is used to assess various hazards for windthrow. 2. Three hazard components (topographic, stand and soil) are assessed and then brought together in a ranking table to provide an overall biophysical hazard for windthrow. The three components take into account location, and characteristics of the stand and soil median - all factors critical to assess the inherent hazard of the area for windthrow — i.e., the biophysical hazard. Biophysical Hazard — the intrinsic stability of the stand in its pre-treatment condition. The inherent ability to resist wind damage is the cumulative result of topographic, soils and stand features interacting as the stand develops with endemic windloading. 3. The biophysical hazard is then used along with an estimate of treatment hazard (activity associated with development) to rank the likelihood of windthrow occurring on the edge segment. Treatment Hazard — is the way in which a particular treatment increases or decreases the windloading or wind resistance of trees. A simple example of treatment hazard is the influence of land clearing to expose new edges. Treatment hazard can be reduced by further treatments such as pruning, or topping. 17 Page 393 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 394 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Treatment hazard ranges from low to high depending on howor where land clearing will be applied. The two working together give an indication of how likely windthrow will be on the edge or within a retained forest stand, (i.e., the likelihood of windthrow). | TN HighLacihood~ Scenarios 4. Once the likelihood of windthrow is determined, consequences are considered to provide an assessment of windthrow risk. Windthrow risk is the combination of the likelihood of windthrow and the potential consequences of that windthrow. Windthrow risk reflects the risk associated with the site plan, considering the likelihood of windthrow against limits (thresholds) that are set based on consequences. Windthrow risk is not equal to the likelihood of windthrow. If considerable windthrow is expected, but there are no consequences, there is little risk. Windthrow impact definitions © Windthrow Likelihood - is the expected level of damage from endemic winds. It combines Biophysical Hazard and Treatment Hazard. ¢ Windthrow Consequences - is the probable level of impact on specific management objectives, or sensitivity of those objectives, if the expected level of windthrow occurs. © Windthrow Risk - is the potential for a negative consequence from windthrow caused by endemic winds. It is the combination of Windthrow Likelihood and Consequence. 18 Page 394 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 395 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Windthrow treatment, when prescribed, is necessary to retain and/or enhance riparian habitat and reduce hazard (to workers, residents, visitors, structures).
