Where not safe, consider retaining Coarse CWD may be a Woody Debris to enhance biodiversity consideration 24 Page 400 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 401 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Assessment Results Windthrow risk assessed at two segments of Holland Creek Tributary 1 SPEA at Holland Creek Partnership Stages 6 & 7 is rated Moderate. Windthrow likelihood is Moderate. Eleven (11) trees assessed as hazard trees are recommended for removal (falling into the SPEA). Tree size and species were major determinants of windthrow risk. Large big leaf maples rated highest for highest windthrow risk. Of the eleven trees, eight (8) were big-leaf maple, two (2) were smaller Douglas-fir, and one (1) was a smaller western hemlock near the stream crossing. Except for one Class 4 big leaf maple, all other trees assessed as hazard trees were live trees. However, many larger maples in the area feature as dominant trees nearing the end of biological rotation. Observations during the field assessment indicated that some trees along the edge of the SPEA have incurred physical damage, likely as a result of land clearing for development. Signs of tree damage included stem scars, root removal, and, in one case, evidence of “pushover” of a whole tree. Care must be taken during development to avoid disturbance within the drip line of trees along the edges of the SPEA. Damaged trees can be more susceptible to windthrow and disease. The coast of British Columbia is subjected to severe storms in the fall/winter. The subject site is somewhat protected from prevailing winds by local topographic features (nearby hills, mid-slope position). Recent removal of surrounding, protective tree cover from lands on either side of the riparian area of Tributary 1 could exacerbate effects of winter storms. Extended periods of little precipitation — as occurred in the summer of 2021 — can cause severe stress to trees. Long dry spells make trees more susceptible to fungi and insects. In a prolonged drought, studies indicate tree deaths can occur as a result of carbon starvation because trees close their stomata, blocking entry of carbon needed for photosynthesis. Drought-damaged, weakened trees are extra susceptible to damage from heavy winds and rain in severe storms. Hazard mitigation is recommended for hazard trees. Identified hazardous trees have defects which could increase susceptibility to wind damage, which poses a risk to workers and future residents. Dead/dying trees along the upper edge of the SPEA, adjacent to future homes, contribute to woody fuel that could be a potential interface fire risk. 25 Page 401 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 402 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Best management practices to manage windthrow risk and hazard trees typically involves a variety of treatments, including spiral pruning, coppicing (to remove dead/dying high branches and reduce height while encouraging lateral branching) and removal (with options for high stumping and / or retention of coarse woody debris). In this case, removal (directional falling into SPEA) is recommended. High stumping is recommended for the maples, which can be expected to coppice. Nesting boxes for bats and birds could be considered for high stumps. As noted in the Post-Clearing Tree Risk Assessment conducted by Vancouver Island Tree Service (July 2021), large maples at the north-east side of the development (bottom of the slope) could be pruned to remove any large diameter deadwood from the canopy. Appropriate treatment must be implemented prior to clearing/construction in order to ensure the site is safe for the uses intended. e During site preparation and construction, monitor clearing and construction within the RAA adjacent to the SPEA by a QEP. e Use a qualified Arborist for the treatment work. e Assign a qualified monitor to oversee tree retention and protection activities within the development area throughout the length of the project. e Wherever safely possible, attempt to retain existing tree cover within the SPEA, in order to maintain bank stability. e Minimize disturbance to roots of trees within the RAA and on the edge of the SPEA. Limit ground disturbance within the drip line (at least 3 m from boles of trees) within the RAA from the edge of the SPEA. e Retain native ground cover in SPEA (salal, Oregon grape, salal, ferns, mosses, etc.) e Promptly re-vegetate any areas disturbed within and surrounding the SPEA with native trees and shrub species ecologically suited to the site (as per direction from a QEP, and under direction of a qualified landscaper). Implementation of mitigative actions (e.g., hazard tree treatment and remediation of the SPEA) will yield a net environmental improvement. Remediation will increase resiliency of riparian forest at Tributary 1. Decadent, hazardous maples in the second- growth forest stand at Tributary 1 are very likely to fall down in the near future, especially given predicted intensity of storms associated with climate change. Remediation will provide a better outcome for this forest. Remediation will compensate identified deficiencies with species diversification (overstorey and understorey) and habitat diversity (increased levels of coarse woody debris). Species and habitat diversification will result in succession to a more maintenance-free and safer forest. If the measures identified in this report to protect the integrity of the SPEA and surrounding riparian habitat are implemented by the developer, there will be no harmful alteration, disruption or destruction of natural features, functions and conditions that support fish life processes in (and/or downstream of) the riparian assessment area. Strategies to sustain tree cover will help enhance local biodiversity of both riparian and upland habitats. Finally, if the recommendations contained in this report are followed during planning and construction, risk associated with windthrow and hazard trees can be mitigated to ensure the safety of the intended development. 28 Page 404 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 405 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Appendix 1. Page 410 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 411 PROJECT: Holland Creek Area, Stage 5, Ladysmith, BC { FILE NO.: F9446.01 DATE: March 26, 2021 1.0 INTRODUCTION 1.1 Background a. For the purposes of this report “the Property” is defined as the Holland Creek Area Stage 5. The Property is located on the east coast Vancouver Island within the ToL. b. The proposed development for the Property at the time of this report includes the construction of a twenty (20) lot residential subdivision with associated civil utilities and hard surfacing. c. The Property is located within DPA 6, as per the ToL, OCP Map 2 — Development Permit Areas. d. For more information, please reference the civil plans prepared by the project’s Civil Engineer — NEL. e. LEA has carried out an assessment in order to provide an overview of the site conditions, BMPs, determination of areas susceptible to erosion and sediment transport and the proposed ESCP. f. In preparation of this report, we have reviewed the most current and relevant technical documents provided by EGBC, DFO, MoE, and CoN. 2.0 SITE CONDITIONS 2.1 Physical Setting a. The Property is located in the central region of the ToL. The site is situated on the south side of Dogwood Drive and is accessed via Rollie Rose Drive. 2.2 Climate and Vegetation a. The climate is characterized with long, wet and mild winters. Significant rainfall during the winters with occasional snowfall events, followed by a sunny, relatively dry-summer season.* b. The Property is located in the “Coastal western hemlock zone: western hemlock sub zone”.? 2.3 Terrain and Features a. LEA visited the property on March 23, 2021, and conducted a visual site assessment. At the time of our assessment, the Property was undeveloped. b. In general, the topography of the Property slopes south to north, with approximately 31.0m of vertical relief over the length of the Property. 2.4 Watercourses and Existing Stormwater Infrastructure a. The Property does not contain any defined watercourses within its boundaries. The closest notable watercourse near the Project boundaries is “Tributary 1” as by the attached civil site plan. Tributary 1 is a 1 Page 411 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 412 PROJECT: Holland Creek Area, Stage 5, Ladysmith, BC { FILE NO.: F9446.01 DATE: March 26, 2021 tributary to the Holland Creek watercourse. b. There is no existing storm drainage infrastructure currently on site. However, the previous stages of development leading from Dogwood Drive to the Property contain a number of catch basins and manholes, that discharge storm water into the tributaries of Holland Creek. 2.5 Soil and Bedrock Conditions a. A subsurface investigation was not included as part of the ESCP assessment. b. Published surficial geology mapping identifies the area as part of the Qualicum formation, a soil formation consisting of glaciofluvial deposits. Particles consist of a mixture of boulders, sand, silt and clay.” 2.6 Groundwater Conditions a. Given the mapped soil conditions, specifically the dense fine-grained glacial till subgrade, we expect that a shallow “perched” groundwater table is present seasonally. We expect that the groundwater flows. associated with this perched condition would be related directly to the volume and frequency of storm events b. Groundwater levels can be expected to fluctuate seasonally with cycles of precipitation. 3.0 DISCUSSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 3.1 Project Staging a. In general, there will be four major development stages specific to this project: i. Clearing and grubbing of the existing site vegetation ii. Surface preparation for construction staging. iii. Civil utilities install iv. Final grading and surfacing. 3.2 Water Management a. Site soils in the area are considered imperfectly draining, suggesting that some infiltration of surface water may occur but will likely remain in a perched condition overlying the impermeable silty glacial till soils. b. The critical area for water management will be ensuring that the quality of site runoff remains acceptable and does not negatively affect the neighboring tributaries and Holland Creek. The Contractor is expected to cover exposed erodible soils and direct site runoff into vegetated areas. For more details see attached Page 412 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 413 PROJECT: Holland Creek Area, Stage 5, Ladysmith, BC { FILE NO.: F9446.01 DATE: March 26, 2021 LEA — ESCP Drawing. It is expected that the retained vegetated area will be able to absorb/infiltrate the expected site runoff. 3.3 Erosion and Sediment Sources a. In general, coarse grained soils (cobbles, gravels, coarse sand) are susceptible to erosion but have a relatively low potential for sedimentation and/or sediment transport. Fine grained soils (fine sand, silt, clay) are typically susceptible to both erosion and sedimentation. It is our expectation that the subject project will likely encounter both fine- and coarse-grained soils during development. b. Sources of erosion and sedimentation include but are not limited to soil areas exposed during clearing and grubbing, stockpiled soils created during the excavation and earthworks phase as well as any exposed soils left in place as part of the final grading and or landscaping. Special attention must be followed where large areas relative the total parcel size (>50%) are left exposed along with exposed soils located near project boundaries. c. Construction traffic leading to and from site may also lead to significant erosion of the site soils and transport of deleterious material onto existing roads, causing sedimentation of the existing storm service. d. Critical areas prone to erosion and sedimentation specific to the Property include areas stripped of vegetation and left bare. Special attention should also be paid to exposed soils in areas along project boundaries. 3.4 Best Management Practices a. BMPs are intended to reduce erosion and sedimentation by protecting/stabilizing exposed soils and/or reducing surface flow runoff velocities that aid in the mitigation of sediment transport offsite. Commonly implemented BMPs include the following: i. Retaining vegetated areas and buffers. ii. Installation of drainage paths (swales/ditches) uphill from the proposed areas of disturbance. This will allow surface/groundwater to be diverted away and around areas of disturbance. iii. Surface roughening to reduce water velocities (contouring). iv. Covering exposed soil slopes with coco matting to prevent rill and surface erosion. ve Protect natural drainage channels and ditches with check dams, sediment traps and armoring. vi. To limit erosion and sedimentation earthworks should be conducted during periods of dry weather. b. Descriptions of the planned BMPs can be found on the attached ESCP. 3.5 Erosion and Sediment Control Plan a. Measures shown in the attached ESCP must be installed prior to the related stage of development and Page 413 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 414 PROJECT: Holland Creek Area, Stage 5, Ladysmith, BC { FILE NO.: F9446.01 DATE: March 26, 2021 maintained and monitored throughout the course of development. b. Implementation of the ESCP will be the responsibility of the Contractor. It is best practice that the Contractor designate a site person to inspect to ESC measures daily and maintain if necessary. c. ESCPs are dynamic and adaptive documents that require ongoing inspection, maintenance and re- evaluation of the effectiveness of the prescribed ESC measures. If the Contractor finds that the prescribed ESC measures are not functioning adequately the following steps should be taken: i. Ensure ESC measures are installed correctly as per the most up to date ESCP. ii. | Determine if other BMPs may be best suited to mitigate the specific scenario. iii. | Assess to see if increased maintenance of existing ESC measures is required. iv. | Contact the ESC Professional if required. d. 48 hours prior to any significant storm event, the designated site person should inspect the ESC measures and ensure that the works are adequately installed to protect the site during the storm event. 4.0 CONCLUSIONS 4.1 Responsibilities a. Implementation and routine maintenance of the ESCP will be the responsibility of the Contractor. Ata minimum, the Contractor is to inspect all required BMPs weekly and provide inspection reports to the Engineer for review. The Contractor is also to inspect the ESC measures 48 hours prior to any significant storm event to ensure that the prescribed ESC measures are adequately installed. If not, they are to inform the ESC Professional so that work can be modified to best protect the site during the storm event. b. Acopy of this report along with the attached ESCP should be kept on-site at all times and made available to all personnel responsible for the installation and maintenance of the Project’s ESC measures. 4.2 Acknowledgements a. ASSESSMENT OBJECTIVES Our assessment, as summarized within this report, is intended to meet the following objectives: Determine whether the land is considered safe for the use intended (defined for the purposes of this report as construction of a residential development including the installation of associated on and off site civil works and services), with the probability of a geotechnical failure resulting in property damage of less than 10 percent (10%) in 50 years, with the exception ofgeohazards due to a seismic event which are to be based on a2 percent (2%) probability of exceedance in 50 years, provided the recommendations in this report are followed. Identify any geotechnical deficiency that might impact the design and construction of the development, and prescribe the geotechnical works and any changes in the standards of the design and construction of the development that are required to ensure the land, buildings, and works and services are developed and maintained safely for the use intended. iii. Acknowledge that Approving and/or Building Inspection Officer may rely on this report when making a decision on applications for the development ofthe land. ASSESSMENT METHODOLOGY The subsurface geotechnical investigation was carried out over three consecutive days from September 23 to 25, 2013 using a Hitachi Zaxis 200 excavator provided by Parksville Heavy Equipment Ltd. A total of fifty-seven (57) test pits (TP 13-01 to TP 13-57) were excavated within the proposed development property. All test pits were backfilled upon completion. Site plans showing the extent of the development area, as well as the approximate locations ofthe test pits are attached as Figures 1 through 5, following the text of this report. SITE CONDITIONS 51 General The subject development area is approximately 141 acres (57.05 hectares) in total size and consists of three separate legal properties. It is not known as this time whether the residential subdivision process will consist of a strata or fee simple type of development, or portions ofeach. The majority of the proposed development area has been selectively logged, with an area within the western portion of the site clear-cut in recent years. The proposed development property is located to the immediate west of the Town of Ladysmith, and is bound to the south by the limits of the Town of Ladysmith. The southern and western perimeters of the development area include BC Hydro (BCH) and Fortis right-of-ways (ROWs) to accommodate existing underground and overhead transmission line services. BCH also has a second ROW running north/south through the eastern portion of the proposed development area. Access to the subject properties is currently limited. The development area can be accessed on foot from Arbutus Drive and Dogwood Drive along the eastern extents of the development area, or by vehicle along the existing gated services roads within the BCH and Fortis ROWs. Heart Creek and two smaller tributaries run approximately southwest to northeast through the property. We understand that the potential impact on the existing creek and tributaries, relative to the proposed development, will be carried out by others. g Topography within the property is complex, with varying slopes throughout. Relatively flat plateaus exist in the western portion of the development area. Preliminary survey data indicates geodetic elevations varying from 125m at the southern extents of the property to 20m at the northern extents of the property for a total of 105m of total vertical relief sloping Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 420 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 421 Client: 0885538 BC Ltd. L Project: Holland Creek Residential Development File: F0391.04 Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 4 of 15 downhill from south to north (approximately). 5.2 Soil Conditions The proposed subdivision plan, and the existing terrain within the development area dictated that the majority of the subsurface explorations (test pits) were excavated within the southern portions of the development area. Soil conditions within the southern portion of the anticipated development area consisted of typical alluvial sands and gravel underlain by an over-consolidated silt, sand, and gravel matrix (glacial till). Glacial till was encountered throughout the southern portion of the development property at a mean depth of 1.1m. Soil conditions within the northern portion of the anticipated development area consisted of more substantial alluvial deposits. Sand and gravel, or minor variations of, were encountered predominantly throughout the northern portion of the development property. Granular materials were encountered at depths from 0.2m to a maximum depth of 3.4m. Please note, the total depth of the naturally deposited granular soils was not determined due to the dense nature of the material, the depth of the material, and the limitations of the excavation equipment. Sporadic localized subgrade soil conditions were encountered in some areas during the field investigation. i, TP 13-15 revealed a layer of “re-worked” site materials to a depth of 0.4m. We expect that re-worked site materials will be encountered throughout the property given the logging activities in the area. We expect the nature of these materials to be negligible given the scope of the anticipated earthworks associated with the proposed development. ii, TP 13-21 revealed soft, wet, organic soils to a depth of0.6m, underlain by a loose to Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 421 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 422 Client: 0885538 BC Ltd. L Project: Holland Creek Residential Development File: F0391.04 Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 5 of 15 compact silty gravel to a depth of 2.2m, with groundwater seepage observed throughout the test pit excavation. Ponded water was noted at surface in proximity to the test pit location. In addition, equipment access to the area in proximity to TP 13-21 was limited given the soft, wet nature of the surface soils. Visual reconnaissance of the are was conducted as conditions permitted. We do not expect the extent of this soft area to be significant. However, additional investigation may be warranted to determine the volume of unsuitable materials with respect to the proposed roadway construction in the area. iii, TP 13-51, TP 13-52, and TP 13-54 revealed a bearing material of very stiff to hard silt with a trace of sand and clay. While dissimilar in general composition from the glacial till discussed above, the engineering properties of this material are similar to the glacial till. We do not expect that this fine-grained stratum, given its consistency, will impact the proposed development. e. Depths are referenced to the existing ground surface at the time of our field investigation. Soil classification terminology is based on the Modified Unified classification system, The relative proportions of the major and minor soil constituents are indicated by the use of appropriate Group Names as provided in ASTM D2487 Figures 1a, 1b, and 2. Other descriptive terms generally follow conventions of the Canadian Foundation Engineering Manual. 5.3 Bedrock a. As discussed above, glacial till was encountered predominantly throughout the site, with areas of granular deposits in the northern portion of the site. b. Please note, effective refusal in TP 13-35 was reached due to either a large boulder or shallow bedrock. c. Large cobbles and boulders are common to the type ofglacial till soils encountered during Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 422 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 423 Client: 0885538 BC Ltd. L Project: Holland Creek Residential Development File: F0391.04 Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 6 of 15 the field investigation. d. As bedrock was not encountered or observed in any other areas of the property, it is reasonable to assume that that the effective refusal in TP 13-35 consisted of a large boulder. 5.4 Groundwater a. There was groundwater seepage observed, as outlined above, in TP 13-21. Groundwater was not encountered during the remainder ofthe field investigation. b. Note, the test pitting investigation was conducted during an extended period of dry weather. Given the dense, impervious nature of the subgrade soils documented during the field investigation (shallow glacial till), it is reasonable to assume that a shallow, perched groundwater table is present during the “wet” season, particularly in the southern portion of the development property. We expect that this seasonal perched condition will be directly related to the volume and frequency of storm events. c. Groundwater levels can be expected to fluctuate seasonally with cycles of precipitation. Groundwater conditions at other times and locations can differ from those observed within the bore holes at the time of our assessment. 5.5 Review of Available Mine Information a. We considered the potential impact to the proposed development by abandoned coal mines. As part of this assignment, we have reviewed historical documents with respect to coal mining activities rumored to have occurred in the area. b. Based on our review, there was no documented underground coal mining activities in proximity to the subject development area. c. Historical information indicates that the closest underground mining activities were located approximately 23km to the north. Documented mines in this area included the “Reserve Mine,” the “Morden Mine,” and the “Black Track Mines.” Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 6.1 General a. From a geotechnical point of view, the land is considered safe for the use intended (defined for the purposes of this report as construction of a residential development including the installation ofassociated on and off site civil works and services), with the probability of a geotechnical failure resulting in property damage of less than 10 percent (10%) in 50 years, with the exception of geohazards due to a seismic event which are to be based on a 2 percent (2%) probability of exceedance in 50 years, provided the recommendations in this report are followed. b. Site development for the study area is understood to require grading (general excavation, embankment construction, and earthworks typical of this type of development) to establish or improve roadways and proposed building lots. Therefore, lots are subject to re- examination during and after area grading but prior to building permit issuance. We have taken this issue into account in formulating our recommendations. c. We recommend that setbacks from steep slope crests be provided for proposed structures and roadways as a precautionary measure against slope degradation due to erosion from extreme storm events or from seismic action. Slopes that require setbacks are defined here as having an inclination exceeding 30 degrees from horizontal. Based on an examination of slopes within this development site, we conclude that there are natural slopes within the property that require setbacks from slope crests. i. Where buildings and roadways are set above slopes with an inclination greater than 45 degrees a minimum setback of 8m is recommended where slopes are between 4m to 8m in total height. Where the total slope height is less than 4m, a setback equal to the height of the slope is required; where total slope height is greater than 8m, the Geotechnical Engineer should be contacted to provide information specific to the localized slope. As a conservative estimate, for slope greater than 8m in total height, a setback equal to the Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 424 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 425 Client: Project: File: 0885538 BC Ltd. Holland Creek Residential Development F0391.04 EA) Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 8 of 15 height of the slope may be used for preliminary design purposes. ii. Where buildings and roadways are to be set above slope with an inclination of 30 - 45 degrees the set back should be a minimum of 6m where slopes are between 3m to 6m in total height. Where the total slope height is less than 3m, a setback equal to the height of the slope is required; where total slope height is greater than 6m, the Geotechnical Engineer should be contacted to provide information specific to the localized slope. As a conservative estimate, for slope greater than 6m in total height, a setback equal to the height of the slope may be used for preliminary design purposes. iii, Where buildings and roadways are set below natural slopes with a grade 30 degrees from horizontal or greater, the setback shall be the total height of the slope (as measured vertically from the toe to crest of the slope). . There is the possibility for the setbacks to be reduced given more in depth analysis of particular features or exposures. Fills may be created to establish building and roadway levels that differ from existing conditions. In this case, a building setback of3.0 metres shall be established for fills ranging from 1.5m to 3.0m high, and 5.0m where the fill exceeds 3.0m in thickness. Fill slopes shall not exceed an inclination of 2H : 1V. Fill shall be compacted to achieve a uniform and dense relative density as per our recommendations for structural fill placement and compaction. Structural fill shall be evaluated and be approved by the Geotechnical Engineer for the project. Natural soil faces shall not be undercut without subsequent support by permanent retaining walls designed and constructed to support the slope face. In general, retaining wall back slopes should be flattened to a configuration no steeper than 2H : 1V to allow for disturbance such as from temporary excavation. The Geotechnical Engineer for the project should review temporary sub-cutting such as for retaining or foundation walls deeper than 1.2m. A more detailed geotechnical analysis on a lot by lot basis may be necessary at the Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 425 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 426 Client: Project: File: 0885538 BC Ltd. Holland Creek Residential Development F0391.04 EA) Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 9 of 15 time of construction. This may be accomplished using a standard BC Building Code Quality Assurance Schedules B and C. 6.2 Structural Fill Where fill is required to raise areas that will support buildings, slabs, or pavements, structural fill should be used. The Geotechnical Engineer should first approve the exposed subgrade to confirm the removal of all unsuitable materials. Structural fill should be inorganic sand and gravel, or well-graded blasted/broken rock (subject to the review and approval of the Geotechnical Engineer). If structural fill placement is to be carried out in the wet season, material with a fines content limited to 5% passing the 75um sieve should be used, as such a material will not be overly sensitive to moisture, allowing compaction during rainy periods of weather. Structural fill should be compacted to a minimum of 95% of Modified Proctor maximum dry density (ASTM D1557) in foundation and floor slab areas, and a minimum of 95% in paved roadway and parking areas. Structural fills under foundations should include the zone defined by a plane extending down and outward a minimum 0.5m from the outer edge of the foundation at an angle of 45 degrees from horizontal to ensure adequate subjacent support. Compaction of fill should include moisture conditioning as needed to bring the soils to the optimum moisture content and compacted using vibratory compaction equipment in lift thickness appropriate for the size and type of compaction equipment used. A general guideline for maximum lift thickness is no more than 100mm for light hand equipment such as a ‘jumping-jack,’ 150mm for a small roller and 300mm for a large roller or heavy (>500 kg) vibratory plate compactor or a backhoe mounted hoe-pac or a large excavator mounted hoe-pac, as measured loose. It should be emphasized that the long-term performance of buildings, slabs, and pavements Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 426 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 427 Client: Project: File: 0885538 BC Ltd. Holland Creek Residential Development F0391.04 EA) Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 10 of 15 is highly dependant on the correct placement and compaction of underlying structural fills. Consequently, we recommend that structural fills be observed and approved by the Geotechnical Engineer. This would include approval of the proposed fill materials and performing a suitable program of compaction testing during construction. 6.3 Foundation Design & Construction — Proposed Residential Construction Prior to construction, the building area should be stripped to remove all unsuitable materials to provide an undisturbed natural soil subgrade for the footing support. Foundation loads should be supported on natural undisturbed soil approved for use as a bearing stratum by our office, or structural fill, and may be designed using the following values. For foundations constructed on structural fill, as outlined in Section 6.3 of this report, a Service Limit State (SLS) bearing pressure of 150 kPa, and an Ultimate Limit State (ULS) of 200 kPa may be used for design purposes. These values assume a minimum 0.6m depth of confinement or cover. For foundations constructed on dense, naturally deposited sand and gravel (or similar), or glacial till, an SLS bearing pressure of 150 kPa, and a ULS of 200 kPa may be used for design purposes. These values assume a minimum 0.6m depth of confinement or cover ron Exterior footings should be provided with a minimum 0.6m depth of ground cover for frost protection purposes. d. Prior to placement of concrete footings, any bearing soils that have been softened, loosened, or otherwise disturbed during the course of construction should be removed, or else compacted following our recommendations for structural fill. Compaction will only be feasible if the soil has suitable moisture content and if there is access to heavy compaction equipment. If no structural fill is placed, a smooth-bladed clean up bucket should be used to finish the excavation. Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 427 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 428 Client: 0885538 BC Ltd. L Project: Holland Creek Residential Development File: F0391.04 Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 11 of 15 6.4 Seismic Issues a. A localized area of potentially liquefiable and/or compressible soil was encountered in proximity to TP 13-21. Based on the remainder of the field investigation, and a visual reconnaissance of the area in proximity to TP 13-21, we expect the scope and total extent of the soft soils to be limited. We expect that the area of soft soil can be excavated and replaced with competent structural fill materials as required to facilitate the proposed subdivision development and associated residential construction. b. Based on the 2012 British Columbia Building Code, Division B, Part 4, Table 4.1.8.4.A, ‘Site Classification for Seismic Site Response,’ the soils and strata encountered during the test pitting investigation would be ‘Site Class D’ (Stiff Soil). 6.5 Permanent Dewatering Conventional requirements of the 2012 British Columbia Building Code pertaining to building drainage are considered suitable at this site. Once final plans and tentative elevations are determined, the Geotechnical Engineer should be consulted to provide further dewatering data. 6.6 Erosion Control Since the site consists of some erodible surfaces, erosion control is expected to be an issue of significance during the development of this property. Overland storm water controls should take into account the potential impact of concentrated runoff as it may impact adjacent sensitive areas. This should generally take the form of runoff from construction activities being directed to retention areas prior to entry to sensitive areas. Erosion and sediment control plans can be provided by our office prior to any construction activities to ensure appropriate practices are documented. Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 428 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 429 Client: 0885538 BC Ltd. { Project: Holland Creek Residential Development File: F0391.04 Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 12 of 15 6.7 Undermining Discussions and Recommendations a. Based on a review of the available information, there was no underground coal mining activity in proximity to the proposed development area. b. Historical documentation indicates that the Ladysmith Harbour, located approximately 3 km northeast of the subject development area, was used as a shipping port for coal. We do not expect that the documented shipping and/or export activities will have any impact on the proposed development. c. The proposed development should not be impacted by abandoned coal mine workings or ancillary coal mining activities. 6.8 Trenching and Utility Installation a. We understand through conversations with the civil consultant and a cursory review of the design civil drawings, that the installation of the civil works and services will include substantial excavation depths in some areas. b. Given our knowledge of subgrade soil conditions, we offer the following preliminary recommendations with respect to trenching and civil utility installation: i, The subgrade soil conditions are expected to consist primarily of very dense glacial till. ii. A continuous vertical excavation depth of 3.0m should be feasible given the anticipated subgrade conditions. This is subject to the field review and approval of the Geotechnical Engineer at the time of construction. iii, | Any excavation depths exceeding 3.0m in depth shall be sloped at a configuration of 1H : 2V beyond 4.0m in height. iv. Consideration may be given for excavation depths exceeding 3.0m in depth, subject to the field review and approval of the Geotechnical Engineer at the time of construction. Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 429 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 430 Client: 0885538 BC Ltd. Project: Holland Creek Residential Development File: F0391.04 Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 13 of 15 v. All excavations shall be protected from environmental conditions as required during the course of construction. Surface water and seepage shall me monitored closely during construction. vi. All excavation work shall conform to applicable criteria as outlined by Worksafe BC. Any trenching or general excavation depth that exceeds the depths outlined by Worksafe BC shall be reviewed in the field by the Geotechnical Engineer. 7. GEOTECHNICAL ASSURANCE AND QUALITY ASSURANCE The 2012 British Columbia Building Code requires that a geotechnical engineer be retained to provide Geotechnical Assurance services for construction of this nature. Geotechnical Assurance services include review of the geotechnical components of the plans and supporting documents, and responsibility for field reviews of these components during construction. LIMITATIONS The conclusions and recommendations submitted in this report are based upon the data obtained from a limited number of widely spaced subsurface explorations. The nature and extent of variations between these explorations may not become evident until construction or further investigation. The recommendations given are based on the subsurface soil Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 430 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 431 Client: Project: File: 0885538 BC Ltd. No other warrantee, expressed or implied, is made. Due to the geological randomness of many soil formations, no interpolation of soil conditions between or away from the test pits has been made or implied. Soil conditions are known only at the test pit locations. The changes to be made in and about the stream are: Culvert installation buried at a depth greater than 2m. The location of the works are at the following coordinates, as provided by the applicant: 48.97578, -123.81295 All works shall be completed in accordance with: a. Construction Environmental Protection Plan for Holland Estates Stage 5 — Culvert Installation Tributary 1. Prepared by D.R. Clough Consulting. March 2021; b. Construction Environmental Management Plan — Course Woody Debris Addition for Holland Estates Stage 5 — Culvert Crossing. Prepared by D.R. Clough Consulting. June 2021; c. Culvert Maintenance Schedule. Prepared by Drew Beiderwieden and the Town of Ladysmith agrees. June 2021; d. Private Driveway and Town Owned Watermain, Tributary 1 Crossing. VOY BES Fax: (250) 731-3010 Development Web: Resource Management https www2.gov.be calgovleontenvenvironment/air- land-water/water Page 504 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 505 August 27, 2021 Job Number: 118024 File Number: 1005133 The works authorized shall be completed within the “least fish window” June 15 — September 15. Must be obtain a Riparian Area Development Permit issued by the Town of Ladysmith prior to any works occurring. A Qualified Environmental Professional/Monitor with the authority to halt work shall be on site during all phases of construction. Temporary fencing must be installed prior to construction to sufficiently protect the upstream and downstream areas from encroachment by construction staff, construction and development activity. The fencing must have signage that identifies the area as environmentally sensitive. Trees to remain adjacent to the disturbance area and the construction zone must be protected from damage. Do not allow fill material to bury the base of trees. Install temporary fencing around the drip line of trees adjacent to construction zones to prevent compaction of root systems by heavy machinery. Disturbed riparian areas must be seeded with native grasses and mesh or fiber materials utilized to prevent erosion and promote grass growth. Must use sediment fence/filtration system in the stream channel and on adjacent slopes where practical to prevent and reduce the introduction of sedimentation into the stream. Must prevent unnecessary spillage/storage of construction material in the stream bed and contingency measures must be adhered to as addressed by the Qualified Professional. Construction site bed must be covered if there are erodible substrates (i.e., clay) every night to prevent loss of material. No concrete works, including concrete laden water, either by pore-in-place or grouting be allowed to enter the stream during works. All rock used in the works shall be clean and free of sediment producing material, durable, non-acid generating and suitably graded. Water flow in the stream must be bypassed around the work site and return to the stream bed just below the site. Must use turnouts, sumps and swales in the drainage and ditches leading to the work site to reduce site water from entering fish habitat. In addition, sump pumps must be used as necessary to directed dirty construction water outside the stream environment away from the streamside protection and enhancement area (SPEA). Page 2 of3 Ministry of Forests, Lands, Natural Mailing Address: Phone: (250) 731-3000 Resource Operations, and Rural 4885 Cherry Creek Road, Fax: (250) 731-3010 Development Port Alberni British Columbia Web: hts /www2.gov.be.calgovicontentienvironment/air-land- Resource Management vey 8&9 wateriwater Page 505 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 506 August 27, 2021 Job Number: 118024 File Number: 1005133 Course Woody Debris Plan must be implemented in the interface areas between the proposed development and forested areas adjacent to the riparian area. Equipment used in close proximity to wetted perimeter must be free of deleterious materials (e.g. hydrocarbons) and in good mechanical condition (e.g. no fuel or hydraulic leaks). Spill kits must be on site. Fuelling and servicing of vehicles and equipment must occur a minimum of 30 metres away from all streams, lakes and waterbodies. Keep a spill containment kit on site and train onsite staff in its use. Immediately report any spill ofa substance that is toxic, polluting, or deleterious to aquatic life of reportable quantities to the Dangerous Goods Incident Report 24-hour phone line at 1-800-663-3456. The works shall not result in depressions that have the ability to trap fish and other aquatic life. The holder of this approval shall take reasonable care to avoid damaging any land, works, trees, or other property and shall make full compensation to the owners for any damage or loss resulting from the exercise ofthe rights granted with this approval. All material utilized during construction shall be contoured and placed in a stable area such that it is not able to mobilize and managed to avoid entry into any stream or watercourse. Measures must be taken to ensure that no harmful material (e.g. fuel and other hydrocarbons, soil, road fill, or sediment) which could adversely impact water quality, fish and other aquatic life, and/or fish habitat, be allowed to enter the wetted perimeter as a result of the project activities. The activities authorized under this approval may be halted at any time by an Order in writing from a Water Manger under the Water Sustainability Act to ensure compliance with the terms and conditions authorized herein. All work shall be carried out in accordance with the Provincial "Standards and Best Practices for In-stream Works" (2004). The Provincial guidance document can be found at the following link: http://www.env.gov.be.ca/wld/documents/bmp/iswstdsbpsmarch2004.pdf. VOR 2HO 250-390-2901 drclough@shaw.ca March 24, 2021 Page 507 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 508 Introduction: This report is an Environmental Protection Plan to address environmental values during the installation ofa900mm diameter concrete culvert over Tributary 1 in Holland Creek Estates. Newcastle Engineering provided the culvert design and Erosion Sediment Control Plan (ESC) on their drawings. D.R. Clough Consulting will be the environmental monitor for the project. This environmental protection plan is to ensure safe environmental practices are conducted with regard to work in and around water. Specific environmental concerns are: 1. Introduction of silt and debris into the stream and the associated impacts on water quality and fish habitat downstream of the construction site. 2. Containment of a hydrocarbon spill (e.g., oil, fuel) during construction. Project Construction Contacts $22 Jim Dickinson Owner Drew Beiderwieden, P.Eng | Newcastle Engineering | 250-616-8075/756-9553 office Mike Shepherd Newcastle Engineering | 250-714-3584 Dan Verkley, Supervisor Johnson Bros. 250-927-5963 Contracting David Clough, RPBio Environmental Monitor | 250-714-5416/390-2901 office Brad Remillard, RPBio Environmental Monitor | 250-616-2174 Glenn Carey Owner Representative | 250-390-1475 Danu Vandermark Bennett Land 778-227-7683/754-5518 Surveyors Project environmental description and location: Tributary 1 is a small non-fish channel that leads to Holland Creek. It is a seasonal stream fed by the upland forestry and hydro road ditches and drainages. It then passes through Stage 5 of Holland Estates to travel 750m down to Holland Creek. There is a fish barrier falls (5m) in the City Park at Holland Creek. Schedule of Work The work is scheduled in the general least risk fish window for Vancouver Island of June 15 — September 15. The stream has a seasonal flow regime. Instream work will not begin until the stream is either dry or at low flow and in dry weather. These conditions are expected by July 1, 2021. The start date must be reviewed and approved by the environmental monitor. Work instream installing culvert sections and headwalls is expected to be up to a week. docx Holland_Stage SCulvertCEMP2021 Page 2 of 6 Page 508 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 509 The contractors must be prepared for the environmental limitations and risks associated with this project timing; e The contractor must be prepared for rain events and be prepared to protect the site from sediment and erosion by having all materials on site. The environmental monitor may request a stop work for environmental protection reasons. e The contractor will be responsible for sediment control and any flow bypass installed before work starts. The environmental monitor must approve these measures or work will not be permitted. Construction Environmental Management Plan Check List This CEMP is meant to guide the project monitoring and environmental practices by the contractor. The guiding documents the contractor will follow are; e Newcastle Culvert ESC (attached Fig. 1) ¢ Permit conditions from FLNROD e General construction for the new stage 5 site will have an ESC by Lewkowich Engineering Associates (LEA) before construction begins. 1. Pre-Work —A job safety and environmental pre-work meeting will be done by the Environmental Monitor (EM). All will be informed of the site environmental liabilities from the Section 11 Notification terms and conditions as well as the Newcastle Engineering ESC for the Culvert installation. All copies of environmental plans and permits will be kept and accessible at the site. Environmentally sensitive areas must be identified before work with flagging, signage and fencing. There must be no disturbance outside the identified work boundaries. 2. Monitoring — Environmental monitoring will be conducted to ensure the Section 11 permit conditions, and the Newcastle engineering ESC is followed. The EM will routinely inspect and record procedures that follow the ESC. In the event of a concerns or excedence, the EM will request a stop work until the work follows the ESC procedures. monitors will be there during sensitive work activities, such as the culvert installation. The EM work will primarily be undertaken by D.R. Clough Consulting and Newcastle Engineering Staff but may involve other qualified personnel. 3. Excavation preparation; e the site must be flagged, fenced and have signage to mark the limits of excavation (Approx 30m by 30m). e The site must have a sediment fence/filtration system in the stream channel and on adjacent slopes. e Any water flow must be bypassed around the work site and return the water to the stream bed just below the site. Holland_Stage SCulvertCEMP2021 docx Page 3 of 6 Page 509 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 510 e There shall be no spillage/storage of construction material in the stream bed. e All strippings not suitable for backfill are to be trucked off site. Clean excavated fill must be stored with sediment control /covers. e Sump pumps used to dispose of dirty construction water must be placed outside the stream environment away from the Stream SPEA area. e The construction site bed must be covered if there are erodible substrates (i.e. clay) every night to prevent loss of material. e Grouting sawing and grinding must be isolated from the wetted perimeter habitat. Concrete or grout works require isolation for until cured with no release of material (typically 48hours). Backfill must be covered in the event of rain. Fill slopes not armoured must be covered with seed, mesh or fibre materials to prevent erosion and promote grass seed growth. 5. Erosion/Drainage — Drainage and ditches leading to the work site require installation of turnouts, sumps and swales to reduce site water entry directly to fish habitat. Installation of guard rails, geotextile, rock armour, hay, plastic and grass seed must be applied as required to address runoff and protect fish habitat from deleterious substances (i.e., sediment laden water). . Clough Consulting tan ae Page 514 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 515 Introduction: This is an addendum to provide detailed guidance on the utilization of Coarse Woody Debris (CWD) for wildlife habitat. The reason for this prescription is to compensate for the lack of wood on the forest floor that is important for wildlife habitat. The lack of CWD was identified from the environmental assessment. The lack of CWD can be compensated for by following this plan. Coarse Woody Debris Function The function of coarse woody debris in coastal forests is very important for wildlife. The material is a food supply for invertebrates that are the base of the food chain for birds, amphibians and mammals. The wood is also an important home for cavity nesting and it acts as shade or moisture storage which creates a more diverse plant community on or adjacent these piles of wood. Coarse woody debris is a key ecological component of a healthy forest. Description of Fisheries Resources Values and a Description of the Development proposal (Provide as a minimum: Species present, type of fish habitat present, description of current riparian vegetation condition, connectivity to downstream habitats, nature of development, specific activities proposed, timelines) Unnamed trib to Holland Creek - Thetis Drive The purpose of this Riparian Area Protection Report (RAPR) is to determine the Riparian Assessment Area (RAA) boundaries, as well as the designated Streamside Protection and Enhancement Areas (SPEA) zones for the subject property located at the end of Thetis Drive. Located in the Town of Ladysmith, the assessment is required as the property owner wishes to construct a single family home. The property is presently identified as Lot 8. At the time of our assessment in March of 2022, there was one stream that met the definition of a watercourse as identified by the Fish-Stream Identification Guidebook (1998). The stream has one reach within the subject property. All works proposed are for the right bank of the watercourse. Stream 1- Reach | The subject watercourse has been classified as a stream and runs southwest to northeast along the northwestern flank of the subject property. At the time of our assessment, Reach | has an average gradient of 9.5% and an average bankfull width of 2.00m resulting in step-pool morphology. The substrate is dominated by gravels with patches of mineral alluvium and cobble. The canopy closure fluctuates seasonally but in general ranges from 80-90%. The riparian understory is comprised primarily of sword fern and salal with an overstory consisting of western red cedar, Douglas fir as well as grand fir in the young forest stage of development with occasional older secondary growth polygons. At the time of our assessment, the lot (Lot 8) had been cleared historically as part of the previous subdivision works and application. Although no FISS reports were available for this watercourse, fish presence is assumed given the proximity to fish bearing watercourses downstream (Holland Creek) and an absence of upstream barriers to fish. Note: All stormwater controls and utilities are being kept outside of the designated RAA. Stormwater from the impermeable surfaces on the property is being sent to a rock pit to reduce the overall scouring potential of the stormwater flows during peak rain events. Specific Recommendations for Lot 8 — Thetis Drive Works outside of the designated SPEA zone and within 30m of the RAPR watercourse e Areas designated as the SPEA will be flagged with high visibility flagging tape and temporary fencing. e Prior to construction, a sediment and erosion control plan will be developed to prevent the discharge of sediment laden water into the SPEA or any watercourses identified on-site. This will include the installation of sediment fencing/hay bales as determined by on-site biologist prior to the initiation of construction activities. ¢ No works shall be undertaken within areas designated as SPEA. All works Scheduled Within 30m of a Watercourse and Outside of the SPEA will adhere to all recommendations as outlined in the BMP - Develop with Care: Environmental Guidelines for Urban and Rural Land Development in British Columbia. As well: o Ensure construction will proceed smoothly without harmful alteration of habitat; o Provide long-term monitoring for disturbed sites until green-up is established and the soils at the site are stable. e Heavy equipment (excavators etc.) working within 30m of the watercourse will be monitored for leaks (oil, hydraulic fluid etc.). e Disturbed areas outside the SPEA and within 30m of a waterbody will be revegetated with native plants of a size that will quickly re-establish riparian cover when construction activities are deemed complete. ¢ Detailed direction to contractors will be given to ensure that no erosion or sediment movement will occur and that no silt will be released to the waterbody during the construction and post construction phase. e The site will be monitored by the designated QEP (once every two weeks or as required due to high rainfall events - >30mm/24 hour period) during the Form 1 Page 12 of 19 Page 538 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 539 FORM 1 Riparian Areas Regulation - Qualified Environmental Professional - Assessment Report construction period. Any contraventions of the RAR will be communicated to the builder as well as local municipal staff and RAR staff. A post construction report generated by the designated QEP will be submitted to RAPR and local municipal staff within 4 months after activities are deemed complete. Specific Recommendations for Lot 18 — Thetis Drive Works outside of the designated SPEA zone and within 30m of the RAPR watercourse e Areas designated as the SPEA will be flagged with high visibility flagging tape and temporary fencing. ¢ Prior to construction, a sediment and erosion control plan will be developed to prevent the discharge of sediment laden water into the SPEA or any watercourses identified on-site. This will include the installation of sediment fencing/hay bales as determined by on-site biologist prior to the initiation of construction activities. ¢ No works shall be undertaken within areas designated as SPEA. All works Scheduled Within 30m of a Watercourse and Outside of the SPEA will adhere to all recommendations as outlined in the BMP - Develop with Care: Environmental Guidelines for Urban and Rural Land Development in British Columbia. As well: o Ensure construction will proceed smoothly without harmful alteration of habitat; o Provide long-term monitoring for disturbed sites until green-up is established and the soils at the site are stable. e Heavy equipment (excavators etc.) working within 30m of the watercourse will be monitored for leaks (oil, hydraulic fluid etc.). e Disturbed areas outside the SPEA and within 30m of a waterbody will be revegetated with native plants of a size that will quickly re-establish riparian cover when construction activities are deemed complete. ¢ Detailed direction to contractors will be given to ensure that no erosion or sediment movement will occur and that no silt will be released to the waterbody during the construction and post construction phase. e The site will be monitored by the designated QEP (once every two weeks or as required due to high rainfall events - >30mm/24 hour period) during the Form 1 Page 11 of 19 Page 558 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 559 FORM 1 Riparian Areas Regulation - Qualified Environmental Professional - Assessment Report construction period. Any contraventions of the RAR will be communicated to the builder as well as local municipal staff and RAR staff. A post construction report generated by the designated QEP will be submitted to RAPR and local municipal staff within 4 months after activities are deemed complete. Phone #: Secondary QEP Details Name: Company Address Email Phone Page 584 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 585 May 31, 2022 Jane Hawthornwaite Marban Construction and Design 112 Evelyn Crescent Nanaimo BC RE: 109 BURNS PLACE LADYSMITH BC RAPR POST CONSTRUCTION INSPECTION ASSESSMENT 1.0 INTRODUCTION Aquaparian Environmental Consulting Ltd (Aquaparian) was retained by Marban Construction and Design (Marban) to complete a post construction assessment for 109 Burns Place in Ladysmith BC. This parcel was previously identified as Lot 4 Cook Street / Giovando Way during the subdivision and lot development phase in 2018. A site location map has been included as Figure 1. A site plan is included as Figure 2. Because the subdivision was located in proximity of a non-fish bearing tributary of Tyee Creek (Rocky Creek), a Riparian Areas Regulation (RAR) assessment was completed for the subdivision and reviewed by the province (Assessment #5138) which determined a 10m Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA) for this tributary. This regulation was replaced in 2019 by the Riparian Areas Protection Regulation (RAPR). The stream reach adjacent to the subject parcel is between Giovando Way and Fourth Avenue and is approximately 100 m in length; however, approximately 65m of the channel north of Giovando Way flows underground as it was buried with fill some time in the past and appears to have been done during the sanitary main located on the east side of the creek and cuts across the ravine slope. The open section of the channel is 35m in length and confined within a ravine reach adjacent to the subject parcel. The stream flows under 4TM Avenue in a culvert and the confluence with Tyee Creek is immediately north of the north side of 4° Avenue. 2.0 RESULTS Aquaparian visited the site on May 26, 2022. Site photographs have been included in Appendix A. The parcel has been constructed with a single-family house and small fenced yard. The fence is located at the top of a steep slope above the dirt road / sanitary alignment within the park dedication. As identified in the RAR assessment, the Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA) is located in the side of the ravine outside the property boundaries. 203-321 Wallace St. Nanaimo, BC V9R 5B6, 250-591-2258 Cell SARAH BONAR 250-714-8446 CHRIS ZAMORA 250-714-8864 Page 585 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 586 109 Burns Pi May 2022 2 There was no evidence of any negative impact to the SPEA or migration of fines into the SPEA from the development of this parcel. A fence has been installed along the property boundary. The slope adjacent to the parcel above the sanitary alignment is steep, roughly 3m high and with a slope of approximately 1H:1V with a narrow strip of vegetation along the top if the slope with a slight overhang where roots are exposed. Some erosion is evident but it appears stable. 3.0 CONCLUSION This property was developed in compliance with the measures included in the RAR assessment. No additional recommendations are warranted at this time. Aquaparian trusts that the information provided in this report meets your requirements. Any questions regarding information provided in this document, please contact the undersigned at (250) 591-2258. Description of Fisheries Resources Values and a Description of the Development proposal (Provide as a minimum: Species present, type of fish habitat present, description of current riparian vegetation condition, connectivity to downstream habitats, nature of development, specific activities proposed, timelines) Description of Proposed Development The proposed development of Stage 6 and Stage 7 of Holland Creek Estates is part ofa multi year and multi staged development process. Stage 6 and Stage 7 are situated on 3.74 ha ofa total lot area of 22.02 ha located off of Rollie Rose Drive in the Town of Ladysmith. The proposed development along Tributary 1 (T1), will be adjacent to approximately 347 m of riparian habitat on the northwest side of T1, 95 m on the southeast side of T1, and 133 m on the northeast side of Ditch 1 (D1). T1 eventually discharges into Holland Creek. The proposed development includes the subdivision of lots and a road right of way over T1 with culvert crossing to connect the lot parcels between Stage 6 and Stage 7. The road right of way will be fully prepared and constructed as part of this proposed development. Full servicing will be laid in the road right of way and finishing completed as per the site plans and updated detailed site servicing plan from Newcastle Engineering Ltd. (Full PFD maps available in appendices)’ All works are to only occur within the road right of way. Under Section 11 of the Water Sustainability Act (WAS) a Change Approval and Notification (Changes In and About a Stream) was submitted to Forests, Lands and Natural Resource Operations (FLNRO) for a culvert crossing at T1 on April 30th, 2021; a Change Approval for the culvert installation was approved under Section 11 of the WSA and received on August 30th, 2021 (File 1005133). The majority of the proposed lots are slated for the construction of single-family residential homes, other portions will remain as greenspace or be used as road right of ways. The total area covered by housing footprints, access roads and other structures will not be available until the lots are registered, sold, and a building permit is applied for and approved. The Site Plan map along with Newcastle Engineering Ltd. site plan maps are available in Section 3 of this report. T1 and D1 fall within the Development Permit Area (DPA) 6 of the Town of Ladysmith. A detailed Riparian Areas Protection Regulation (RAPR) is required to obtain a Development Permit (DP) for the proposed subdivision of lots, the proposed culvert crossing and road right of way, and construction of residential housing in Stage 6 and Stage 7. Recently site preparation activities including clearing vegetation occurred between 2020 and 2021, without an approved development permit in DPA 6. These activities occurred within the RAAs of T1 and D1 of Stage 6 and 7. A Condition and Impact Assessment (CIA) report was required to address the historically completed site preparation activities with further detailed measures to protect, maintain, and enhance the SPEA. The CIA report is attached to this detailed RAPR. This detailed RAPR with supporting reports/documents and CIA will be used as a planning document for the DP process with the Town of Ladysmith. This document sets the framework for SPEA protection, maintenance, and enhancement associated with the proposed development activities within Stage 6 and Stage 7. Description of Fisheries Resources Value A site visit was completed on the 1% of October 2021 with D.R. Clough Consulting. Stream and ditch survey data for this detailed RAPR assessment report for T1 and D1 was supplied by D.R. Clough Consulting. ' Newcastle Engineering Ltd. 2021. Site Plans and Site Servicing Plans. Form 1 Page 4 of 32 Page 602 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 603 FORM 1 Riparian Areas Protection Regulation - Qualified Environmental Professional - Assessment Report A second Site visit for the CIA was completed on the 24" of March 2022. The CIA Site inspection focused on assessing potential impacts to the SPEAs from unauthorized historical vegetation clearing in the RAA/DPA of Tributary 1 and D1 as well as identifying mitigation measures. Tributary 1 is a non fish tributary that flows into Holland Creek near the Dogwood Avenue bridge. T1 has had considerable disturbance and alteration of the channel within the proposed development areas and associated RAAs within Stage 6 and 7. The T1 channel is comprised of several reach segments: T1-R1, T1-R2, T1-R3. The proposed development area was logged in the past using clear-cut methods and allowed to regenerate naturally. There are active logging roads as well as abandoned roads that are completely grown in with trees. A mixture of regenerating Red Cedar, Douglas Fir, Red Alder and Broad Leaf Maple comprise the dominant tree species in the RAA as well as the total development area. No old growth trees were observed in the RAA. Extensive areas of the RAA were dominated by moss (in and near T1), salal and ferns as well as by weedy species such as Spurge-Laurel, Foxglove, Himalayan Blackberry, Canada Thistle, Queen Anne’s Lace. In the lower reaches below the development area in Stage 6 and 7, the channel was historically redirected for logging, service of BC Hydro electrical lines, a water line corridor, as well as access for a garbage dump. In the upper reaches above the Stage 6 and 7 development area, the BC Hydro transmission line, Fortis Natural Gas line and forestry road corridors disrupted the channels with poorly located culverts or lack of culverts, alternate routes, drainage ditches and braiding. Reach 1 begins at the confluence with Holland Creek above an 8 m bedrock waterfall which flows year-round from ground water seepage and provides critical summer flow to Holland Creek. The reach is 370 m in length, has an average width of 2.17 m, and an average gradient of 9%. It is comprised of step pool complexes. Large woody debris is scattered throughout the reach, in channel and along the banks. This reach ends below the Stage 6 and 7 proposed development area. The lower portion of Reach 1 outside of the proposed development area has been developed under an earlier phase of works. The watercourse was culverted underneath a road right of way and runs along the side of the road heading north to Holland Creek. Reach 2 begins approximately at the downstream end of the proposed development for Stage 6 on the northwest bank, which coincides with a Hydro line crossing. Upstream on the east bank the proposed development for Stage 7 is present. This section is confined in a ravine for most of it's 320 m length. This reach also provides summer flow via groundwater seepage to Holland Creek. The average width of this reach is 2.86 m with a much steeper gradient of 21% when compared to Reach 1. It is comprised of step pool complexes. Large woody debris is scattered throughout the reach, in channel and along the banks. Reach 3 begins at the presence of unconfined channel and lower gradient near the proposed road right of way on the property, which connects Stage 6 and Stage 7. The reach is 140 m in length, has an average width of 2.07 m, and an average gradient of 9%. This reach was significantly altered by historic logging activities and road building. It has seasonal flow and is fed by steep slopes and groundwater above the BC Hydro transmission line, Fortis Natural Gas line and forestry road corridors which have disturbed the capture of water for T1. There is ditching with recent machine maintenance where road runoff collects along the BC hydro line road and right of way that discharges into D1 and into T1-R3. Ditch 1 is a 120m long non fish bearing drainage. The ditch is manmade, it is a machine dug channel with segments along an old logging/skid road to accommodate runoff, it discharges into T1-R3. This waterway drains from the BC hydro line road and right of way which includes a Fortis Natural Gas line and forestry road corridors. This ditch and others were dug to accommodate logging and draining the BC hydro line road and right of way. It has ephemeral flow. Form 1 Page 5 of 32 Page 603 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 604 FORM 1 Riparian Areas Protection Regulation - Qualified Environmental Professional - Assessment Report The proposed development area is within the Coastal Douglas Fir Biogeoclimatic Zone which is a Red Listed Plant Community. No specific Red or Blue listed plants other than the CDF Community are found in the B.C. Government Ecosystem Explorer for this site. Coastal Cutthroat Trout and Red Legged Frogs are two provincial blue listed endangered species historically observed during previous studies? around the lower fish bearing drainages. Fish Assessment T1 does not support anadromous or residential fish populations. It is located above the 8 m bedrock waterfall which acts as a fish barrier located at the confluence with Holland Creek. The steep gradients in Reach 2 and intermittently dry channel in Reach 1 eliminate the potential for resident fish. An electroshock of the wetted areas of the lower end of T1 in 2010 confirmed there were no fish*. Holland Creek, the downstream receiving waters from T1 is located outside of the proposed development area. The creek has perennial flow and anadromous fish access from its’ lower reaches to water falls upstream which act as a fish barrier. The creek supports a diverse mix of anadromous and resident fish species including cutthroat and rainbow trout along with chum and coho salmon’. There has been enhancement of coho and chum salmon through small numbers of hatchery fry augmentation as well as extensive and successful habitat restoration with construction of four different off channel sites as well as much instream work to stabilize the banks and create fish habitat®. ? If a specific measure is not being recommended a justification must be provided. 1. Danger Eleven trees were assessed as hazard trees and are recommended for removal Trees (falling into the SPEA). Where safe, high stumping is recommended to retain value for wildlife. Where not safe, consider retaining Coarse Woody Debris for SPEA to enhance biodiversity. Vegetation management and mitigation measures will be undertaken in multiple ways such as tree replacement planting and enhancement to bolster the vegetation in and around the SPEA which will increase biodiversity and habitat values. This is an extensive riparian area with potential for further danger trees over time, however the drainages are generally incised in SPEA areas putting the trees in the SPEA at lower elevations than potential building areas. As lots are sold, it is recommended that all houses and development be located to allow for setbacks away from the SPEA beyond the effect of potential new danger trees over time, as determined by a QEP under the new lot owner. The eastern portion of the RAA along T1 is windward to prevailing winds, and more prone to wind damage; both the windward and leeward segments contained hazardous trees according to the assessment. Treatment to prevent windthrow should follow standard strategies to minimize disturbance to rooting layers during clearing and construction, including not creating windthrow, protecting trees in the SPEA (especially along the SPEA boundary), and retaining wildlife trees in the SPEA.
