(TerraWest) was retained by Jim Dickinson and represented by GlenCar Consultants Inc. (the ‘Client') to complete a Condition and Impact Assessment (CIA) of the property located at the Stage 6 and 7 area of Holland Creek Estates development in Ladysmith, BC, herein referred to as the ‘Subject Property’ and/or the ‘Site’. Activities conducted within the defined Site boundaries are herein referred to as “on-Site”. 2.0 Background Prior to the initiation of development activities on the Subject Property, the Client obtained a Qualified Environmental Professional (QEP) to complete a Riparian Areas Regulation (RAR) assessment in 2014. The RAR report (no. 3279A) was completed and notification of approval was received by the Town of Ladysmith on November 26", 2014 from Forests, Lands and Natural Resource Operations (FLNRO) of British Columbia. The Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA), for the Site was determined to be 10m for Tributary 1, Reach 1, 2 and 3 (T1-R1, T1-R2 and T1-R3), and 2m for the associated Ditches (D1, D2, and D3). The Client was given verbal approval from BC Hydro to complete maintenance and repair the ditch line along the BC hydro line road and right of way. This maintenance was completed off Site, south of Stage 6 and 7. Current runoff Environmental Management and Consulting Page 632 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 633 Zg \/ Condition and Impact Assessment Holland Creek Partnership TerraWest Project: JDHC22-02 Page 2 of 8 collected along the BC hydro line road and right of way discharges solely into D3 (D1 under the 2021 RAPR), and into Tributary 1. Under Section 11 of the Water Sustainability Act (WAS) a Change Approval and Notification (Changes In and About a Stream) was submitted to FLNRO for a culvert crossing on Tributary 1 to connect Stage 6 and 7 on April 30t, 2021; a Change Approval for the culvert installation was approved under Section 11 of the WSA and received on August 30', 2021 (File 1005133). Based on the results and previous approval of the 2014 detailed riparian assessment, the verbal approval from BC Hydro for road water management ditching activities on their right of way, and the Change Approval from FLNRO for the culvert installation on Tributary 1, the Client completed Site preparation activities. These activities occurred within the Development Permit Area (DPA) 6 prior to the acquisition of a relevant Development Permit (DP) from the Town of Ladysmith. The Client was under the impression that the 2014 RAR was still applicable and thus the Change Approval from FLNRO was as well to the current proposed road right of way subdivision and for the proposed subdivision of lots and construction of residential housing on the Site; and that conducting clearing activities in the Riparian Assessment Areas (RAAs) but outside of the SPEAs, with the exception of the Tributary 1 crossing as per the Section 11 approval, was acceptable. The Client was also under the impression since road ditching was changed along the BC Hydro right of way and D1 was redirected off Site into D3, D1 was no longer a functional ditch within the Site and subsequently was cleared. TerraWest was retained by the Client in October of 2021 to complete a new detailed assessment under the current Riparian Areas Protection Regulation (RAPR) due to the time lapsed from the original RAR in 2014. RAR/RAPR as of the updated 2019 Riparian Areas Protection Regulation now expire within five years of which a copy of the report is provided to the local government. Due to the fact Site preparation activities within the RAAs of Stage 6 and 7 occurred between 2020 and 2021, more than five years after the 2014 RAR, and prior to the Site assessment and submission of the current 2021 RAPR or the acquisition of a DP, a Condition and Impact Assessment (CIA) was required to address the historically completed site preparation activities. The local government, being the Town of Ladysmith, is required to review and approve this CIA. Once written approval of the CIA is obtained by the Town of Ladysmith, both documents will be submitted as attachments along with the updated RAPR to the province. Once the RAPR package is approved by the province it will be used to assist in the Development Permit application and approval process through the Town of Ladysmith prior to any new development on Site. The 2021 RAPR was carried out identifying a tributary and a ditch on the Site, RAA/DPA and SPEA boundaries are identified in the RAPR and shown on the Site Plan where determined, see Appendix A. Tributary 1 and Ditch 1 boundary locations and development boundaries were based on previous surveys supplied by the Client's current contractor Bennett Land Surveying (Coastal) Ltd. Environmental Management and Consulting Page 633 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 634 Zg \/ Condition and Impact Assessment Holland Creek Partnership TerraWest Project: JDHC22-02 Page 3 of 8 3.0 Riparian Impact Assessment This CIA outlines the historical disturbance that has occurred inside the RAA/DPA of Tributary 1 and D1. With an approved Section 11 Notification for culvert installation and road construction the CIA generally does not include clearing inside a road right of way, however it is provided here for context. Aerial photos in Appendix B show the progression of historical development activities in and around the Subject Property. Vegetation clearing on Site within the SPEA has occurred, clearing was only observed to be within the surveyed road right of way of Tributary 1. The clearing was completed as part of the approved Section 11 works for the culvert installation and construction of road crossing on Tributary 1 in order to connect Stage 6 and 7. The Subject Property has had site preparation activities including vegetation clearing occur inside the RAA/DPA of Tributary 1 as well as D1, however the SPEA remained intact as confirmed during the detailed 2021 RAPR field assessment and March 24th, 2022 CIA Site inspection; see March 24th, 2022 Site photos in Appendix C. The CIA Site inspection focused on assessing potential impacts to the SPEAs from unauthorized historical vegetation clearing in the RAA/DPA of Tributary 1 and D1 as well as identifying mitigation measures. RARP reports are to be submitted and approved prior to development activities inside RAA/DPA areas. This ensures appropriate measures will be set up and in place to protect SPEAs prior to development activities. It is important to protect the biological functions of the SPEAs associated with the different Zones of Sensitivity (ZOS). The ZOS within the SPEA provides benefit to fish and fish habitat by way of Large Woody Debris/Bank Stability, Litter Fall and Insect Drop, and Shade. Each of the ZOS are determined by field measurements based on the application of current RAPR methodology. Based on the current RAPR methodology the SPEAs of Tributary 1 (10m) and D1 (2m) were determined. 4.0 SPEA Protective Measures 4.1. Danger Trees and Windthrow A windthrow and hazard tree assessment of the Site was completed by Strathcona Forestry Consulting in October 2021. The assessment was prompted due to the clearing of vegetation and removal of trees outside of the determined SPEA but within the RAA/DPA areas along Tributary 1 and D1 of Site. The clearing activities created an exposed tree line along the edge of the SPEA. Forest cover on Site along the east and west sides of Tributary 1 was assessed, resulting in a moderate windthrow risk classification. The eastern portion of the RAA is windward to prevailing winds, and more prone to wind damage. There were no observations of windthrow during the Site assessment, however observations of some trees along the SPEA edge indicated signs of physical damage. The damage most likely was the result of previous land clearing in the RAA/DPA. Environmental Management and Consulting Page 634 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 635 TerraWest Project: JDHC22-02 Page 4 of 8 Hazard mitigation was recommended for hazard trees, identified hazard trees have defects which could increase susceptibility to wind damage. Hazard trees pose a risk to workers, future residents/homes, and increased fire risk. The assessment resulted in eleven (11) trees assessed as hazard trees. Best management for these trees is determined to be removal (directional falling into the SPEA). Where determined safe, high stumping is recommended to retain value for wildlife, and where determined not safe consider retaining for Coarse Woody Debris within the SPEA for enhanced biodiversity. Tree replacement is to occur for each hazard tree that is slated for removal as part of enhancing a remediating the SPEA. Implementation of mitigative actions will be overseen by a QEP (e.g., hazard tree treatment and remediation of the SPEA) as discussed in the windthrow and hazard tree assessment with recommended guidelines in conjunction with the provincial RAR Revegetation Guidelines will yield a net environmental improvement. In the case of needing to replace trees, BC provincial criteria must be followed for tree replacement as per the guidelines below. ¢ Omm- 151 mm (6") dbh 2 replacement trees (min height 1.5 m), or, 4 shrubs (for up to 50% of trees being replaced in this range); e =152 mm - 304mm (12") dbh 3 replacement trees (min height 1.5 m); e 305mm - 456mm (18") dbh 4 replacement trees (min height 2.0 m); e 457mm - 60? mm (24") dbh_ 6 replacement trees (min height >" 2.0 m); e 610mm -914mm (36") dbh 8 replacement trees (min height > 2.0 m) o Trees > 914 mm dbh (36") will require individual approval and replacement criteria prior to removal. o Every effort must be made to retain 20% of trees > 304 mm dbh (12") as wildlife snags at minimum height of 3 m. If the measures identified in the windthrow and hazard tree assessment are followed and implemented by the developer to protect the integrity of the SPEA and surrounding riparian habitat, it is determined there will be no harmful alteration, disruption or destruction of natural features, functions and conditions that support fish life processes in (and/or downstream of) the riparian assessment area. 4.2 Slope Stability Previous land clearing activities in the affected RAA/DPA have not resulted in impacts related to slope stability. 4.3 Protection of Trees It is important to take steps and protect trees within the SPEA as they can be damaged by construction activities taking place on adjacent land outside of the SPEA. Tree roots may extend outwards from their base to multiple times their own height, thus making them susceptible even if ground disturbance is outside the SPEA. In addition, the Environmental Management and Consulting Page 635 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 636 Zg \/ Condition and Impact Assessment Holland Creek Partnership TerraWest Project: JDHC22-02 Page $ of 8 operation of heavy equipment close to the SPEA has the potential to cause damage to trees. Indirect impacts may also occur over the rooting zone in the form of paving or altering the ground level under trees. Observations during the windthrow and hazard tree assessment of some trees along the SPEA edge, outside the surveyed road right of way of Tributary 1, indicated some signs of physical damage. The damage most likely was the result of previous land clearing in the RAA/DPA. There has been no apparent deep excavations or large soil moving activities (only clearing and grubbing observed), inside the affected RAA/DPA areas on Site which suggests the tree drip zones have most likely been maintained. To protect the trees from harm a 7.5m drip zone beyond the marked SPEA is to be implemented to protect the tree roots as well as the placement of fencing along SPEA buffers. Activities that must not take place near SPEA trees are: significant changes to ground level, release of pollutants, moving equipment, parking or storing construction equipment. A QEP will observe for compliance during development inspections and any other practices that may impact SPEA tree health. Removal of any danger trees in the SPEA will require the services of a professional danger tree assessor. Work identified as being harmful to the SPEA but not within such as excavation, clearing, erection of permanent structures has to be done in such a way to protect the SPEA trees from harm. The approved Section 11 Notification for culvert installation and road construction in this CIA generally does not include clearing inside a road right of way, however it is provided here for context. The SPEA conditions prior to clearing were observed during a previous breeding bird nest survey conducted on March 23’, 2021 for D.R. Clough Consulting by TerraWest Environmental. The SPEA conditions prior to vegetation removal were consistent with the current upstream/downstream right/left bank SPEA habitat on Site. TerraWest Environmental was not involved in assessing the culvert crossing location and road right of way for mitigation methods and submission of the Section 11 application. The clearing inside of the designed road right of way appears to conform to the Site plans, it is unknown how many trees were removed during the clearing activities from the SPEA. The clearing works has not appeared to have impacted the upstream/downstream, right/left bank trees growing adjacent in the SPEA. The currently approved Section 11 Notification for culvert installation and road construction was received on August 30'", 2021 (File 1005133). 4.4 Encroachment SPEA encroachment is a significant cause of riparian habitat loss and stream degradation. Plant disturbance and loss due to construction activities, dumping and yard waste, trampling due to hiking, and domesticated animals all contribute to riparian degradation. As plants and stream bank stabilization decrease due to disturbance, run off and siltation may occur harming the aquatic ecosystem including fish, their spawning Environmental Management and Consulting Page 636 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 637 Zg \/ Condition and Impact Assessment Holland Creek Partnership TerraWest Project: JDHC22-02 Page 6 of 8 gravels, and aquatic invertebrates (fish food sources). Apart from the clearance of vegetation as part of the yet to come Culvert installation and road construction on Tributary 1, there has been no other observed SPEA encroachment based on the 2021 Detailed RAPR Assessment. Unauthorized encroachment into the RAA/DPA areas on Site have occurred which is the trigger for this CIA. In order to prevent any further encroachment into the RAA/DPA 30m setback, as shown on the Site Plan, high visibility orange “snow fencing” must be erected and maintained along the RAA/DPA extant. Currently snow fencing is erected along the northwest RAA Tributary 1 boundary within Stage 6, as well as at the clearing boundaries of the road right of way over Tributary 1. Snow fencing was not erected along the southeast RAA Tributary 1/D1 boundary within Stage 7; however this was deemed acceptable based on no further works taking place in the area. No further clearing or grubbing has been or will be completed in Stage 6 or 7 until an approved DP from the Town of Ladysmith is in place. A QEP will perform a Site visit to confirm the snow fencing has been erected. Disturbance within the RAA/DPA will only be permitted upon approval of the Detailed Assessment submitted under RAPR and successfully obtaining a development permit from the Town of Ladysmith. The developer understands that the access to SPEAs in the long term needs to be restricted. There should be no encroachment into SPEAs including any dwellings, clearings, people, domestic animals or vehicles. The SPEAS will be flagged and marked with signage along the lot boundaries asking that the public stay out of and respect the sensitive riparian habitat, as well as the potential for permanent fencing as a barrier. Property owners will be advised about SPEA locations on bills of sale with copies of the RAPR report. Even though the Change Approval and Notification (Changes In and About a Stream) was submitted to FLNRO for the culvert crossing on Tributary 1 to connect Stage 6 and 7 on April 30%, 2021; and a Change Approval for the culvert installation was approved under Section 11 of the WSA and received on August 30", 2021 (File 1005133), the Town of Ladysmith requires that these activities only proceed after obtaining an approved DP. The approved Section 11 activities involve the installation of a culvert on Tributary 1 to allow for road construction in the road right of way. These construction activities involve SPEA encroachment as permitted under the approved Section 11 (File 1005133). 4.5 Erosion and Sediment Control (ESC) SPEA areas and stream channels must be protected from the proposed property developments from erosion and sediment issues. An erosion and sediment control plan by Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. was developed and implemented in 2021 for Stage 5 and 6 of the Site which had been cleared and grubbed in the RAA/DPA; Stage 7 of the Site is currently only cleared within the RAA/DPA. Stage 7 ground conditions were left rough after tree clearing within the RAA/DPA, with stumps left in place, woody debris left on the ground, and shrubs/herbs present. This ground cover is currently acting as a form sediment and erosion control, decreasing the chance of sedimentation and runoff Environmental Management and Consulting Page 637 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 638 Zg \/ Condition and Impact Assessment Holland Creek Partnership TerraWest Project: JDHC22-02 Page 7 of 8 leading downslope into Tributary 1. Prior to development activities in Stage 7, an erosion and sediment control plan must be completed, and once activities begin it must be implemented. A QEP will complete Site inspections to ensure the implementation of erosion and sediment control measure are correctly in place and maintained. Further guidance on sediment and erosion control as land clearing and development occurs can be taken from the Develop With Care - Environmental Guidelines for Urban and Rural Land Development in B.C. Best Management. 4.6 Stormwater Management The majority of the RAA/DPA area around Tributary 1 and D1 consists low lying vegetation in Stage 7 and bare soil in Stage 6 and is considered raw and undeveloped. Clearing activities within the RAA/DPA have not appeared to cause increases in stormwater runoff into the SPEA and subsequently Tributary 1 or D1. The future development of the Site must ensure that runoff patterns and water quality are not altered. Impermeable surfaces increase stormwater runoff and could impact Tributary 1 and D1 if not managed correctly. Site servicing and stormwater management plans were prepared by Newcastle Engineering Ltd. for the Site. Further guidance and practices as lots are developed can be found in the publication; Stormwater Planning; A Guide for British Columbia. 4.7 Floodplain Concerns Clearing activities withing the RAA/DPA of Tributary 1 and D1 have not been observed to cause concerns related to floodplains. 5.0 Closure The unauthorized clearing activities that occurred without an approved Development Permit from the Town of Ladysmith on Site within the RAA/DPAs associated with Tributary 1 and D1, appear to have had very little, if any effect on their associated SPEAs. As discussed in Section 4.4, activities involving SPEA encroachment did occur as permitted under the approved Section 11 (File 1005133), which involved vegetation clearing in preparation for the installation of a culvert on Tributary 1 to allow for road construction in the road right of way. However even though an approved Section 11 was obtained clearing activities were completed again prior to receiving an approved Development Permit. It is imperative that this CIA along with the current RAPR are approved by local and provincial government prior to any further disturbances or works within the RAA/DPA areas on Site. One immediate requirement that must be met is the installation of further snow fencing and the maintenance of currently installed snow fencing for the identification of the RAA/DPA 30m boundary on Site. A follow up Site visit will be Environmental Management and Consulting Page 638 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 639 \; Condition and impact Assessment Hollond Creek Partnership Terrawest Project: JOHC22-02 Page 8 of8 completed to ensure the fencing has been placed in the correct locations and no further disturbances have occurred withing the RAA/DPA. Environmental Management and Consulting Page 651 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 652 D. R. Clough Consulting Fisheries Resource Consultants 6966 Leland Road Lantzville B.C. VOR 2HO Ph/Fax: 250-390-2901 Cell: 250-714-5416 email:drclough@shaw.ca March 20, 2013 Attn: 0885538BC Ltd and Stzuminus First Nation c/o Glenn Carey, Project Manager 6774 Dickinson Road Nanaimo, BC V9V 1A2 Ph: 250-390-1475 email: s.22 RE: Holland Creek Watershed, Ladysmith B.C. Environmental Assessment Introduction: In the proposal for the development on property on the south side of Holland Creek we were asked to provide a preliminary Biological assessment during the winter. The objectives of the assessment were to determine; 1.) Stream and drainage mapping: There are two unnamed drainages as well as Heart Creek and Holland Creek in the development area. We will identify the location in the field with flagging and GPS the location of the unnamed drainages for upload files preliminary planning maps. 2.) Stream Fish Habitat values: The streams will be assessed with a standard fish habitat assessment to determine the physical status of the channel as well as potential for fish presence and type. Po Inspect the proposed bridge crossing area on Heart Creek. Consultation: The importance of this watershed to Stzuminus First Nations, Ladysmith Sportsmen Club and Town of Ladysmith will result in consultation to determine their interest and input in fisheries values. There will be a site visit and meeting to explain findings and listen to concerns. Methods Stream mapping Brad Remillard, RPBio and Dave Clough, RPBio undertook the stream channel assessments in January and February 2013. We began at either the top or bottom of the major drainages and flagged stations and tributaries as we inspected the channels for habitat characteristics. Hand held Garmin (450) GPS was used with a cellular GPS application (Everytrail) and a photo and location reference as well. GPS data was edited on Garmin Mapsource software and uploaded to Google Earth for display. The survey area is bounded by Holland Creek on the north east and the Hydro line on the south west. Stream Habitat Each stream was inspected bya biologist for fish habitat suitability. Fish habitat features such as barriers, rearing and spawning habitat as well as flow regimes were analyzed. We also referred to past fish presence information from past electroshock surveys and information from local stream stewardship groups. Holland Ck Lot 103 Biological Assessment DRCMar13.doc 1 Page 652 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 653 Bridge Site Inspection The general area (taken from the preliminary mapping) suggested approximately 100m of area along Heart Creek. This area was walked to determine the best site based on a narrow confined channel that would result in least impact to fish habitat values. Consultation The Stzuminus First Nation was consulted at their bad office on January 27, 2013 to discuss the development and the possibility of a fish hatchery. The Ladysmith Sportsmen attended on-site tour with the proponent and a follow up inspection of hatchery locations on the 27" of February. Results Study Area Overview; Holland Creek is a salmon and trout stream its entire length adjacent the subject property. The salmon swim upstream under the E&N Railway culvert adjacent the island Highway Bridge then upstream approximately 400m inside the Holland Creek Park to the Dogwood Avenue Bridge. To this point the river is heavily utilized by Chum salmon spawners in October and November. The river then continues upstream past the Lot 103 tributaries in a confined valley. Salmon access lives approximately 1.8km above Dogwood Avenue at Crystal falls, a 10m bedrock barrier. The reach above Dogwood is used by Coho spawners as well as Cutthroat. Crystal Falls is the first of many in a long (8.5 km) steep climb up to Holland Lake (670m elev.). There are resident Cutthroat trout and Rainbow Trout above the falls to Holland Lake. Holland Lake is impounded and used as part of the Town of Ladysmith water supply (Company Dam). Holland Creek is protected by a second growth forest that is 30 to 100m in width on each side to the park boundaries and beyond. The forest was logged; the stumps show it was historically dominated by Douglas Fir with Red Cedar near the water. The forest is regenerating with those species as well as Red Alder, Broad Leaf Maple and many shrub species including Willow, Indian Plum, Ocean Spray, Salmonberry, Sword Fern and Blackberry. There are a few veteran Douglas Fir in the forest. This same forest type extends upland into Lot 103 area with the largest trees found in the Heart Creek valley. Lot 103 also has many polygons of younger stands of trees just emerging from the brush as well as a recent logging above either side of Heart Creek. The Holland Creek foot trail encircles the creek on both sides, with a bridge over each of the Lot 103 tributaries near their entrance to Holland Creek. The Hydro line provides the southwest boundary to the property and Holland Creek/Heart Creek are on the northeast boundary of the lot. The Holland Creek watershed has seen a concerted effort of salmon enhancement and habitat restoration over the last 20 years. There are now hundreds of pieces of wood debris placed for fish habitat. Four sidechannel areas have been dug out in the lower reaches increasing the summer wetted habitat and winter flood refuge significantly in Holland Creek. This work has been done bya partnership led by the Ladysmith Sportsmen Club working with Stzuminus First Nation Fisheries Program and Town of Ladysmith. There is a hatchery on Bush Creek that incubates approximately 15,000 coho fry and 50,000 Chum fry from this creek annually. There are plans to consider relocation of the Bush Creek hatchery to Holland Creek due to the better water quality, easier access and safety. Assessment results are presented overleaf with a Map, and Photos for each drainage. Stream Mapping/Fish Habitat Streams were at medium to high flow levels during the survey allowing for identification of the mainstems as well as smaller tributaries. There are three Holland Creek tributaries that drain the proposed development area; Tributary 1, 2 and Heart Creek respectively from downstream to up (Figure 1). Holland Ck Lot 103 Biological Assessment DRCMar13.doc 2 Page 653 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 654 Tributaries 1 and 2 are unnamed drainages that enter Holland Creek over bedrock water falls (5m) with no fish access. Table 1) Holland Creek Lot 103 Fish Habitat Summary. Drainage Fish Access/Habitat Holland Creek Yes Tributary 1 No Tributary 2 No Heart Creek Yes Tributary 1 The mainstem is 830 m long through the property from the hydro line to Holland Creek. It enters over a 5m bedrock falls just north of the Dogwood Avenue Bridge parking lot. The channel is approximately 2.1m wide. The lower reach to the first hydro line (200m) is relatively low gradient at 4-11%. This reach appears to have been diverted from its historic route as the channel has evidence of recent formation with no natural stream characteristics. It was likely diverted west to make way for Dogwood Avenue. Above the old Hydro right of way the channel appears natural but disturbed by historic logging lacking large woody debris. The channel gradient increases to more than 20% and is confined in a small valley with vegetated sidewalls to just below (150m) the Hydro Line where it is fed by three seasonal channels T1, T1-2, T1-3, that braid across the Hydro Line. The channel furthest north is the strongest (T1). The Hydro Line and logging roads appear to have disrupted the natural course in this area such that the historical location is difficult to determine above the split in channels. There is no fish access into this channel. An electroshock in 2010 found no fish in the 200 m along the lower reach where the gradient is less than 20%. The tributary has perennial water flow to Holland Creek. Tributary 2 The main channel of Tributary 2 is 930m long upstream Hydro line crossing. It has two short tributaries (2B, 2C,) that enter it within the Lot 103 area. Beginning at Holland Creek there is a 4.5m bedrock falls that denies fish access. Upstream this channel was disturbed by historic logging lacking pools and large woody debris. It lies in a semi-confined channel with vegetated sidewalls. The creek channel is 1.7m wide in the lower reach on a gradient of 1-7% above the barrier. It loses its confinement at the Hydro line crossing where it is dry in summer. Water flow is perennial to Holland Creek and in summer this water accrues below the hydro line. Heart Creek This is the longest and largest tributary with length of 1.2 km from the Hydro line to Holland Creek. Heart Creek has a 240m long reach of salmon access, ending at a 5m bedrock water falls. Above the falls there is a confined and deep (20-50m) treed valley that creates an isolated reach of Heart Creek to the Hydro Line where the canyon ends. The average channel width was 4.1m on a 10% slope. Heart Creek goes approximately 1.0 km further upstream to its source at Heart Lake. The entire length of Heart Creek is habitat for resident Cutthroat & Rainbow Trout which occupy the lake as well as perennial pockets in the lower reach. The fish are seeded into the entire length of the stream from Heart Lake. The upper reaches above the Hydro line are more disturbed by historic logging and are seasonal while below the Hydro line, there is flow recovery in summer with perennial flow into Holland Creek. Heart Creek Bridge Site Inspection The mid reach of Heart Creek is the location of a proposed road location. We inspected the stream channel widths in this area and found the channel width and floodplain ranged between 5.0 and 6.3m. The cross section sites were flagged in the field as XS (see Fig.1). The valley walls in the area were 25% slope on the south and 50% slope on a 10m bank on the north side. There were no significant fish habitat features in the area, pools were shallow and the channel had little LWD. The banks were steep but Holland Ck Lot 103 Biological Assessment DRCMar13.doc 3 Page 654 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 655 vegetated and stable. The stream substrates are Boulder/Cobble/Gravel. There were no significant veteran trees in the vicinity. Consultation/Planning for Hatchery Ladysmith Sportsmen Club operate the Bush Creek Hatchery. They built the hatchery with the full support of the Stzuminus First Nation in 1995 after both parties agreed there was a local need. Since then there has been a shared use of the facility. The hatchery enhances Chum and Coho stocks in five local streams; Stocking, Holland, Bush, Walker and the Chemainus River. They have 10 heath stacks and a capacity for 400,000 eggs. Over the years since the hatchery was developed the water quality in Bush Creek has declined. The gravity fed water is colder, carries more sediment and dries to a trickle in early summer. The water supply plugged this year and the eggs were all transported to Nanaimo Hatchery by the club in January. The hatchery also has no electrical power other than a generator so the alarm and fish feeders work off solar power. Its remote location 2.5 km up a logging road has resulted in vandalism and robbery constantly. The new location is next to town and walking distance from local schools allowing the education programs conducted by the Club to expand. The new building may have a classroom for workshops and school programs. The developers of the property have offered their land for a hatchery at a time when the operators of the hatchery were considering relocation. Consultation meetings have been held this winter, the relocation was discussed by both groups, and they walked the sites. There is an opportunity to use T1 and T2 as well as Heart Creek which all have flowing water year round. An inspection this winter found the water temperatures to be 1-3C warmer than Bush Creek which hasa significant effect on egg development timing. The Holland Creek hatchery idea was taken to the DFO Community Programs Community Advisor for advice and permitting. This permit will require a more detailed design to identify the flow and space requirements. CONCLUSIONS The assessment of the drainages was made to determine preliminary planning for a residential development. No lot or road determinations are finalized. The developer had instructed us to provide this environmental information such that they could plan around the environmental aspects. The environmental aspects of this area show Tributary 1 and 2 to be lacking fish access but important water supplies to Holland Creek. The summer water flow contribution of these two streams is approximately 25%. Heart Creek is a fish bearing channel which has a salmon reach to the base of the falls and is populated with resident trout above. Heart Creek is protected by a deep treed ravine which provides shade and habitat to the stream. The T1 and T2 channels are confined or semi-confined in treed depressions. To determine the riparian setback of these channels a Riparian Area Assessment (RAR) will need to be done. The RAR identifies the requirement for building setbacks as well as stormwater management, construction environmental protection as well as Danger Trees, Windthrow, Floodplain, Slope Stability, and Tree Protection. The development of the hatchery will follow a series of regulatory steps, which are out of the control of the proponents but the DFO are indicating their support (they haven't said no) and they should be able to assist in getting the approvals from their auditors and provincial agencies. Heart Creek at Hydro Line culvert, Holland Ck Lot 103 Biological Assessment DRCMar13.doc 9 Page 660 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 661 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Stages 6 & 7, Holland Creek Partnership, Ladysmith, BC Windthrow & Hazard Tree Assessment Prepared for: Holland Creek Partnership Jim Dickenson, c/o Glen Carey, Project Manager, GlenCar Consultants Inc. Prepared by: Strathcona Forestry Consulting PO Box 387 Stn Mn Duncan BC V9L 3X5 strathcona.fc@shaw.ca 24 October 2021 Page 661 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 662 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Executive Summary Strathcona Forestry Consulting was retained by Jim Dickenson, property owner, c/o Glenn Carey, Project Manager, GlenCar Consultants Inc., to prepare a_windthrow and hazard tree assessment of the riparian area at Stages 6 & 7 of the Holland Creek Partnership. Stages 6 & 7 comprise residential lots being developed on Colonia Drive, off Rollie Rose Drive, in Ladysmith, B.C. The development straddles Tributary 1 of Holland Creek. The RARP (Riparian Areas Protection Regulation) Project lead is Derek Nickel RPBio at Terra West Environmental Inc. The Riparian Assessment Area (RAA) boundary is 30m; the Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA) is 10 m forTributary 1 and 2 m for Ditch 1. Boundaries were determined by TerraWest Environmental Inc., D.R.Clough Consulting, and Bennett Land Surveying (Coastal) Ltd. A Post-Clearing Tree Risk Assessment conducted by Vancouver Island Tree Service in July 2021 identified trees deemed to have an elevated likelihood of failure. The purpose of this report is to determine whether there are windthrow concerns within and adjacent to the SPEA as a result of the proposed development, and, where necessary, to prescribe windthrow protection measures. Forest cover at two edge segments (east and west sides of Tributary 1) was assessed. Windthrow risk at was rated MODERATE. Likelihood of windthrow was rated MODERATE. The eastern portion of the RAA is windward to prevailing winds, and more prone to wind damage; both the windward and leeward segments contained hazardous trees. Eleven trees, including eight (8) big-leaf maples, were identified as hazard trees. Recommended hazard mitigation comprises felling (including options for high stumping and/or retention of coarse woody debris) and coppicing (maple). Coppicing will reduce tree height and remove any dangerous limbs, while encouraging lateral branching. High stumping will retain perching and nesting sites, while also providing opportunities for installing nesting boxes and bat boxes. Planting with ecologically suitable native trees and shrubs is recommended to rehabilitate the SPEA. Page 662 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 663 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Treatment to prevent windthrow should follow standard strategies to minimize disturbance to rooting layers during clearing and construction, including not creating windthrow, protecting trees in the SPEA (especially along the SPEA boundary), and retaining wildlife trees in the SPEA. Measures to avoid disturbance to existing trees will decrease potential for additional hazard trees, enhance biodiversity, and help to maintain a carbon sink. If the measures identified in this report to protect the integrity of the SPEA and surrounding riparian habitat are implemented by the developer, there will be no harmful alteration, disruption or destruction of natural features, functions and conditions that support fish life processes downstream of the riparian assessment area. Mitigative actions (treatment of hazardous trees and remediation of the SPEA) will yield a net environmental improvement. Recommended strategies will enhance local biodiversity of both riparian and upland forest areas by increasing resiliency. Additionally, if the recommendations contained in this report are followed during planning and construction, risks associated with windthrow and hazard trees can be mitigated to reduce long-term maintenance while also enhancing safety within and surrounding the riparian forest stand. Page 663 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 664 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Introduction Strathcona Forestry Consulting was retained by Jim Dickenson, property owner, c/o Glenn Carey, Project Manager, GlenCar Consultants Inc., to prepare a windthrow and hazard tree assessment at Stages 6 & 7 of the Holland Creek Partnership. Stages 6 & 7 comprise residential lots being developed on Colonia Drive, off Rollie Rose Drive, in Ladysmith, B.C. Tributary 1 of Holland Creek flows northeast between Stages 6 & 7. The RARP Project lead is Derek Nickel RPBio at Terra West Environmental Inc. The Riparian Assessment Area (RAA) boundary is 30m; the Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA) is 10 m forTributary 1 and 2 m for Ditch 1. Boundaries were determined by TerraWest Environmental Inc., D.R.Clough Consulting, and Bennett Land Surveying (Coastal) Ltd. A Post-Clearing Tree Risk Assessment conducted by Vancouver Island Tree Service in July 2021 identified five (5) big leaf maple trees “deemed to have an elevated likelihood of failure, and which pose an unacceptable level of risk to proposed structures and dwellings.” The report recommended that these (5) trees be removed to mitigate the risk. The report also noted that large maples at the north-east side of the development (bottom of the slope) should be pruned to remove any large diameter deadwood from the canopy. The purpose of this report is to determine whether there are windthrow concerns within and adjacent to the SPEA as a result of the proposed development, and, where necessary, to prescribe windthrow protection measures. The intent is to maintain tree cover where safely possible in conjunction with the planned development. The Riparian Area is to be dedicated to the Town of Ladysmith as parkland. Riparian Areas Protection Regulation The Riparian Areas Protection Regulation (RAPR) defines “stream” to encompass any watercourse — natural or human-made-—that provides fish habitat, contains water on a perennial or seasonal basis, is scoured by water or contains observable deposits of mineral alluvium, and has a continuous channel bed, including a watercourse that is Page 664 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 665 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting obscured by overhanging or bridging vegetation or soil mats. A watercourse may not itself be inhabited by fish, but may provide water, food and nutrients to streams that do support fish. Under the Riparian Areas Regulation, a proponent must prepare a Riparian Assessment report in support of their application to local government for development approval if development is proposed within 30 m of a stream or the top of a ravine bank of a stream. The Assessment Report must be prepared by a Qualified Environmental Professional (or group of professionals) who understands the interaction of various features, functions, and conditions of riparian areas. The RAR Assessment Report prescribes the specific requirements of the SPEA (streamside protection and enhancement area) and ZOS (zone of sensitivity). The width of the SPEA, determined through appropriate methodology, outlines required measures to maintain the integrity of the SPEA. The ZOS, determined through detailed assessment procedures under the RAR, identifies a zone of sensitivity adjacent to a waterbody within which disturbance is restricted, i.e., an undisturbed riparian buffer. The effects of the biophysical processes through which riparian vegetation influences in stream conditions vary continuously with buffer width. Under the RAPR, a fixed buffer width is generally selected in order to maintain in stream conditions similar to those found in undisturbed forests, and/or to target specific species such as salmonid fishes. Specific experts (i.e., geotechnical advisors, windthrow specialists) may be called on to provide their relative expertise on site characteristics that may pose specific problems or concerns. The Riparian Assessment report for the proposal must demonstrate appropriate assessment methods have been followed, and must certify: |. if the development is implemented as proposed there will be no harmful alteration, disruption, or destruction of natural features, functions, and conditions that support fish life processes in the riparian assessment area, or ll. if the streamside protection and enhancement areas identified in the report are protected from the development and the measures identified in the report as necessary to protect the integrity of those areas from the effects of the development are implemented by the developer, there will be no harmful alteration, disruption or destruction of natural features, functions and conditions that support fish life processes in the riparian assessment area Page 665 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 666 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Next pages: Holland Creek RAR and Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek Partnership Page 666 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 667 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting SKETCH PLAN TO ACCOMPANY RIPARIAN AREAS PROTECTION REGULATION REPORT FOR STAGE 6 AND STAGE 7 OF HOLLAND CREEK HOLLAND CREEK ‘ra Ps hows TH LOCATION OF LE FEATURES CRY, WO DOES HOT IRscaTe oreeo CENAES Tat HAY ENT ON OR ARON To DORSET ‘commen comecr bennett o {ano SURVEWING (COASTAN LTD. tsar omeer eae weer Seoevemn co a Roma commen ATES STANT SS SO ORAS ESP SETONESER TORT Ts POUANO REAR) ET IONS Holland Creek RAR. To the west are cleared areas with new and future residential development, to the south (upslope) is a BC Hydro right-of-way; immediately to the northeast is forest, while further to the northeast is established residential development along Dogwood Drive and Arbutus Crescent. To the east is mature forest (scheduled for future development). The SPEA is dedicated to the Town of Ladysmith for parkland. Signs of previous human activities (e.g. historical logging) were evidenced by a brushed- in, old skid trail and partially buried choker cables. The Town of Ladysmith does not have a Tree Protection bylaw. Water Courses Tributary 1 of Holland Creek flows northeast between Stages 6 & 7 and discharges into Holland Creek, which discharges into Ladysmith Harbour, less than a kilometre to the northeast. Biogeoclimatic Classification The subject site is classified in the Coastal Douglas-fir Moist Maritime Subzone (CDFmm). The CDFmm has warm dry summers and moist mild winters. Prevailing winds in winter are generally southeasterly (to southwesterly). Ecosystems in the assessed area were classified as CDFmm_04/05/01. Vegetation The SPEA is forested with mature to maturing second-growth forest cover. Forest cover is “mixed” — with coniferous and deciduous trees. Coniferous trees dominate - mainly Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga heterophylla), with lesser amounts of western redcedar (Thuja plicata), and a minor components of grand fir (Abies grandis), and western hemlock (Tsuga heterophylla). Deciduous cover is dominated by big leaf maple (Acer Page 671 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 672 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting macrophyllum), with a lesser component of red alder (A/nus rubra). Many of the big leaf maples are dominant trees in the canopy. The understorey is characterized by a discontinuous shrub layer (sword fern, salal, and Oregon grape) and a discontinuous moss layer (Hylocomium splendens, Kindbergia oregana, Rhytidiadelphus triquetus). Observations of historical blowdown indicate trees in the local area are fairly windfirm. Forest cover was recently removed from lands on either side of Tributary 1 in conjunction with development of Phases 6 and 7. After the prolonged drought in the summer of 2021, trees could be vulnerable to windthrow this fall and winter, especially if saturation from heavy rains coincides with strong windstorms. Forest cover along the eastern side ofthe SPEA is likely more vulnerable to blowdown due to direction of prevailing winds in winter. Soils in the area developed in moderately deep, sandy gravelly fluvial, fluvioglacial and/or marine deposits. Soils are well to imperfectly drained. Very gravelly to gravelly loamy sand is the usual texture in the upper horizons; subsoils consist of very gravelly loamy and or very gravelly sand. The coarse fragment content is at least 35% and usually exceeds 50% by volume. A weak to moderate cemented layer is generally present at depths between 35 and 90 cm; relatively unweathered parent material is encountered at depths between 1.5 and 2 m. The usual taxonomic classification is Orthic Dystric Brunisol; the lesser common soil is a Duric Dystric Brunisol (MoE Technical Report 17). Site Visit Field work took place on October 14, 2021. At the time of the assessment, the Top of Bank (Top of Bank) and SPEA were flagged and surveyed in with hard pins. The development site had been cleared up to the RAPR setbacks. Lots were not marked. Trees had not been previously tagged. As part of this study, potentially hazardous trees were flagged and numbered, but were not GPS referenced, due to inclement weather on the day of the assessment. 12 Page 672 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 673 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Stages 6 and 7 and Holland Creek Tributary 1 SPEA Stages 6 & 7- Development site cleared up to the RAR setback. Fie Big leaf maples constituted the majority of hazardous trees. 14 Page 674 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 675 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Efforts are encouraged to retain wildlife trees in the SPEA / future parkland. 15 Page 675 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 676 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Windthrow - Background Discussion Windthrow (Tree fall) — tree uprooting or stem breakage that results when wind loads exceed stem or anchorage strength. The purpose of windthrow assessment is to determine whether there are windthrow concerns as a result of proposed development and prescribe windthrow protection measures outside of the SPEA. In coastal BC, the most common cause of stand damaging winds is the western movement of extra-tropical low pressure systems from the Pacific Ocean. These storms produce counter-clockwise rotating regional-scale wind fields that interact with local geography and terrain. Pacific low pressure systems are strongest during the coolest months (i.e. October to April) when they are accompanied by gusty winds and high rainfall. The long duration of these storms and the high rainfall can be significant factors in windthrow risk because root-soil cohesion breaks down as trees rock back and forth in wet soil. In routine events, local geography and terrain produce predictable differences in local wind speeds. Catastrophic damage patterns during intense systems are less dependent on local terrain. WIND TURNING MOMENT During strong Pacific low systems with wind and heavy rains, root-soil cohesion breaks down as trees rock back and forth in wet soil (left). Intense winds can cause boles to “snap” (right). 16 Page 676 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 677 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting The other large scale weather systems which can cause stand damaging winds are arctic ridges of high pressure. These cold, dry systems occasionally move south over the interior of BC and outward toward the coast. Strong outflow winds through major valleys are associated with these winter systems, particularly when there is an offshore low pressure system and therefore a steep differential gradient in surface air pressure (high to low). In the summer, local wind effects are created where strong differences in air temperature develop. On-shore winds develop in the afternoon as the land heats up relative to the ocean. Windthrow Assessment Windthrow hazard and likelihood assessment is conducted on those areas in the stand (edge segments) that have a risk to values or objectives as a result of windthrow. 1. A set of diagnostic questions is used to assess various hazards for windthrow. 2. Three hazard components (topographic, stand and soil) are assessed and then brought together in a ranking table to provide an overall biophysical hazard for windthrow. The three components take into account location, and characteristics of the stand and soil median - all factors critical to assess the inherent hazard of the area for windthrow — i.e., the biophysical hazard. Biophysical Hazard — the intrinsic stability of the stand in its pre-treatment condition. The inherent ability to resist wind damage is the cumulative result of topographic, soils and stand features interacting as the stand develops with endemic windloading. 3. The biophysical hazard is then used along with an estimate of treatment hazard (activity associated with development) to rank the likelihood of windthrow occurring on the edge segment. Treatment Hazard — is the way in which a particular treatment increases or decreases the windloading or wind resistance of trees. A simple example of treatment hazard is the influence of land clearing to expose new edges. Treatment hazard can be reduced by further treatments such as pruning, or topping. 17 Page 677 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 678 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Treatment hazard ranges from low to high depending on howor where land clearing will be applied. The two working together give an indication of how likely windthrow will be on the edge or within a retained forest stand, (i.e., the likelihood of windthrow). | TN HighLacihood~ Scenarios 4. Once the likelihood of windthrow is determined, consequences are considered to provide an assessment of windthrow risk. Windthrow risk is the combination of the likelihood of windthrow and the potential consequences of that windthrow. Windthrow risk reflects the risk associated with the site plan, considering the likelihood of windthrow against limits (thresholds) that are set based on consequences. Windthrow risk is not equal to the likelihood of windthrow. If considerable windthrow is expected, but there are no consequences, there is little risk. Windthrow impact definitions © Windthrow Likelihood - is the expected level of damage from endemic winds. It combines Biophysical Hazard and Treatment Hazard. ¢ Windthrow Consequences - is the probable level of impact on specific management objectives, or sensitivity of those objectives, if the expected level of windthrow occurs. © Windthrow Risk - is the potential for a negative consequence from windthrow caused by endemic winds. It is the combination of Windthrow Likelihood and Consequence. 18 Page 678 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 679 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Windthrow treatment, when prescribed, is necessary to retain and/or enhance riparian habitat and reduce hazard (to workers, residents, visitors, structures). Where not safe, consider retaining Coarse CWD may be a Woody Debris to enhance biodiversity consideration 24 Page 684 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 685 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Assessment Results Windthrow risk assessed at two segments of Holland Creek Tributary 1 SPEA at Holland Creek Partnership Stages 6 & 7 is rated Moderate. Windthrow likelihood is Moderate. Eleven (11) trees assessed as hazard trees are recommended for removal (falling into the SPEA). Tree size and species were major determinants of windthrow risk. Large big leaf maples rated highest for highest windthrow risk. Of the eleven trees, eight (8) were big-leaf maple, two (2) were smaller Douglas-fir, and one (1) was a smaller western hemlock near the stream crossing. Except for one Class 4 big leaf maple, all other trees assessed as hazard trees were live trees. However, many larger maples in the area feature as dominant trees nearing the end of biological rotation. Observations during the field assessment indicated that some trees along the edge of the SPEA have incurred physical damage, likely as a result of land clearing for development. Signs of tree damage included stem scars, root removal, and, in one case, evidence of “pushover” of a whole tree. Care must be taken during development to avoid disturbance within the drip line of trees along the edges of the SPEA. Damaged trees can be more susceptible to windthrow and disease. The coast of British Columbia is subjected to severe storms in the fall/winter. The subject site is somewhat protected from prevailing winds by local topographic features (nearby hills, mid-slope position). Recent removal of surrounding, protective tree cover from lands on either side of the riparian area of Tributary 1 could exacerbate effects of winter storms. Extended periods of little precipitation — as occurred in the summer of 2021 — can cause severe stress to trees. Long dry spells make trees more susceptible to fungi and insects. In a prolonged drought, studies indicate tree deaths can occur as a result of carbon starvation because trees close their stomata, blocking entry of carbon needed for photosynthesis. Drought-damaged, weakened trees are extra susceptible to damage from heavy winds and rain in severe storms. Hazard mitigation is recommended for hazard trees. Identified hazardous trees have defects which could increase susceptibility to wind damage, which poses a risk to workers and future residents. Dead/dying trees along the upper edge of the SPEA, adjacent to future homes, contribute to woody fuel that could be a potential interface fire risk. 25 Page 685 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 686 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Best management practices to manage windthrow risk and hazard trees typically involves a variety of treatments, including spiral pruning, coppicing (to remove dead/dying high branches and reduce height while encouraging lateral branching) and removal (with options for high stumping and / or retention of coarse woody debris). In this case, removal (directional falling into SPEA) is recommended. High stumping is recommended for the maples, which can be expected to coppice. Nesting boxes for bats and birds could be considered for high stumps. As noted in the Post-Clearing Tree Risk Assessment conducted by Vancouver Island Tree Service (July 2021), large maples at the north-east side of the development (bottom of the slope) could be pruned to remove any large diameter deadwood from the canopy. Tree protection fencing must be in place to ensure appropriate setbacks. (See Site Plan and tree list, Appendix 1) ¢ Prior to commencement of clearing/construction, an ocular survey should take place to identify any additional Danger Trees that may result from conditions occurring after this assessment took place. Appropriate treatment must be implemented prior to clearing/construction in order to ensure the site is safe for the uses intended. e During site preparation and construction, monitor clearing and construction within the RAA adjacent to the SPEA by a QEP. e Use a qualified Arborist for the treatment work. e Assign a qualified monitor to oversee tree retention and protection activities within the development area throughout the length of the project. e Wherever safely possible, attempt to retain existing tree cover within the SPEA, in order to maintain bank stability. e Minimize disturbance to roots of trees within the RAA and on the edge of the SPEA. Limit ground disturbance within the drip line (at least 3 m from boles of trees) within the RAA from the edge of the SPEA. e Retain native ground cover in SPEA (salal, Oregon grape, salal, ferns, mosses, etc.) e Promptly re-vegetate any areas disturbed within and surrounding the SPEA with native trees and shrub species ecologically suited to the site (as per direction from a QEP, and under direction of a qualified landscaper). Numbers of plantings may need to be adjusted pending a post-clearing survey by a QEP. Implementation of mitigative actions (e.g., hazard tree treatment and remediation of the SPEA) will yield a net environmental improvement. Remediation will increase resiliency of riparian forest at Tributary 1. Decadent, hazardous maples in the second- growth forest stand at Tributary 1 are very likely to fall down in the near future, especially given predicted intensity of storms associated with climate change. Remediation will provide a better outcome for this forest. Remediation will compensate identified deficiencies with species diversification (overstorey and understorey) and habitat diversity (increased levels of coarse woody debris). Species and habitat diversification will result in succession to a more maintenance-free and safer forest. If the measures identified in this report to protect the integrity of the SPEA and surrounding riparian habitat are implemented by the developer, there will be no harmful alteration, disruption or destruction of natural features, functions and conditions that support fish life processes in (and/or downstream of) the riparian assessment area. Strategies to sustain tree cover will help enhance local biodiversity of both riparian and upland habitats. Finally, if the recommendations contained in this report are followed during planning and construction, risk associated with windthrow and hazard trees can be mitigated to ensure the safety of the intended development. 28 Page 688 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 689 Stages 6 & 7 Holland Creek ace strathcona Forestry Consulting Appendix 1. Page 694 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 695 PROJECT: Holland Creek Area, Stage 5, Ladysmith, BC { FILE NO.: F9446.01 DATE: March 26, 2021 1.0 INTRODUCTION 1.1 Background a. For the purposes of this report “the Property” is defined as the Holland Creek Area Stage 5. The Property is located on the east coast Vancouver Island within the ToL. b. The proposed development for the Property at the time of this report includes the construction of a twenty (20) lot residential subdivision with associated civil utilities and hard surfacing. c. The Property is located within DPA 6, as per the ToL, OCP Map 2 — Development Permit Areas. d. For more information, please reference the civil plans prepared by the project’s Civil Engineer — NEL. e. LEA has carried out an assessment in order to provide an overview of the site conditions, BMPs, determination of areas susceptible to erosion and sediment transport and the proposed ESCP. f. In preparation of this report, we have reviewed the most current and relevant technical documents provided by EGBC, DFO, MoE, and CoN. 2.0 SITE CONDITIONS 2.1 Physical Setting a. The Property is located in the central region of the ToL. The site is situated on the south side of Dogwood Drive and is accessed via Rollie Rose Drive. 2.2 Climate and Vegetation a. The climate is characterized with long, wet and mild winters. Significant rainfall during the winters with occasional snowfall events, followed by a sunny, relatively dry-summer season.* b. The Property is located in the “Coastal western hemlock zone: western hemlock sub zone”.? 2.3 Terrain and Features a. LEA visited the property on March 23, 2021, and conducted a visual site assessment. At the time of our assessment, the Property was undeveloped. b. In general, the topography of the Property slopes south to north, with approximately 31.0m of vertical relief over the length of the Property. 2.4 Watercourses and Existing Stormwater Infrastructure a. The Property does not contain any defined watercourses within its boundaries. The closest notable watercourse near the Project boundaries is “Tributary 1” as by the attached civil site plan. Tributary 1 is a 1 Page 695 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 696 PROJECT: Holland Creek Area, Stage 5, Ladysmith, BC { FILE NO.: F9446.01 DATE: March 26, 2021 tributary to the Holland Creek watercourse. b. There is no existing storm drainage infrastructure currently on site. However, the previous stages of development leading from Dogwood Drive to the Property contain a number of catch basins and manholes, that discharge storm water into the tributaries of Holland Creek. 2.5 Soil and Bedrock Conditions a. A subsurface investigation was not included as part of the ESCP assessment. b. Published surficial geology mapping identifies the area as part of the Qualicum formation, a soil formation consisting of glaciofluvial deposits. Particles consist of a mixture of boulders, sand, silt and clay.” 2.6 Groundwater Conditions a. Given the mapped soil conditions, specifically the dense fine-grained glacial till subgrade, we expect that a shallow “perched” groundwater table is present seasonally. We expect that the groundwater flows. associated with this perched condition would be related directly to the volume and frequency of storm events b. Groundwater levels can be expected to fluctuate seasonally with cycles of precipitation. 3.0 DISCUSSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 3.1 Project Staging a. In general, there will be four major development stages specific to this project: i. Clearing and grubbing of the existing site vegetation ii. Surface preparation for construction staging. iii. Civil utilities install iv. Final grading and surfacing. 3.2 Water Management a. Site soils in the area are considered imperfectly draining, suggesting that some infiltration of surface water may occur but will likely remain in a perched condition overlying the impermeable silty glacial till soils. b. The critical area for water management will be ensuring that the quality of site runoff remains acceptable and does not negatively affect the neighboring tributaries and Holland Creek. The Contractor is expected to cover exposed erodible soils and direct site runoff into vegetated areas. For more details see attached Page 696 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 697 PROJECT: Holland Creek Area, Stage 5, Ladysmith, BC { FILE NO.: F9446.01 DATE: March 26, 2021 LEA — ESCP Drawing. It is expected that the retained vegetated area will be able to absorb/infiltrate the expected site runoff. 3.3 Erosion and Sediment Sources In general, coarse grained soils (cobbles, gravels, coarse sand) are susceptible to erosion but have a relatively low potential for sedimentation and/or sediment transport. Fine grained soils (fine sand, silt, clay) are typically susceptible to both erosion and sedimentation. It is our expectation that the subject project will likely encounter both fine- and coarse-grained soils during development. Sources of erosion and sedimentation include but are not limited to soil areas exposed during clearing and grubbing, stockpiled soils created during the excavation and earthworks phase as well as any exposed soils left in place as part of the final grading and or landscaping. Special attention must be followed where large areas relative the total parcel size (>50%) are left exposed along with exposed soils located near project boundaries. Construction traffic leading to and from site may also lead to significant erosion of the site soils and transport of deleterious material onto existing roads, causing sedimentation of the existing storm service. Critical areas prone to erosion and sedimentation specific to the Property include areas stripped of vegetation and left bare. Special attention should also be paid to exposed soils in areas along project boundaries. 3.4 Best Management Practices a. BMPs are intended to reduce erosion and sedimentation by protecting/stabilizing exposed soils and/or reducing surface flow runoff velocities that aid in the mitigation of sediment transport offsite. Commonly implemented BMPs include the following: Retaining vegetated areas and buffers. Installation of drainage paths (swales/ditches) uphill from the proposed areas of disturbance. This will allow surface/groundwater to be diverted away and around areas of disturbance. Surface roughening to reduce water velocities (contouring). Covering exposed soil slopes with coco matting to prevent rill and surface erosion. Protect natural drainage channels and ditches with check dams, sediment traps and armoring. vi. To limit erosion and sedimentation earthworks should be conducted during periods of dry weather. b. Descriptions of the planned BMPs can be found on the attached ESCP. 3.5 Erosion and Sediment Control Plan a. Measures shown in the attached ESCP must be installed prior to the related stage of development and Page 697 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 698 PROJECT: Holland Creek Area, Stage 5, Ladysmith, BC { FILE NO.: F9446.01 DATE: March 26, 2021 maintained and monitored throughout the course of development. b. Implementation of the ESCP will be the responsibility of the Contractor. It is best practice that the Contractor designate a site person to inspect to ESC measures daily and maintain if necessary. c. ESCPs are dynamic and adaptive documents that require ongoing inspection, maintenance and re- evaluation of the effectiveness of the prescribed ESC measures. If the Contractor finds that the prescribed ESC measures are not functioning adequately the following steps should be taken: i. Ensure ESC measures are installed correctly as per the most up to date ESCP. ii. | Determine if other BMPs may be best suited to mitigate the specific scenario. iii. | Assess to see if increased maintenance of existing ESC measures is required. iv. | Contact the ESC Professional if required. d. 48 hours prior to any significant storm event, the designated site person should inspect the ESC measures and ensure that the works are adequately installed to protect the site during the storm event. 4.0 CONCLUSIONS 4.1 Responsibilities a. Implementation and routine maintenance of the ESCP will be the responsibility of the Contractor. Ata minimum, the Contractor is to inspect all required BMPs weekly and provide inspection reports to the Engineer for review. The Contractor is also to inspect the ESC measures 48 hours prior to any significant storm event to ensure that the prescribed ESC measures are adequately installed. If not, they are to inform the ESC Professional so that work can be modified to best protect the site during the storm event. b. Acopy of this report along with the attached ESCP should be kept on-site at all times and made available to all personnel responsible for the installation and maintenance of the Project’s ESC measures. 4.2 Acknowledgements a. Dear Mr. Dickinson: 1. INTRODUCTION As requested, Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. (LEA) has carried out a geotechnical assessment of the above referenced property. This report provides a summary of our findings and recommendations. 2. BACKGROUND LEA understands the proposed development consists of a residential subdivision including the installation of associated on and off site civil works and services. We also understand the scope, extent, and general layout of the subject residential development is still in the design stage. ASSESSMENT OBJECTIVES Our assessment, as summarized within this report, is intended to meet the following objectives: Determine whether the land is considered safe for the use intended (defined for the purposes of this report as construction of a residential development including the installation of associated on and off site civil works and services), with the probability of a geotechnical failure resulting in property damage of less than 10 percent (10%) in 50 years, with the exception ofgeohazards due to a seismic event which are to be based on a2 percent (2%) probability of exceedance in 50 years, provided the recommendations in this report are followed. Identify any geotechnical deficiency that might impact the design and construction of the development, and prescribe the geotechnical works and any changes in the standards of the design and construction of the development that are required to ensure the land, buildings, and works and services are developed and maintained safely for the use intended. iii. Acknowledge that Approving and/or Building Inspection Officer may rely on this report when making a decision on applications for the development ofthe land. ASSESSMENT METHODOLOGY The subsurface geotechnical investigation was carried out over three consecutive days from September 23 to 25, 2013 using a Hitachi Zaxis 200 excavator provided by Parksville Heavy Equipment Ltd. A total of fifty-seven (57) test pits (TP 13-01 to TP 13-57) were excavated within the proposed development property. All test pits were backfilled upon completion. Site plans showing the extent of the development area, as well as the approximate locations ofthe test pits are attached as Figures 1 through 5, following the text of this report. Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 703 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 704 Client: 0885538 BC Ltd. Project: Holland Creek Residential Development File: F0391.04 Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 3 of 15 5. SITE CONDITIONS 51 General The subject development area is approximately 141 acres (57.05 hectares) in total size and consists of three separate legal properties. It is not known as this time whether the residential subdivision process will consist of a strata or fee simple type of development, or portions ofeach. The majority of the proposed development area has been selectively logged, with an area within the western portion of the site clear-cut in recent years. The proposed development property is located to the immediate west of the Town of Ladysmith, and is bound to the south by the limits of the Town of Ladysmith. The southern and western perimeters of the development area include BC Hydro (BCH) and Fortis right-of-ways (ROWs) to accommodate existing underground and overhead transmission line services. BCH also has a second ROW running north/south through the eastern portion of the proposed development area. Access to the subject properties is currently limited. The development area can be accessed on foot from Arbutus Drive and Dogwood Drive along the eastern extents of the development area, or by vehicle along the existing gated services roads within the BCH and Fortis ROWs. Heart Creek and two smaller tributaries run approximately southwest to northeast through the property. We understand that the potential impact on the existing creek and tributaries, relative to the proposed development, will be carried out by others. g Topography within the property is complex, with varying slopes throughout. Relatively flat plateaus exist in the western portion of the development area. Preliminary survey data indicates geodetic elevations varying from 125m at the southern extents of the property to 20m at the northern extents of the property for a total of 105m of total vertical relief sloping Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 704 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 705 Client: 0885538 BC Ltd. L Project: Holland Creek Residential Development File: F0391.04 Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 4 of 15 downhill from south to north (approximately). 5.2 Soil Conditions The proposed subdivision plan, and the existing terrain within the development area dictated that the majority of the subsurface explorations (test pits) were excavated within the southern portions of the development area. Soil conditions within the southern portion of the anticipated development area consisted of typical alluvial sands and gravel underlain by an over-consolidated silt, sand, and gravel matrix (glacial till). Glacial till was encountered throughout the southern portion of the development property at a mean depth of 1.1m. Soil conditions within the northern portion of the anticipated development area consisted of more substantial alluvial deposits. Sand and gravel, or minor variations of, were encountered predominantly throughout the northern portion of the development property. Granular materials were encountered at depths from 0.2m to a maximum depth of 3.4m. Please note, the total depth of the naturally deposited granular soils was not determined due to the dense nature of the material, the depth of the material, and the limitations of the excavation equipment. Sporadic localized subgrade soil conditions were encountered in some areas during the field investigation. i, TP 13-15 revealed a layer of “re-worked” site materials to a depth of 0.4m. We expect that re-worked site materials will be encountered throughout the property given the logging activities in the area. We expect the nature of these materials to be negligible given the scope of the anticipated earthworks associated with the proposed development. ii, TP 13-21 revealed soft, wet, organic soils to a depth of0.6m, underlain by a loose to Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 705 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 706 Client: 0885538 BC Ltd. L Project: Holland Creek Residential Development File: F0391.04 Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 5 of 15 compact silty gravel to a depth of 2.2m, with groundwater seepage observed throughout the test pit excavation. Ponded water was noted at surface in proximity to the test pit location. In addition, equipment access to the area in proximity to TP 13-21 was limited given the soft, wet nature of the surface soils. Visual reconnaissance of the are was conducted as conditions permitted. We do not expect the extent of this soft area to be significant. However, additional investigation may be warranted to determine the volume of unsuitable materials with respect to the proposed roadway construction in the area. iii, TP 13-51, TP 13-52, and TP 13-54 revealed a bearing material of very stiff to hard silt with a trace of sand and clay. While dissimilar in general composition from the glacial till discussed above, the engineering properties of this material are similar to the glacial till. We do not expect that this fine-grained stratum, given its consistency, will impact the proposed development. e. Depths are referenced to the existing ground surface at the time of our field investigation. Soil classification terminology is based on the Modified Unified classification system, The relative proportions of the major and minor soil constituents are indicated by the use of appropriate Group Names as provided in ASTM D2487 Figures 1a, 1b, and 2. Other descriptive terms generally follow conventions of the Canadian Foundation Engineering Manual. 5.3 Bedrock a. As discussed above, glacial till was encountered predominantly throughout the site, with areas of granular deposits in the northern portion of the site. b. Please note, effective refusal in TP 13-35 was reached due to either a large boulder or shallow bedrock. c. Large cobbles and boulders are common to the type ofglacial till soils encountered during Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 706 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 707 Client: 0885538 BC Ltd. L Project: Holland Creek Residential Development File: F0391.04 Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 6 of 15 the field investigation. d. As bedrock was not encountered or observed in any other areas of the property, it is reasonable to assume that that the effective refusal in TP 13-35 consisted of a large boulder. 5.4 Groundwater a. There was groundwater seepage observed, as outlined above, in TP 13-21. Groundwater was not encountered during the remainder ofthe field investigation. b. Note, the test pitting investigation was conducted during an extended period of dry weather. Given the dense, impervious nature of the subgrade soils documented during the field investigation (shallow glacial till), it is reasonable to assume that a shallow, perched groundwater table is present during the “wet” season, particularly in the southern portion of the development property. We expect that this seasonal perched condition will be directly related to the volume and frequency of storm events. c. Groundwater levels can be expected to fluctuate seasonally with cycles of precipitation. Groundwater conditions at other times and locations can differ from those observed within the bore holes at the time of our assessment. 5.5 Review of Available Mine Information a. We considered the potential impact to the proposed development by abandoned coal mines. As part of this assignment, we have reviewed historical documents with respect to coal mining activities rumored to have occurred in the area. b. Based on our review, there was no documented underground coal mining activities in proximity to the subject development area. c. Historical information indicates that the closest underground mining activities were located approximately 23km to the north. Documented mines in this area included the “Reserve Mine,” the “Morden Mine,” and the “Black Track Mines.” Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd.
