CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 6.1 General a. From a geotechnical point of view, the land is considered safe for the use intended (defined for the purposes of this report as construction of a residential development including the installation ofassociated on and off site civil works and services), with the probability of a geotechnical failure resulting in property damage of less than 10 percent (10%) in 50 years, with the exception of geohazards due to a seismic event which are to be based on a 2 percent (2%) probability of exceedance in 50 years, provided the recommendations in this report are followed. b. Site development for the study area is understood to require grading (general excavation, embankment construction, and earthworks typical of this type of development) to establish or improve roadways and proposed building lots. Therefore, lots are subject to re- examination during and after area grading but prior to building permit issuance. We have taken this issue into account in formulating our recommendations. c. We recommend that setbacks from steep slope crests be provided for proposed structures and roadways as a precautionary measure against slope degradation due to erosion from extreme storm events or from seismic action. Slopes that require setbacks are defined here as having an inclination exceeding 30 degrees from horizontal. Based on an examination of slopes within this development site, we conclude that there are natural slopes within the property that require setbacks from slope crests. i. Where buildings and roadways are set above slopes with an inclination greater than 45 degrees a minimum setback of 8m is recommended where slopes are between 4m to 8m in total height. Where the total slope height is less than 4m, a setback equal to the height of the slope is required; where total slope height is greater than 8m, the Geotechnical Engineer should be contacted to provide information specific to the localized slope. As a conservative estimate, for slope greater than 8m in total height, a setback equal to the Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 708 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 709 Client: Project: File: 0885538 BC Ltd. Holland Creek Residential Development F0391.04 EA) Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 8 of 15 height of the slope may be used for preliminary design purposes. ii. Where buildings and roadways are to be set above slope with an inclination of 30 - 45 degrees the set back should be a minimum of 6m where slopes are between 3m to 6m in total height. Where the total slope height is less than 3m, a setback equal to the height of the slope is required; where total slope height is greater than 6m, the Geotechnical Engineer should be contacted to provide information specific to the localized slope. As a conservative estimate, for slope greater than 6m in total height, a setback equal to the height of the slope may be used for preliminary design purposes. iii, Where buildings and roadways are set below natural slopes with a grade 30 degrees from horizontal or greater, the setback shall be the total height of the slope (as measured vertically from the toe to crest of the slope). . There is the possibility for the setbacks to be reduced given more in depth analysis of particular features or exposures. Fills may be created to establish building and roadway levels that differ from existing conditions. In this case, a building setback of3.0 metres shall be established for fills ranging from 1.5m to 3.0m high, and 5.0m where the fill exceeds 3.0m in thickness. Fill slopes shall not exceed an inclination of 2H : 1V. Fill shall be compacted to achieve a uniform and dense relative density as per our recommendations for structural fill placement and compaction. Structural fill shall be evaluated and be approved by the Geotechnical Engineer for the project. Natural soil faces shall not be undercut without subsequent support by permanent retaining walls designed and constructed to support the slope face. In general, retaining wall back slopes should be flattened to a configuration no steeper than 2H : 1V to allow for disturbance such as from temporary excavation. The Geotechnical Engineer for the project should review temporary sub-cutting such as for retaining or foundation walls deeper than 1.2m. A more detailed geotechnical analysis on a lot by lot basis may be necessary at the Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 709 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 710 Client: Project: File: 0885538 BC Ltd. Holland Creek Residential Development F0391.04 EA) Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 9 of 15 time of construction. This may be accomplished using a standard BC Building Code Quality Assurance Schedules B and C. 6.2 Structural Fill Where fill is required to raise areas that will support buildings, slabs, or pavements, structural fill should be used. The Geotechnical Engineer should first approve the exposed subgrade to confirm the removal of all unsuitable materials. Structural fill should be inorganic sand and gravel, or well-graded blasted/broken rock (subject to the review and approval of the Geotechnical Engineer). If structural fill placement is to be carried out in the wet season, material with a fines content limited to 5% passing the 75um sieve should be used, as such a material will not be overly sensitive to moisture, allowing compaction during rainy periods of weather. Structural fill should be compacted to a minimum of 95% of Modified Proctor maximum dry density (ASTM D1557) in foundation and floor slab areas, and a minimum of 95% in paved roadway and parking areas. Structural fills under foundations should include the zone defined by a plane extending down and outward a minimum 0.5m from the outer edge of the foundation at an angle of 45 degrees from horizontal to ensure adequate subjacent support. Compaction of fill should include moisture conditioning as needed to bring the soils to the optimum moisture content and compacted using vibratory compaction equipment in lift thickness appropriate for the size and type of compaction equipment used. A general guideline for maximum lift thickness is no more than 100mm for light hand equipment such as a ‘jumping-jack,’ 150mm for a small roller and 300mm for a large roller or heavy (>500 kg) vibratory plate compactor or a backhoe mounted hoe-pac or a large excavator mounted hoe-pac, as measured loose. It should be emphasized that the long-term performance of buildings, slabs, and pavements Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 710 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 711 Client: Project: File: 0885538 BC Ltd. Holland Creek Residential Development F0391.04 EA) Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 10 of 15 is highly dependant on the correct placement and compaction of underlying structural fills. Consequently, we recommend that structural fills be observed and approved by the Geotechnical Engineer. This would include approval of the proposed fill materials and performing a suitable program of compaction testing during construction. 6.3 Foundation Design & Construction — Proposed Residential Construction Prior to construction, the building area should be stripped to remove all unsuitable materials to provide an undisturbed natural soil subgrade for the footing support. Foundation loads should be supported on natural undisturbed soil approved for use as a bearing stratum by our office, or structural fill, and may be designed using the following values. For foundations constructed on structural fill, as outlined in Section 6.3 of this report, a Service Limit State (SLS) bearing pressure of 150 kPa, and an Ultimate Limit State (ULS) of 200 kPa may be used for design purposes. These values assume a minimum 0.6m depth of confinement or cover. For foundations constructed on dense, naturally deposited sand and gravel (or similar), or glacial till, an SLS bearing pressure of 150 kPa, and a ULS of 200 kPa may be used for design purposes. These values assume a minimum 0.6m depth of confinement or cover ron Exterior footings should be provided with a minimum 0.6m depth of ground cover for frost protection purposes. d. Prior to placement of concrete footings, any bearing soils that have been softened, loosened, or otherwise disturbed during the course of construction should be removed, or else compacted following our recommendations for structural fill. Compaction will only be feasible if the soil has suitable moisture content and if there is access to heavy compaction equipment. If no structural fill is placed, a smooth-bladed clean up bucket should be used to finish the excavation. Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 711 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 712 Client: 0885538 BC Ltd. L Project: Holland Creek Residential Development File: F0391.04 Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 11 of 15 6.4 Seismic Issues a. A localized area of potentially liquefiable and/or compressible soil was encountered in proximity to TP 13-21. Based on the remainder of the field investigation, and a visual reconnaissance of the area in proximity to TP 13-21, we expect the scope and total extent of the soft soils to be limited. We expect that the area of soft soil can be excavated and replaced with competent structural fill materials as required to facilitate the proposed subdivision development and associated residential construction. b. Based on the 2012 British Columbia Building Code, Division B, Part 4, Table 4.1.8.4.A, ‘Site Classification for Seismic Site Response,’ the soils and strata encountered during the test pitting investigation would be ‘Site Class D’ (Stiff Soil). 6.5 Permanent Dewatering Conventional requirements of the 2012 British Columbia Building Code pertaining to building drainage are considered suitable at this site. Once final plans and tentative elevations are determined, the Geotechnical Engineer should be consulted to provide further dewatering data. 6.6 Erosion Control Since the site consists of some erodible surfaces, erosion control is expected to be an issue of significance during the development of this property. Overland storm water controls should take into account the potential impact of concentrated runoff as it may impact adjacent sensitive areas. This should generally take the form of runoff from construction activities being directed to retention areas prior to entry to sensitive areas. Erosion and sediment control plans can be provided by our office prior to any construction activities to ensure appropriate practices are documented. Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 712 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 713 Client: 0885538 BC Ltd. { Project: Holland Creek Residential Development File: F0391.04 Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 12 of 15 6.7 Undermining Discussions and Recommendations a. Based on a review of the available information, there was no underground coal mining activity in proximity to the proposed development area. b. Historical documentation indicates that the Ladysmith Harbour, located approximately 3 km northeast of the subject development area, was used as a shipping port for coal. We do not expect that the documented shipping and/or export activities will have any impact on the proposed development. c. The proposed development should not be impacted by abandoned coal mine workings or ancillary coal mining activities. 6.8 Trenching and Utility Installation a. We understand through conversations with the civil consultant and a cursory review of the design civil drawings, that the installation of the civil works and services will include substantial excavation depths in some areas. b. Given our knowledge of subgrade soil conditions, we offer the following preliminary recommendations with respect to trenching and civil utility installation: i, The subgrade soil conditions are expected to consist primarily of very dense glacial till. ii. A continuous vertical excavation depth of 3.0m should be feasible given the anticipated subgrade conditions. This is subject to the field review and approval of the Geotechnical Engineer at the time of construction. iii, | Any excavation depths exceeding 3.0m in depth shall be sloped at a configuration of 1H : 2V beyond 4.0m in height. iv. Consideration may be given for excavation depths exceeding 3.0m in depth, subject to the field review and approval of the Geotechnical Engineer at the time of construction. Lewkowich Engineering Associates Ltd. Page 713 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 714 Client: 0885538 BC Ltd. Project: Holland Creek Residential Development File: F0391.04 Date: February 7, 2014 Page: 13 of 15 v. All excavations shall be protected from environmental conditions as required during the course of construction. Surface water and seepage shall me monitored closely during construction. vi. All excavation work shall conform to applicable criteria as outlined by Worksafe BC. Any trenching or general excavation depth that exceeds the depths outlined by Worksafe BC shall be reviewed in the field by the Geotechnical Engineer. 7. Must be obtain a Riparian Area Development Permit issued by the Town of Ladysmith prior to any works occurring. A Qualified Environmental Professional/Monitor with the authority to halt work shall be on site during all phases of construction. Temporary fencing must be installed prior to construction to sufficiently protect the upstream and downstream areas from encroachment by construction staff, construction and development activity. The fencing must have signage that identifies the area as environmentally sensitive. Trees to remain adjacent to the disturbance area and the construction zone must be protected from damage. Do not allow fill material to bury the base of trees. Install temporary fencing around the drip line of trees adjacent to construction zones to prevent compaction of root systems by heavy machinery. Disturbed riparian areas must be seeded with native grasses and mesh or fiber materials utilized to prevent erosion and promote grass growth. Must use sediment fence/filtration system in the stream channel and on adjacent slopes where practical to prevent and reduce the introduction of sedimentation into the stream. Must prevent unnecessary spillage/storage of construction material in the stream bed and contingency measures must be adhered to as addressed by the Qualified Professional. Construction site bed must be covered if there are erodible substrates (i.e., clay) every night to prevent loss of material. No concrete works, including concrete laden water, either by pore-in-place or grouting be allowed to enter the stream during works. All rock used in the works shall be clean and free of sediment producing material, durable, non-acid generating and suitably graded. Water flow in the stream must be bypassed around the work site and return to the stream bed just below the site. Must use turnouts, sumps and swales in the drainage and ditches leading to the work site to reduce site water from entering fish habitat. In addition, sump pumps must be used as necessary to directed dirty construction water outside the stream environment away from the streamside protection and enhancement area (SPEA). Newcastle Engineering provided the culvert design and Erosion Sediment Control Plan (ESC) on their drawings. D.R. Clough Consulting will be the environmental monitor for the project. This environmental protection plan is to ensure safe environmental practices are conducted with regard to work in and around water. Specific environmental concerns are: 1. Introduction of silt and debris into the stream and the associated impacts on water quality and fish habitat downstream of the construction site. 2. Containment of a hydrocarbon spill (e.g., oil, fuel) during construction. There is a fish barrier falls (5m) in the City Park at Holland Creek. Schedule of Work The work is scheduled in the general least risk fish window for Vancouver Island of June 15 — September 15. The stream has a seasonal flow regime. Instream work will not begin until the stream is either dry or at low flow and in dry weather. These conditions are expected by July 1, 2021. The start date must be reviewed and approved by the environmental monitor. Clough Consulting tan ae Page 799 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 800 Introduction: This is an addendum to provide detailed guidance on the utilization of Coarse Woody Debris (CWD) for wildlife habitat. The reason for this prescription is to compensate for the lack of wood on the forest floor that is important for wildlife habitat. The lack of CWD was identified from the environmental assessment. The lack of CWD can be compensated for by following this plan. Coarse Woody Debris Function The function of coarse woody debris in coastal forests is very important for wildlife. The material is a food supply for invertebrates that are the base of the food chain for birds, amphibians and mammals. The wood is also an important home for cavity nesting and it acts as shade or moisture storage which creates a more diverse plant community on or adjacent these piles of wood. Coarse woody debris is a key ecological component of a healthy forest. Clough (drclough@shaw.ca) <drclough@shaw.ca>; Drew Beiderwieden <drew.beiderwieden@newcastleengineering.com> Subject: Holland Creek Phase 5- Culvert Maintenance Hi Ryan As discussed yesterday, we had a meéting with the Ministry of Forest Lands, Natural Resources and Rural Development which is the department that reviews the culvert crossing application. As this culvert will have more than 2m of fill on top of it there is a concern of the culvert becoming block by debris and the subsequent ponding could cause a collapse of the road fill. To mitigate this risk the Ministry would like some assurances on the maintenance schedule that the Town will have in place for the culvert. To that end | have prepared the following recommendations for the inspection and maintenance of the system: 1. Maintain inlet sump, inlet grill, outlet grill, pipe and manhole free of debris at all times. Scheduled maintenance for the removal of debris should be planned for each fall prior to the start of the rainy season. Periodic inspection and debris removal should occur throughout the rainy season especially prior to and during any forecast heavy rainfall events. 2. Inspect the system including the inlet headwall, pipe, manhole, outlet headwall and grills for any structural damage or degradation yearly in the summer when flow is lowest. 3. Complete any repairs identified in the yearly inspection as critical to the culvert structure integrity or flow capacity prior to the start of the rainy season. | understand that Ladysmith has a crew for the maintenance of the Towns stormwater infrastructure and that culverts are part of the ongoing work that this crew undertakes. !f you could review the above mentioned maintenance inspection and provide a response regarding if the Town will be adding this culvert to the existing maintenance schedule as well as if the above noted items will be part of that maintenance plan? Plan VIP42164 Prepared by: Brittany Brooks, BNRP, BIT : Bob Crandall, QEP Report prepared for: MNP Recreation LTD February 27", 2022 Page 820 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 821 Background The subject property is in the Cowichan Lake District, located at 8396 Sa-Seen-Os Road, Youbou, BC. VOR2G0. Parcel PID: 001-282-131. The total lot size is around 0.439661 hectares, and the riparian length is roughly 36 metres. The Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA) is on Cowichan Lake and the watershed code is 920-257700. The development was a machine constructed retaining wall built with large quarry rock and a structural geotextile fabric woven between each layer with no approval or authorization. A sediment fence will need to be erected prior to work commencing. Materials must be disposed of properly. The shoreline is on a north-western exposure and during high winds prevailing from the west it becomes scoured by waves. Naturally the substrate is a ¥” to 2” plus and supports less aquatic plant species due to the water movement. Figure 2. Civic Map of property outlined in yellow. 3 of 21 Page 822 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 823 Plan When the retaining wall was built the area of development was striped to soil, removing native species such as mature Nootka rose, bracken fern, and perennial grasses. In addition, invasive and introduced species such as Himalayan blackberry, Daphne laurel, and English holly were also removed. The property owners will be instructed to replant the area with sun to part shade native shoreline plants and remove all invasive species. There will be 1 zone - terrestrial. Riparian restoration planting will commence after the removal of a geotextile landscape fabric which runs the length of the shoreline roughly 12’ wide. We will be hand-planting a selection of native ground cover, shrubs, and tree species within bagged soil. In the area of protection there was around 100 plants removed, this includes invasives (see appendix A). We will plant the equal number of native plants in the invasives place as well as return plants of the same species and maturity back where they once grew. Removal of invasive plant species will be integral for all new plants survival and invasive volunteers will need to be removed twice annually in early Spring and managed throughout the year. It will take multiple years to fully eradicate the invasive species present on site. It will take time and the plants that get established will depend on propagation from nearby colonizing species, so variation may be 4of21 Page 823 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 824 limited. The site is liable to be colonized by non-native species. These can form dense single species stands that prevent a varied ecology of native plants from developing. By revegetating with a variety of native plants, riparian zone vegetation can be jump-started with ecological diversity and companion species can be appropriately grouped. The purpose of planting is to augment, and jump start the natural succession of the site not to try and replicate or replace what previously existed in one season. This is accomplished by: 1. Preparing the area for planting by carefully (taking care not to disturb any volunteer native plants that may be returning) removing invasive species that are attempting to colonize. 2. Documenting the existing native plants (volunteers) that are attempting to re- colonize the site and making sure they are protected. 3. Planting native species suitable for the site in appropriate initial densities leaving room for natural re-colonization between planted plants. 4. Monitoring at least three times per year to: a) remove invasives as soon as they appear. b) check survival of planted plants and volunteers. c) Prepare a plan for next year’s invasive species control. Small erect twiggy rhizomatous shrub. Rapidly spreading root system has excellent soil-binding characteristics. 10 (Pi) Indian Plum * Oemleria cerasiformis - 1.5 to 5 meters. Shrub or small tree. One of the first shrubs to flower in spring in the southern part of Vancouver Island. Full sun to partial shade. Dry to moist. Open woods and streambanks. A valuable riparian component south of Ladysmith on Vancouver Island. Can spread by underground suckers. Important for wildlife. 10 (Ni) Pacific Ninebark * Physocarpus capitatus - To 4 meters. Full sun to full shade. Erect to spreading, arching shrub. Streamside thickets, wet usually open 9 of 21 Page 828 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 829 places, edges of lakes and streams. Root system is excellent for stabilizing stream banks. A common riparian species in our area. Extremely valuable for streamside restoration. 2 (As) Sitka Alder * Alnus sitchensis also known as A. sinuata- 1 to 5 meters. Coarse shrub or small tree. Full sun to part shade. Moist sites along streams, wet meadows, recently de-glaciated areas. Nitrogen fixing. A pioneer species able to naturally colonize bare areas, low nutrient soils, and disturbed sites. High flood and snow resistance. Extremely valuable for restoration work. Suggestions for successful container planting 1. Dig a hole slightly larger than the container size. 2. Fertilizer or bone meal may be added. Note: Some plants may not require fertilizer. 3. Mound soil around the plant to create a depression that will catch moisture. “Water in’ after planting. 5. Establish a watering schedule for the first year to allow the root system to establish. Maintain plants by weeding to keep invasive species out. 7. Monitor plants for browse. If browse is excessive then apply a repellant. 10 of 21 Page 829 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 830 Aftercare During the first year, plant survival can be enhanced by watering thoroughly as required during the dry period. Do not rely on early fall rain to penetrate down to the developing root systems. If plant survival is very poor, replanting in future years may be necessary. Deer and other animals such as elk and rabbits can cause tremendous damage to newly planted areas. There are many methods to prevent browse, but these are often expensive and labour intensive. Browse control should be factored in the project cost and labour should be made available to apply browse protection and monitor its effectiveness. Description of Fisheries Resources Values and a Description of the Development proposal (Provide as a minimum: Species present, type of fish habitat present, description of current riparian vegetation condition, connectivity to downstream habitats, nature of development, specific activities proposed, timelines) Unnamed trib to Holland Creek - Thetis Drive The purpose of this Riparian Area Protection Report (RAPR) is to determine the Riparian Assessment Area (RAA) boundaries, as well as the designated Streamside Protection and Enhancement Areas (SPEA) zones for the subject property located at the end of Thetis Drive. Located in the Town of Ladysmith, the assessment is required as the property owner wishes to construct a single family home. The property is presently identified as Lot 8. At the time of our assessment in March of2022, there was one stream that met the definition ofa watercourse as identified by the Fish-Stream Identification Guidebook (1998). The stream has one reach within the subject property. All works proposed are for the right bank ofthe watercourse. Stream 1- Reach 1 The subject watercourse has been classified as a stream and runs southwest to northeast along the northwestern flank of the subject property. At the time of our assessment, Reach | has an average gradient of 9.5% and an average bankfull width of 2.00m resulting in step-pool morphology. The substrate is dominated by gravels with patches of mineral alluvium and cobble. The canopy closure fluctuates seasonally but in general ranges from 80-90%. The riparian understory is comprised primarily of sword fern and salal with an overstory consisting of western red cedar, Douglas fir as well as grand fir in the young forest stage of development with occasional older secondary growth polygons. At the time of our assessment, the lot (Lot 8) had been cleared historically as part of the previous subdivision works and application. Although no FISS reports were available for this watercourse, fish presence is assumed given the proximity to fish bearing watercourses downstream (Holland Creek) and an absence of upstream barriers to fish. Note: All stormwater controls and utilities are being kept outside of the designated RAA. Stormwater from the impermeable surfaces on the property is being sent to a rock pit to reduce the overall scouring potential ofthe stormwater flows during peak rain events. Update August 14 2022 ~ The maps have been updated to include a driveway access to the house that is outside of the SPEA however within the RAA. Specific Recommendations for Lot 8 — Thetis Drive Works outside of the designated SPEA zone and within 30m of the RAPR watercourse e Areas designated as the SPEA will be flagged with high visibility flagging tape and temporary fencing. ¢ Prior to construction, a sediment and erosion control plan will be developed to prevent the discharge of sediment laden water into the SPEA or any watercourses identified on-site. This will include the installation of sediment fencing/hay bales as determined by on-site biologist prior to the initiation of construction activities. ¢ No works shall be undertaken within areas designated as SPEA. All works Scheduled Within 30m of a Watercourse and Outside of the SPEA will adhere to all recommendations as outlined in the BMP - Develop with Care: Environmental Guidelines for Urban and Rural Land Development in British Columbia. As well: o Ensure construction will proceed smoothly without harmful alteration of habitat; © Provide long-term monitoring for disturbed sites until green-up is established and the soils at the site are stable. e Heavy equipment (excavators etc.) working within 30m of the watercourse will be monitored for leaks (oil, hydraulic fluid etc.). e Disturbed areas outside the SPEA and within 30m of a waterbody will be revegetated with native plants of a size that will quickly re-establish riparian cover when construction activities are deemed complete. ¢ Detailed direction to contractors will be given to ensure that no erosion or sediment movement will occur and that no silt will be released to the waterbody during the construction and post construction phase. ¢ The site will be monitored by the designated QEP (once every two weeks or as required due to high rainfall events - >30mm/24 hour period) during the Form 1 Page 14 of 21 Page 862 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 863 FORM 1 Riparian Areas Regulation - Qualified Environmental Professional - Assessment Report construction period. Any contraventions of the RAR will be communicated to the builder as well as local municipal staff and RAR staff. A post construction report generated by the designated QEP will be submitted to RAPR and local municipal staff within 4 months after activities are deemed complete. Phone #: 2502164313 Secondary QEP Details Name: Company Address Email Phone Margaret Symon Strathcona Forestry Consulting PO Box 387 Stn Mn __ strathcona.fe@shaw.ca 250-715-6983 Duncan Canada Page 879 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 880 September 1, 2022 Ron Vanderplas Rocky Creek Homes 8.22 Via Email: ron.rockycreekhomes@gmail.com RE: 105 BURNS PLACE LADYSMITH BC RAPR POST CONSTRUCTION INSPECTION ASSESSMENT 1.0 INTRODUCTION Aquaparian Environmental Consulting Ltd (Aquaparian) was retained by Rocky Creek Homes to complete a post construction assessment for 105 Burns Road in Ladysmith BC. This parcel was previously identified as Lot 5 Cook Street / Giovando Way during the subdivision and lot development phase in 2018. A site location map has been included as Figure 1. A site plan is included as Figure 2. Because the subdivision was located in proximity of a non-fish bearing tributary of Tyee Creek (Rocky Creek), a Riparian Areas Regulation (RAR) assessment was completed for the subdivision and reviewed by the province (Assessment #5138) which determined a 10m Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA) for this tributary. This regulation was replaced in 2019 by the Riparian Areas Protection Regulation (RAPR). The stream reach adjacent to the subject parcel is between Giovando Way and Fourth Avenue and is approximately 100 m in length; however, approximately 65m of the channel north of Giovando Way flows underground as it was buried with fill some time in the past and appears to have been done during the sanitary main located on the east side of the creek and cuts across the ravine slope. The open section of the channel is 35m in length and confined within a ravine reach adjacent to the subject parcel. The stream flows under 4TM Avenue in a culvert and the confluence with Tyee Creek is immediately north of the north side of 4" Avenue. 2.0 RESULTS Aquaparian visited the site on August 24, 2022. Site photographs have been included in Appendix A. The parcel has been constructed with a single-family house and small fenced yard. The fence is located at the top of a steep slope above the dirt road / sanitary alignment within the park dedication. As identified in the RAR assessment, the Streamside Protection and 203-321 Wallace St. Nanaimo, BC V9R 5B6, 250-591-2258 Cell SARAH BONAR 250-714-8446 CHRIS ZAMORA 250-714-8864 Page 880 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 881 105 Burns PI August 2022 2 Enhancement Area (SPEA) is located in the side of the ravine outside the property boundaries. There was no evidence of any negative impact to the SPEA or migration of fines into the SPEA from the development of this parcel. A fence has been installed along side yard of the property boundary. A short section of retaining wall was constructed using large diameter rock constructed in three terraces to support the slope on the western corner of the lot. A site survey plan shows the toe of the rocks are a few centimeters over the parcel boundary of the park. The rest of the slope adjacent to the parcel above the sanitary alignment is less steep, roughly 3m high and with a slope of approximately 1H:1V with a narrow strip of vegetation along the top of the slope with a slight overhang where roots are exposed. Some erosion is evident but it appears stable. 3.0 CONCLUSION This property was developed in compliance with the measures included in the RAR assessment. No additional recommendations are warranted at this time. Aquaparian trusts that the information provided in this report meets your requirements. Any questions regarding information provided in this document, please contact the undersigned at (250) 591-2258. This parcel was previously identified as Lot 6 Cook Street / Giovando Way during the subdivision and lot development phase in 2018. A site location map has been included as Figure 1. A site plan is included as Figure 2. Because the subdivision was located in proximity of a non-fish bearing tributary of Tyee Creek (Rocky Creek), a Riparian Areas Regulation (RAR) assessment was completed for the subdivision and reviewed by the province (Assessment #5138) which determined a 10m Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA) for this tributary. This regulation was replaced in 2019 by the Riparian Areas Protection Regulation (RAPR). The stream reach adjacent to the subject parcel is between Giovando Way and Fourth Avenue and is approximately 100 m in length; however, approximately 65m of the channel north of Giovando Way flows underground as it was buried with fill some time in the past and appears to have been done during the sanitary main located on the east side of the creek and cuts across the ravine slope. The open section of the channel is 35m in length and confined within a ravine reach within park land adjacent to the subject parcel. The stream flows under 4TM Avenue in a culvert and the confluence with Tyee Creek is immediately north of the north side of 4°" Avenue. 2.0 RESULTS Aquaparian visited the site on September 7, 2022. Site photographs have been included in Appendix A. The parcel has been constructed with a single-family house and small yard. As identified in the RAR assessment, the Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA) is 203-321 Wallace St. Nanaimo, BC V9R 5B6, 250-591-2258 Cell SARAH BONAR 250-714-8446 CHRIS ZAMORA 250-714-8864 Page 889 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 890 101 Burns PI August 2022 2 located in the side of the ravine outside the property boundaries. There was no evidence of any negative impact to the SPEA or migration of fines into the SPEA from the development of this parcel. The subject parcel is separated from the riparian park area by 105 Burns Road. 3.0 CONCLUSION This property was developed in compliance with the measures included in the RAR assessment. No additional recommendations are warranted at this time. Aquaparian trusts that the information provided in this report meets your requirements. Any questions regarding information provided in this document, please contact the undersigned at (250) 591-2258. (d) That the required strategies for protecting the SPEA during and after road construction and service installation are as follows: i. Provide detailed direction to contractors regarding protection of the SPEA; ii. Monitor heavy equipment operating within 30 metres of the watercourse for leaks; iii. Reduce soil compaction by avoiding the use of machinery near retained vegetation whenever possible; and iv. Following road construction and service installation, allow natural succession of vegetation to proceed with minimal disturbance. (e) That for the long term protection of the SPEA: i. Install a permanent fence, a minimum of 1.2 metres in height, along the full side parcel lines of proposed lots 38 and 47, being the north property boundary of the two lots that are adjacent to the SPEA and within the riparian assessment area; and ii. Install permanent signage on the fencing stating that it is a “Protected Area”. Description of Fisheries Resources Values and a Description of the Development proposal (Provide as a minimum: Species present, type of fish habitat present, description of current riparian vegetation condition, connectivity to downstream habitats, nature of development, specific activities proposed, timelines) Unnamed trib to Holland Creek - Thetis Drive The purpose of this Riparian Area Protection Report (RAPR) is to determine the Riparian Assessment Area (RAA) boundaries, as well as the designated Streamside Protection and Enhancement Areas (SPEA) zones for the subject property located at the end of Thetis Drive. Located in the Town of Ladysmith, the i ired as the property owner wishes to construct a single family home. The property is das Lot 8. At the time of our z ment in March of 2022, there was one stream that met the definition of a watercourse as identified by the Fish-Stream Identification Guidebook (1998). The stream has one reach within the subject property. All works proposed are for the right bank of the watercourse, Stream 1- Reach | The subject watercourse has been classified as a stream and runs southwest to northeast along the northwestern flank of the subject property, At the time of our assessment, Reach I has an average gradient of 9.5% and an average bankfull width of 2.00m resulting in step-pool morphology. The substrate is dominated by gravels with patches of mineral alluvium and cobble. The canopy closure fluctuates seasonally but in general ranges from 80-90%. The riparian understory is comprised primarily of sword fern and salal with an overstory consisting of western red cedar, Douglas fir as well as grand fir in the young forest stage of development with occasional older secondary growth polygons. At the time of our assessment, the lot (Lot 8) had been cleared historically as part of the previous subdivision works and application. Although no FISS reports were available for this watercourse, fish presence i umed given the proximity to fish bearing watercourses downstream (Holland Creek) and an absence of upstream barriers to fish. Note: All stormwater controls and utilities are being kept outside of the designated RAA. Stormwater from the impermeable surfaces on the property is being sent to a rock pit to reduce the overall scouring potential of the stormwater flows during peak rain events, Update August 14 2022 — The maps have been updated to include a driveway access to the house that is outside of the SPEA however within the RAA. Specific Recommendations for Lot 8 — Thetis Drive Works outside of the designated SPEA zone and within 30m of the RAPR watercourse e Areas designated as the SPEA will be flagged with high visibility flagging tape and temporary fencing. e Prior to construction, a sediment and erosion control plan will be developed to prevent the discharge of sediment laden water into the SPEA or any watercourses identified on-site. This will include the installation of sediment fencing/hay bales as determined by on-site biologist prior to the initiation of construction activities. e¢ No works shall be undertaken within areas designated as SPEA. All works Scheduled Within 30m of a Watercourse and Outside of the SPEA will adhere to all recommendations as outlined in the BMP - Develop with Care: Environmental Guidelines for Urban and Rural Land Development in British Columbia. As well: o Ensure construction will proceed smoothly without harmful alteration of habitat; o Provide long-term monitoring for disturbed sites until green-up is established and the soils at the site are stable. e Heavy equipment (excavators etc.) working within 30m of the watercourse will be monitored for leaks (oil, hydraulic fluid etc.). e Disturbed areas outside the SPEA and within 30m of a waterbody will be revegetated with native plants of a size that will quickly re-establish riparian cover when construction activities are deemed complete. e Detailed direction to contractors will be given to ensure that no erosion or sediment movement will occur and that no silt will be released to the waterbody during the construction and post construction phase. ¢ The site will be monitored by the designated QEP (once every two weeks or as required due to high rainfall events - >30mm/24 hour period) during the Form 1 Page 14 of 21 Page 919 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 920 FORM 1 Riparian Areas Regulation - Qualified Environmental Professional - Assessment Report construction period. Any contraventions of the RAR will be communicated to the builder as well as local municipal staff and RAR staff. A post construction report generated by the designated QEP will be submitted to RAPR and local municipal staff within 4 months after activities are deemed complete. Subject to the conditions, requirements and standards !mposed and agreed to in section 5 of this Permit. Page 1 of 4 Page 927 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 928 4. This Permit does not have the effect of: a) Authorizing the alteration of any other Riparian Assessment Areas on the Land, except the Riparian Assessment Areas shown in Schedule B; b) Varying the use or density of the Land specified in Town of Ladysmith Zoning Bylaw 2014, No. 1860. 5. The Permittee, as a condition of the issuance of this Permit, agrees: a) To protect the Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA) shown in Schedule B by adhering to the following environmental management procedures in the Riparian Assessment Area (RAA): PRIOR TO CONSTRUCTION i) Prior to construction and at the time of building permit application a property owner must: « Provide a survey plan showing the location of the SPEA and the proposed building location, * Consult a Qualified Environmental Professional (QEP) to approve, inspect, and submit a completion report for the development, «+ Submit to the Town the QEP name and contact information, » Ensure that the QEP inspects at start-up and routinely as work is conducted to ensure the SPEA boundary is marked and not disturbed, and to identify measures ta protect the SPEA during and after construction, il) Prior to construction a job pre-work meeting will be done with the QEP to ensure that all workers understand the environmental objectives and clearly understand the roles and responsibilities to protect the SPEA. iif) Prior to construction the SPEA must be identified with signage, stakes, flagging and a sediment control fence. DURING CONSTRUCTION iv) The SPEA areas must not be encroached, altered or impacted by construction. There must be no storage of materials, garbage or construction of trails in the SPEA. v) If the root zone of a tree in the SPEA is within the RAA then the root zone must be clearly identified with stakes and flagging prior to lot preparation and construction; and must be protected as recommended by the QEP. Machinery fs not to disturb these trees and their roots in any way. Page 2 of 4 Page 928 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 929 vi} Erosion control coverings such as plastic, tarps and hay bales must be used to cover any exposed ground in the RAA. This is very important curing foundation excavation and for spoil pites which must be covered during heavy rains. vii) Drainage and runoff in the work site must be managed and detained, filtered, or infiltrated such that it is clean when it leaves the lot and enters a SPEA. viii) Heavy equipment access must be surfaced with a non-erodible firm substrate to eliminate sedimentation and rutting during the movement of heavy equipment in and out of the site. ix) Spill kits must be located on each piece of heavy equipment. Spills of any kind must be reported to the environmental monitor. x) Machinery and equipment must not be fueled within 30 metres of a watercourse. xl) In any circumstance, whether raining or not, where a potential exists for sediment to escape into the SPEA, the activity must be stopped and mitigating actions taken. xil} After construction exposed areas outside of the SPEA must be re-seeded with grass seed or covered with other non-erodible materials. All construction materials are to be removed from the site. At the time of final inspection and prior to issuance of Occupancy Permit the owner must complete the following steps: i} Provide a post construction monitoring report to the Town of Ladysmith. The report will be completed by a Qualified Environmental Professional (QEP), and it will confirm that the requirements and measures to protect the SPEA were completed and that the SPEA was adequately protected. ii) Construct a permanent fence along the SPEA boundary, which does not contain a gate, gap or other opening that would allow direct access from the property to the SPEA adjacent to each lot (Covenant CA6043367). iif) The fence on each lot must contain a sign stating “Riparian Preserve Area - Please Protect”. Page 3 of 4 Page 929 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 930 c) That for the long term protection of the SPEA: f) An owner of the Land will protect, preserve, and maintain the SPEA in its natural state (Covenant CA6043367). ii) An owner of the Land will repair, maintain and replace the fence adjacent to the SPEA as needed (Covenant CA6043367). iii) A danger tree within the SPEA on the Lands may be felled provided that once fallen, the danger tree must be left on the ground within the SPEA as coarse woody debris. 6. Description of Fisheries Resources Values and a Description of the Development proposal (Provide as a minimum: Species present, type of fish habitat present, description of current riparian vegetation condition, connectivity to downstream habitats, nature of development, specific activities proposed, timelines) Unnamed trib to Holland Creek - Thetis Drive The purpose of this Riparian Area Report (RAR) is to determine the Riparian Assessment Area (RAA) boundaries, as well as the designated Streamside Protection and Enhancement Areas (SPEA) zones for the subject property located at the end of Thetis Drive. Located in the Town of Ladysmith, the assessment is required as the property owner wishes to subdivide the property. At the time of our assessment in April and May of 2017, there was one stream that met the definition of a watercourse as identified by the Fish- Stream Identification Guidebook (1998). The stream has one reach within the subject property. All works proposed are for the right bank of the stream for this Phase of the development. Stream 1- Reach 1 The subject watercourse has been classified as a stream and runs west to east along the center of the subject property. At the time of our assessment, Reach | has an average gradient of 9.5% and an average bankfull width of 2.00m resulting in step-pool morphology. The substrate is dominated by gravels with patches of mineral alluvium and cobble. The canopy closure fluctuates seasonally but in general ranges from 80-90%. The riparian understory is comprised primarily of sword fern and salal with an overstory consisting of western red cedar, Douglas fir as well as grand fir in the young forest stage of development with occasional older secondary growth polygons. Although no FISS reports were available for this watercourse, fish presence is assumed given the proximity to fish bearing watercourses downstream (Holland Creek) and an absence of upstream barriers to fish. Specific Recommendations for Seaside Acres — Phase 2 Works outside of the designated SPEA zone and within 30m of the RAR watercourse e Areas designated as the SPEA will be flagged with high visibility flagging tape and temporary fencing. ¢ Prior to construction, a sediment and erosion control plan will be developed to prevent the discharge of sediment laden water into the SPEA or any watercourses identified on-site. This will include the installation of sediment fencing/hay bales as determined by on-site biologist prior to the initiation of construction activities. ¢ No works shall be undertaken within areas designated as SPEA except for those areas required to access the property (if crossing required for utilities and access to lands beyond) All works Scheduled Within 30m of a Watercourse and Outside of the SPEA will adhere to all recommendations as outlined in the BMP - Develop with Care: Environmental Guidelines for Urban and Rural Land Development in British Columbia. As well: o Ensure construction will proceed smoothly without harmful alteration of habitat; o Provide long-term monitoring for disturbed sites until green-up is established and the soils at the site are stable. e Heavy equipment (excavators etc.) working within 30m of the watercourse will be monitored for leaks (oil, hydraulic fluid etc.). e Disturbed areas outside the SPEA and within 30m of a waterbody will be revegetated with native plants of a size that will quickly re-establish riparian cover when construction activities are deemed complete. ¢ Detailed direction to contractors will be given to ensure that no erosion or sediment movement will occur and that no silt will be released to the waterbody during the construction and post construction phase. e The site will be monitored by the designated QEP (once every two weeks or Form 1 Page 14 of 20 Page 958 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 959 FORM 1 Riparian Areas Regulation - Qualified Environmental Professional - Assessment Report as required due to high rainfall events - >30mm/24 hour period) during the construction period. Any contraventions of the RAR will be communicated to the builder as well as local municipal staff and RAR staff. A post construction report generated by the designated QEP will be submitted to RAR and local municipal staff within 4 months after activities are deemed complete. Ladysmith Hello all, I just wanted to send this out so everyone is aware of the facts and findings from our onsite visit with QEP Dave Clough and Holland Creek Estate Manager Jim Dickinson. Myself, Habitat Officer Kevin Telfer, RAPR Biologist Nick Schwetz, Jim Dickson (Holland Creek Development Manager) and QEP Dave Clough conducted an onsite inspection of Holland Creek tributaries and ditches. It appears the RAR for 2013 was inaccurate and was not used in any development plan. QEP Dave Clough conducted a new RAR plan in 2014 that was used for the development plans to construct Holland Creek Estates subdivision. It appears no WSA non-compliance was noted, however the 2m SPEA areas around ditch 3 was not retained/protected, the ditch connected to Tributary 2 was not identified and the 2m SPEA was not identified or protected, and Tributary 2C 2m ditch SPEA was not identified or protected. Nick Schwetz and Angela Cameron will be following up on these concerns. If you have any further questions please contact me. Thanks for everyone’s assistance with this file, it was very much appreciated. Cheers! Description of the Development Proposal and Fisheries Resources Values The new content in this updated report are: Figures 3 and 4 (pages 10 and 11), with updated information on the sewage treatment and stormwater management locations. The subject site a 1.1ha lot, 3636 Yellow Point Road, in the Cowichan Valley Regional District (Figures 1, 2 and 8). It is the location of a previously developed single family home, which be removed to construct a new dwelling. On December 10, 2021 Lehna Malmkvist, RPBio, and lan Cruickshank, BSc, visited the site to conduct Riparian Areas Protection Regulation (RAPR) assessment and Sensitive Ecosystem Assessment required by the proposed project. Long Lake Creek crosses the southern portion of the property flowing from west to east, into the marine environment in Nicholson Cove. Watershed Context and Fisheries Resource Values The stream is at the downstream end of the watershed, in the last reach which discharges to the marine environment. No gazetted stream name could be found in the provincial mapping for the stream, however, the 1997 Management Direction Statement for Ladysmith Bog Ecological Reserve for BC Parks (know known as Yellow Point Bog Ecological Reserve), describes the stream as Long Lake Creek flowing out of the Reserve from Long Lake / Green Lake (two different names are used in mapping sources). The lake is located on the BC iMap (920-354500-39600 Waterbody ID 306841). The BC Fisheries Inventory Data Queries (FIDQ) database (January 26, 2022) for the lake describes, rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) and cutthroat trout (O. clarkii) as stocked and observed. Given upstream fish populations and unobstructed access from the marine environment, the stream is determined to be fish-bearing and the RAPR applies. The stream channel meanders through the forest from the culvert under Yellow Point Road to the marine environment in a cascade pool channel type, with sections of bedrock substrated, and sections of rock, cobble and gravel. With the exception of the presences of some invasive species (primarily English ivy), the adjacent SPEA and riparian vegetation on both sides is undisturbed. Site Assessment The RAPR assessment reviewed the subject property with a focus on the Riparian Assessment Area (RAA) (30 m from the Top of Bank) and the proposed work area (Figures 2 and 3). The RAA encompasses most of the lot, and the Streamside Protection & Enhancement Areas (SPEA), and stream encompasses the southern half of the lot. The property is previously developed, with an (Figures 2 and 3; Photos 1-9): existing house (unoccupied) (to be removed and new house built in the same location) separate suite/cottage (partially within the SPEA) well and pump house (in the SPEA) foot bridge over the stream driveway (small part in the SPEA) stairs to the marine shoreline (outside the SPEA) existing septic tank (to be removed) Swell Environmental Consulting Ltd. 480 Beach Drive, Victoria, BC V8S 2M6 ph. 250-217-9190 __ e. lehna@swell.ca Page 1016 of 1046 WLR-2023-30462 Page 1017 Riparian Areas Protection Regulation Report: 3636 Yellow Point Road Page 5 of 34 The vegetation on the property is lawn and landscaping on the north side of the driveway, with a fringe of conifer trees around the perimeter (Photos 1-3, 8, 9). The second growth forest south of the driveway on both sides of the stream consisting of is a mature, second growth, dry coastal forest (Photos ). It is a 8-18, 20, 21). Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii) dominated forest, with large component of western redcedar (Thuja plicata), bigleaf maple (Acer marcophyllum), and a few red alder (Alnus rubra) and grand fir (Abies grandis), with understory dominated by dull Oregon- grape (Mahonia nervosa), sword fern (Polystichum munitum), salal (Gaultheria shallon), with June plum (Oemelaria cerasiformis), oceanspray (Holodiscus discolor), red huckleberry (Vaccinium parvifolium), hairy honeysuckle (Lonicera hispidula), trailing blackberry (Rubus ursinus), etc. Along the stream edge, additional species are willow (Salix sp.), salmonberry (Rubus parviflorus), and slough sedge (Carex obnupta). The Douglas-fir/Oregon-grape forest type is a provincially red-listed (threatened) forest ecosystem. This forest is contiguous with forest in Blue Heron Park providing excellent riparian habitat for the stream and general bird and wildlife habitat. The marine shoreline vegetation in the RAA, but outside the SPEA consists of Douglas-fir, bigleaf maple, and arbutus (Arbutus menziesii) with and understory of willow (Salix sp., Nootka rose (Rosa nutkana), hairy honeysuckle, and bracken fern (Pteridium aquifolium), with ornamental plantings, and invasive species (Photo 19). Invasive, non-native species on the property include: extensive English ivy (Hedra helix), sporadic spurge laurel (Daphne /aureola) and English holly (lex aquifolium), Scotch broom (Cytisus scoparius), yellow archangel (Lamium galeobdon), periwinkle (Vinca minor), Himalayan blackberry (Rubus armeniacus), non-native rose (Rosa sp.), bur-chervil (Anthriscus caucalis), thistle (Cirsium sp.), foxglove (Digitalis purpurea), herb-robert (Geranium robertianum),wall lettuce (Lactuca muralis), bindweed (Convolvulus sepium), reed canary grass (Phalaris arundinacea), and other escaped ornamental species (particularly on the shoreline slope). The proposed new house will be constructed in the same location as the exiting house. No tree removals are proposed. Pre-Clearing Nesting Bird Survey Given the potential habitat for Western Screech-Owl in the forest adjacent to the proposed construction, a nesting survey should be conducted if development activities that could disturb owls during breeding will occur during their nesting season, March through May. The survey would be a call-playback and/or automated recording unit surveys for presence of vocal screech-owls. Additionally, while no tree or understory clearing is proposed for the development, if there are changes to the proposed plan during in the detailed design stage (eg. for the stormwater or septic design), a standard pre-clearing nesting bird survey would be required, as described below. Nesting birds and their nests are protected by both the federal Migratory Bird Convention Act and Section 34 of the BC Wildlife Act, and care must be taken to avoid destruction of nests when clearing and/or developing any property. Section 34 of the BC Wildlife Act protects birds and their eggs from possession, molestation or destruction. The nests of eagles, peregrine falcons, gyrfalcons, ospreys, herons, and burrowing owls are protected at all times of the year. The nests of all other species are protected when the birds or their eggs are in the nest. o If apermanently protected nest is adjacent to the construction footprint, the bird biologist will provide recommendations for buffers and protection during construction, as described with the Guidelines for Raptor Conservation during Urban and Rural Land Development in British Columbia (2013): = https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/environment/natural-resource- stewardship/best-management- practices/raptor_conservation_guidelines_2013.pdf Tree removal and vegetation clearing should be conducted between August 15 and February 1 to minimize the risk of damaging nests. Pre-clearing nesting bird surveys should be conducted if tree or vegetation removal will occur during breeding season. While the period between August 15 and March 15 has been identified by Environment Canada and the BC Ministry of Environment as the general period least likely to involve active bird nesting, this time period does not coincide with the breeding and nesting habits of eagles, many owls species, or herons (Grant Bracher, FLNR and Ann Nightingale, VNHS pers. comm. 2018), therefore we recommend a nesting bird survey be conducted if tree and vegetation clearing will occur between February 1 and August 15. The nesting bird survey should be conducted within 1-2 days of the initiation of clearing, depending on the timing during the nesting season. The rest of the calendar dates are zero percent. https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/avoiding-harm-migratory- birds/general-nesting-periods/nesting-periods.html#_zoneA_calendar When work must be conducted within the breeding window, the following document provides information on steps that can be taken to reduce the risk of disturbing a bird nest. https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/avoiding-harm-migratory- birds/reduce-risk-migratory-birds.html Ideally, vegetation removal should be done outside of the breeding season, but the property owners should be aware that there are some birds (Anna’s Hummingbird, Red Crossbill, Great Horned Owl) that nest during the “off” season. In addition to the actual detection of a nest during vegetation removal, the crew should also watch for signs of high agitation by bird, indicating a nest or young are in the immediate area. If during tree and vegetation removal, a nest is discovered: o halt all disruptive activities in the nesting area © move away as quickly and quietly as possible o avoid disturbing the surrounding vegetation, and avoid makinga trail to and from the nest o protect the nest with a buffer zone o avoid the immediate area until the young have naturally left the vicinity of the nest If a nest with young has been exposed to the elements or predation by removal of surrounding vegetation, the nest with young should immediately be taken to the nearest Wildlife Rehabilitation Centre. Contact Environmental Monitors immediately with any concerns. Spill Prevention and Response. Equipment is inspected for leaks prior to beginning work. Environmental Monitoring The owner has been informed of the obligation to protect the Streamside Protection and Enhancement Area (SPEA) and has agreed to retain a QEP to provide environmental monitoring during construction. At a minimum, environmental monitoring should include: ¢ A pre-construction meeting on-site with the QEP and the contractor. * Site visits timed to coincide with key construction activities and based on weather conditions to ensure all development activities remain outside of the SPEA and E&SC protective structures are in good working order, if needed. o After environmental protection measures are installed (e.g. site flagging, and sediment fencing) o During excavation o Heavy rainfall events (e.g. >15 mm) until such time that the QEP is satisfied that the erosion & sediment control and other protective structures are containing heavy rainfall as designed and no sediment laden runoff is leaving the site o Emergencies (e.g. spills). *A post-development visit to inspect works for the conformance statement and post- development report. Photo-point monitoring and site visit checklists should be used for clarity of post-development reporting. The owner must notify the QEP a minimum of 2 weeks prior to the project start up to arrange for the pre-construction meeting. The owner has been informed of the obligation of a QEP to submit a conformance statement and post-development report to the RAR Notification System and have agreed to obtain the services of a QEP to complete this task. A post development report will include a field inspection of the development site and SPEA to ensure that the measures in the RAR report and in Environmental Monitoring plans have been implemented and that no damage has occurred or is expected to occur to the integrity of the SPEA. Reports generated by the Environmental Monitor during construction will be reviewed and the site will be photo-documented. If a QEP is not retained to monitor the project, it may not be possible to provide assurance that the work-site procedures were followed appropriately or the work completed to an acceptable standard, or to sign a conformance statement and submit a post-development report. Statement of Limitations The assessment was carried out using the provincial Riparian Areas Protection Regulation method. The use of this report is restricted to the intended purpose of application for development approval, as described within the report. The measures prescribed in Section 4 assume diligent work practices by the owner and contractors, and implementation of construction best management practices for environmental protection during the site work. If Swell Environmental Consulting Ltd. is not retained to carry out field reviews and environmental monitoring, Swell may not be able to provide assurance that the work-site procedures were followed appropriately or the work completed to an acceptable standard, or to sign a conformance statement and submit a post-development report. The report addresses this site and project only and does not address possible existing or future impacts to fish in the subject streams that cannot be addressed by measures on the subject property. This report should be considered valid for up to five years for the proposed development exactly as described in the report. The report is no longer valid if the proposed development changes. Additional factors that may influence the validity of the report and the recommended measures include, but are not limited to, changes to streamflows due to factors such as alteration of land uses in the watershed, shifting weather patterns (e.g. rainfall intensity, frequency, and/or duration), stormwater infrastructure, and those listed in Section 1, page 6 under “Limitations”.
